manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lemon Juice Reduces Apple BrowningI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Lemon Juice Reduces Enzymatic Browning of Apple SlicesSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To demonstrate that vitamin C in lemon juice reduces enzymatic browning in apples through visual comparison and time-lapse observation.II. MaterialsFresh apple (1), knife, two identical white plates, fresh lemon or bottled lemon juice, spoon or dropper, kitchen counter, camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash the apple. Slice it into evenly sized slices to ensure fair comparison.2. Placement: Place equal numbers of apple slices on two identical white plates. Arrange them in a single layer.3. Treatment: On the left plate, evenly apply lemon juice to the surface of each apple slice using a spoon or dropper. Do not add anything to the right plate.4. Exposure: Leave both plates uncovered on the same kitchen counter under identical environmental conditions.5. Recording: Fix the camera position and focus so both plates are fully visible. Start time-lapse recording.6. Observation Period: Allow the apples to sit while recording, using accelerated time-lapse to capture changes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: All apple slices appear pale and freshly cut.Over Time: The untreated slices on the right plate gradually turn brown. The lemon-treated slices on the left plate show significantly less browning and remain lighter in color.V. Experimental Principle SummaryApple browning is caused by enzymatic oxidation when cut surfaces contact oxygen. Lemon juice contains vitamin C (ascorbic acid), an antioxidant that slows oxidation by reacting with oxygen and inhibiting the browning enzymes. Therefore, apple slices treated with lemon juice brown more slowly than untreated slices.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Eye Convergence During Near FixationSubject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision ScienceObjective: To observe and understand the eye convergence response as a finger moves from far to near while fixation is maintained.II. Experimental EquipmentParticipant (1 person), well-lit room, camera capable of close-up recording, tripod, single finger of participant’s hand.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the participant upright. Position the camera for a close-up of the face, centered on the eyes. Fix the camera focus and do not refocus during recording.2. Initial Position: The participant extends one arm fully, holding one finger at arm’s length directly in front of the face.3. Fixation: The participant keeps their gaze fixed on the fingertip throughout the experiment.4. Core Operation: Slowly move the finger in a straight line toward the bridge of the nose.5. Recording: Capture the process continuously, optionally accelerated as time-lapse, until the finger reaches near the nose.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Eyes are nearly parallel when fixating on the distant fingertip.During Movement: As the finger approaches, both eyes gradually rotate inward.Final State: At near distance, the eyes show clear convergence toward the fingertip.V. Experimental Principle SummaryEye convergence is a binocular vision response. As fixation distance decreases, the medial rectus muscles of both eyes contract, rotating the eyes inward so the image falls on corresponding retinal points. This maintains single, clear binocular vision at near distances.VI. PrecautionsEnsure steady head position; move the finger smoothly; maintain fixed camera focus and stable lighting.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: binocular eye convergence during near fixation. Minimum assumptions: normal binocular vision, visible eyes, straight finger trajectory toward nose, fixed camera focus. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Steaming vs Boiling Broccoli to Preserve NutrientsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Steaming vs Boiling Broccoli2. Subject: Healthcare - Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To compare how steaming and boiling affect broccoli color and texture, illustrating nutrient retention differences through visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh broccoli florets (equal size and weight, two portions), two pots, steaming basket, stove, water, timer, tongs, two plates.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Wash broccoli and cut into equal-sized florets. Add water to both pots; place a steaming basket in the left pot so broccoli sits above water; ensure the right pot has enough water to fully submerge broccoli.Heating: Bring both pots to a gentle simmer simultaneously.Core Operation: Add one portion of broccoli to the steaming basket (left pot) and the other portion directly into boiling water (right pot) at the same time. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Patellar (Knee-Jerk) Reflex with Reflex Hammer TapI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Patellar (Knee-Jerk) Reflex2. Subject: Healthcare – Nursing3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe the patellar reflex, understand the basic neural reflex arc involved, and master the standard operation for eliciting deep tendon reflexes in clinical nursing assessment.II. Experimental EquipmentExamination table or chair, reflex hammer (rubber mallet), adequate lighting; no additional instruments required.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits upright on the examination table, relaxed, with the left leg naturally crossed over the right so the lower leg hangs freely. The examiner stands or sits facing the subject’s knee. Ensure the quadriceps muscle is relaxed.2. Positioning: Expose the left knee area. Identify the patellar tendon located just below the kneecap (patella).3. Core Operation: Using the rubber reflex hammer, the examiner rapidly and lightly taps the patellar tendon once, allowing the hammer to swing freely from the wrist.4. Observation: Keep the camera fixed and focused on the subject’s leg area during the tap and immediately afterward to capture the reflex response.5. Completion: After observing the response, stop the test and allow the subject to relax their leg.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject’s lower leg is relaxed and stationary.2. Upon Tapping: Immediately after the patellar tendon is tapped, the lower leg briefly and involuntarily extends forward (knee jerk).3. After Response: The leg returns to its resting position.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe patellar reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex. Tapping the patellar tendon stretches the quadriceps femoris muscle, activating muscle spindle receptors. Sensory impulses travel via afferent neurons to the spinal cord (L2–L4), where they synapse directly with motor neurons. The motor neurons then stimulate the quadriceps to contract, causing knee extension. This reflex does not require conscious brain involvement and is used clinically to assess the integrity of the peripheral nerves and spinal cord segments.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Clinical demonstration of the patellar (knee-jerk) reflex as a basic nursing assessment skill. Minimum assumptions: a relaxed seated subject, a correctly positioned reflex hammer, and a visible lower limb capable of reflex movement. Phased storyline: (1) static setup with subject seated and leg crossed, camera fixed on knee; (2) examiner delivers a quick tap to the patellar tendon; (3) immediate involuntary knee extension occurs; (4) leg returns to rest. Verification requires a clear side or front view of the knee area, stable framing, and visible cause-effect timing between tap and leg movement.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Photoelectric Effect on a Zinc Plate ElectroscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Photoelectric Effect on a Zinc Plate Electroscope Using UV vs Visible Light2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences (Physics Foundations)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the photoelectric effect by observing the discharge of a negatively charged gold-leaf electroscope with a zinc plate under ultraviolet illumination, and to compare it with visible-light illumination.II. Experimental EquipmentGold-leaf electroscope with zinc plate, charging rod (ebonite or PVC) and fur/cloth, ultraviolet (UV) lamp, visible-light lamp (or incandescent/LED lamp), insulated stand, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse), darkened room (recommended), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the electroscope on an insulated stand. Ensure the gold leaves are clearly visible. Fix the camera position and focus; do not adjust during the experiment.2. Charging: Use the charging rod to negatively charge the electroscope so that the gold leaves diverge noticeably.3. UV Illumination: Turn on the UV lamp and aim it directly at the zinc plate. Maintain steady illumination while recording.4. Visible-Light Illumination: Turn off the UV lamp. Turn on the visible-light lamp and aim it at the zinc plate under the same geometry and distance.5. Completion: Stop recording after observing the leaf behavior. Turn off all lamps and safely discharge the electroscope.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After charging, the gold leaves are widely separated, indicating a negative charge.2. Under UV Light: The gold leaves gradually collapse toward each other, indicating discharge of the electroscope.3. Under Visible Light: The gold leaves show little or no change and remain separated.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe photoelectric effect occurs when photons with sufficient frequency strike a metal surface and eject electrons. Ultraviolet light has photon energy above the threshold frequency for zinc, causing electrons to be emitted from the zinc plate and neutralizing the negative charge on the electroscope. Visible light has insufficient photon energy for zinc and therefore does not cause electron emission or discharge.

Minimum assumptions: zinc plate is negatively charged; UV photons exceed threshold frequency; visible photons do not. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Blink Reflex to Sudden Air PuffI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Blink Reflex to Sudden Air Puff Near the EyeSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Neurophysiology)Objective: To demonstrate the involuntary blink reflex elicited by a sudden air puff near the eye and understand the protective neural mechanism of the corneal reflex.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld air bulb (rubber air blower), chair or standing position for participant, camera positioned in front of participant, adequate lighting.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Ask the participant to face the camera with eyes open and relaxed. Explain that a brief air puff will be delivered without touching the eye.Positioning: Hold the air bulb at close range (about 3–5 cm) to the side of one eye, avoiding physical contact.Core Operation: Squeeze the air bulb once to deliver a brief air puff toward the eye from the side.Observation: Watch the participant’s eyelids immediately after the air puff.Completion: Stop after one clear demonstration; ensure participant comfort.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Eyes open, no blinking.During Air Puff: A sudden stimulus of air reaches the cornea.Result: Immediate, involuntary blinking of the stimulated eye (often both eyes blink).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe blink (corneal) reflex is a protective, involuntary response mediated by the trigeminal nerve (sensory input from cornea) and the facial nerve (motor output to eyelid muscles). Avoid repeated stimulation to prevent discomfort.

manual: Experiment Title: Heating and Cooling of a Cornstarch-Water Slurry to Form a GelI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To observe the process by which a cornstarch-water slurry thickens when heated and forms a gel upon cooling, and to understand starch gelatinization.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentCornstarch (approximately 2 tablespoons), water (approximately 1 cup), saucepan, spoon or spatula, heat source (stove or hot plate), shallow glass dish, measuring cup.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Add cornstarch to water in the saucepan and stir thoroughly to form a uniform, lump-free slurry.2. Heating: Place the saucepan on the heat source and heat gently while stirring continuously.3. Thickening: Continue heating until the slurry turns from a cloudy liquid into a translucent, thick paste.4. Pouring: Carefully pour the hot thickened slurry into a shallow glass dish.5. Cooling: Leave the dish undisturbed at room temperature until the mixture cools and sets into a gel.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: The slurry is a thin, opaque liquid.During heating: The mixture thickens and becomes glossy and translucent.After cooling: The material sets into a soft, stable gel that holds its shape in the dish.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCornstarch contains starch granules. When heated in water, these granules absorb water, swell, and rupture, releasing starch molecules. This process, called starch gelatinization, causes the mixture to thicken. Upon cooling, the starch molecules form a network that traps water, resulting in gel formation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Layered Gelatin Skin Model with Surface Dye DiffusionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Surface Dye Diffusion Through Layered Gelatin Skin Model2. Subject: Healthcare – Occupational Therapy3. Experiment Objective: To simulate human skin layers using gelatin of different densities, observe surface-applied dye diffusing through layers, and understand how material density affects diffusion behavior.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent container (1), gelatin solutions of three concentrations (low, medium, high density), refrigerator, measuring cup, stirring rod, dropper, colored aqueous dye, camera or smartphone with tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Layers: Prepare three gelatin solutions with increasing concentrations. Pour the highest-density gelatin into the container first and refrigerate until set. Sequentially pour and set the medium-density layer, then the lowest-density layer on top, forming three distinct stacked layers.2. Setup for Observation: Place the container on a stable surface with uniform lighting. Fix the camera focus and position for time-lapse photography.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, gently place one drop of colored dye onto the center of the top gelatin layer without disturbing the surface.4. Time-Lapse Recording: Start recording or time-lapse capture immediately and continue as the dye diffuses downward through the layers.5. Completion: Stop recording after the dye front has clearly entered the lower layers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Three clear, colorless gelatin layers with visible boundaries.2. Early Stage: Dye spreads laterally and vertically in the top layer.3. Middle Stage: Dye crosses into the middle layer with a slower diffusion rate.4. Late Stage: Dye gradually penetrates the bottom, densest layer, showing further reduced diffusion speed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDiffusion is driven by concentration gradients, with molecules moving from regions of higher concentration to lower concentration. In this model, gelatin density simulates different skin layers; higher density restricts molecular movement, resulting in slower dye diffusion. This demonstrates how material properties influence substance transport, relevant to topical treatment and skin absorption in occupational therapy.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plant Nitrogen Deficiency vs Adequate Nitrogen (Leaf Color and Growth Rate)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Nitrogen on Plant Leaf Color and Growth Rate2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics (Plant Nutrition)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how adequate nitrogen promotes green leaf color and faster growth, while nitrogen deficiency causes pale leaves and reduced growth, using controlled visual comparison and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical young plants of the same species and size; blue pot (with nitrogen-rich fertilizer); red pot (with nitrogen-free fertilizer); standard potting soil; water source; identical light source; fixed-position camera or phone with tripod; labels for pots.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select two identical young plants. Plant one in a blue pot with nitrogen-rich fertilizer mixed into the soil, and the other in a red pot with nitrogen-free soil.2. Environmental Control: Place both pots side by side under the same light source. Water both plants with the same volume and frequency.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod directly facing both plants. Lock focus, exposure, and framing to avoid changes.4. Recording: Record short daily clips or use time-lapse mode over several days. Do not move pots or camera.5. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Blanching Green Beans and Ice Bath Color PreservationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Blanching Green Beans Followed by Ice Bath to Preserve Bright Green Color2. Subject: Healthcare - Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how blanching green beans in boiling water followed by rapid cooling in an ice bath preserves their bright green color, compared with unblanched green beans left at room temperature.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh green beans (two equal batches), pot with boiling water, stove or induction cooker, bowl with ice water (ice bath), slotted spoon or tongs, kitchen counter or plate for reference batch, timer, camera on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash and trim green beans. Divide them into two equal batches. Set the camera on a tripod, fix focus and framing to include pot, ice bath, and counter reference area.2. Blanching: Bring a pot of water to a rolling boil. Place the first batch of green beans into the boiling water and blanch for about 1–2 minutes.3. Ice Bath Cooling: Immediately remove the blanched green beans with a slotted spoon and transfer them into the ice bath to stop cooking.4. Reference Setup: Leave the second batch of raw green beans on the kitchen counter or plate at room temperature.5. Observation Period: Keep both batches in view and continue time-lapse recording for a short period to compare color changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both batches of green beans appear raw with a natural green color.2. During Blanching: The blanched beans turn a brighter, more vivid green while in boiling water.3. After Ice Bath: Blanched beans retain a bright green color after cooling; the reference batch on the counter appears comparatively duller over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBlanching briefly exposes green beans to high heat, which inactivates enzymes that cause color and nutrient degradation. Rapid cooling in an ice bath stops further cooking and stabilizes chlorophyll, preserving the bright green color. Beans left unblanched do not undergo enzyme inactivation and therefore do not achieve the same color preservation.VI. Experimental PrecautionsAvoid over-blanching to prevent texture loss; ensure immediate transfer to ice bath; maintain fixed camera focus for accurate time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodine Solution Reacting with Starch PasteI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Solution Reacting with Starch Paste (Blue-Black Color Change)2. Subject: Healthcare - Medicine (Basic Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the qualitative identification of starch by iodine through visual color change and to compare the reaction outcome with a control (water).II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass bowls, starch paste (prepared starch in water, opaque white), plain water (colorless and transparent), iodine solution (brownish-yellow), droppers (2), flat stable table, camera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear glass bowls side by side on a flat table. Label one bowl as starch paste and the other as water.2. Sample Setup: Pour an equal volume of starch paste into the first bowl and plain water into the second bowl. Ensure both bowls are clearly visible.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera directly facing the bowls, adjust focus so both bowls are sharp, and keep the camera position unchanged.4. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of iodine solution into the starch paste bowl. Then, using another dropper, add the same amount of iodine solution into the water bowl.5. Observation: Observe and record the color changes in both bowls over a short period using time-lapse or accelerated recording.6. Conclusion and Cleanup: Stop recording after the color change stabilizes. Dispose of solutions properly and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Starch paste is opaque white; water is colorless and transparent; iodine solution is brownish-yellow.2. After Adding Iodine: The starch paste rapidly turns blue-black, while the water remains brownish-yellow with no significant color change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine molecules can insert into the helical structure of starch (amylose), forming a starch–iodine complex that absorbs light and appears blue-black. Plain water lacks starch, so no such complex forms and no blue-black color appears. This reaction is a classic qualitative test for the presence of starch.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use clear glass bowls to ensure easy observation of color changes.2. Add equal amounts of iodine to both bowls for fair comparison.3. Keep the camera fixed to avoid focus or framing changes that affect observation.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Time-lapse Imaging of Eukaryotic Cell Mitosis with Nuclear Envelope BreakdownSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Cell Biology)Objective: To observe mitosis in cultured eukaryotic cells using time-lapse fluorescence microscopy, focusing on nuclear envelope breakdown and chromosome dynamics.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Dialysis Tubing Demonstration of Selective PermeabilityI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Dialysis Tubing Demonstration of Selective PermeabilitySubject: Healthcare - Nutrition & DieteticsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate selective permeability of a semi-permeable membrane by observing the diffusion of small dye molecules through dialysis tubing while large starch molecules are retained.II. Experimental EquipmentClear beaker (1), dialysis tubing (pre-soaked, one piece), string or clips for tying tubing ends, blue food dye solution, starch suspension (cloudy), distilled water, dropper or pipette, camera or smartphone with fixed mount for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Soak dialysis tubing in water until flexible. Tie one end securely. Prepare a mixture of blue food dye and starch suspension.Filling: Use a dropper to fill the tubing with the blue dye–starch mixture, leaving space for expansion. Tie the other end tightly to prevent leakage.Setup: Fill the beaker with clear water. Submerge the tied dialysis tubing completely in the beaker, ensuring it does not touch the sides excessively.Recording: Fix the camera focus and position. Leave the setup undisturbed and begin time-lapse recording.Completion: After sufficient time, stop recording and observe the final state of the water and tubing.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The beaker water is clear and colorless; the dialysis tubing contains a blue, cloudy mixture.During the Experiment: Blue color gradually appears in the surrounding water, spreading outward from the tubing, while the liquid inside the tubing remains cloudy.Final State: The surrounding water becomes light blue; the tubing contents remain cloudy, indicating starch retention.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDialysis tubing acts as a semi-permeable membrane. Small dye molecules diffuse through the membrane down their concentration gradient into the surrounding water, while large starch molecules are unable to pass through due to their size. This demonstrates selective permeability, a key concept in nutrient absorption and cellular transport in Nutrition & Dietetics.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure knots are tight to prevent leakage. Do not disturb the setup during observation. Maintain a fixed camera position to accurately capture diffusion over time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Liquid Bacterial Culture Treated with a Bactericidal Agent Showing Clearing Over TimeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Title: Effect of a Bactericidal Agent on a Liquid Bacterial Culture2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Microbiology)3. Objective: To observe the time-dependent clearing of a cloudy bacterial culture after treatment with a bactericidal agent and to verify loss of bacterial viability by transfer to fresh medium.II. Experimental MaterialsGlass flasks (2, sterile), liquid bacterial culture (cloudy, actively growing), bactericidal antibiotic solution, sterile fresh liquid growth medium, pipette or dropper, sterile swirling stopper or cap, timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a glass flask containing a visibly cloudy bacterial culture on the bench.2. Antibiotic Addition: Add a measured dose of bactericidal antibiotic into the flask.3. Mixing: Gently swirl the flask to ensure even distribution of the antibiotic.4. Time-Lapse Observation: Allow the flask to stand and observe over time; record changes in turbidity as time progresses (time-lapse or accelerated observation).5. Transfer Step: After visible clearing, transfer a small volume of the treated culture into a second flask containing fresh sterile medium.6. Post-Transfer Observation: Observe the fresh medium for signs of turbidity or clarity over a short observation period.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Experimental Principle SummaryBactericidal agents kill bacteria rather than merely inhibiting growth. As bacterial cells die and lyse, light scattering decreases, leading to visible clearing of the culture. Transferring treated culture to fresh medium tests viability: absence of renewed turbidity indicates that bacteria were killed rather than temporarily inhibited.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Enzyme Catalysis of Hydrogen Peroxide by Catalase in PotatoI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Catalase in Potato Decomposes Hydrogen Peroxide2. Subject: Healthcare - Medicine (Biochemistry / Enzyme Catalysis)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate enzyme catalysis by observing how catalase in raw potato rapidly decomposes hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, producing visible foam.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass cup (2 identical cups), raw potato (fresh), knife and cutting board, hydrogen peroxide solution (3%), measuring cup or dropper, tray or paper towels, safety gloves (recommended).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place two identical clear glass cups side by side on a stable surface. Label one as potato cup and leave the other empty as control. Chop the raw potato into small, uniform pieces.Setup: Put an equal amount of chopped raw potato into one glass cup. Ensure the other cup remains empty and clean.Core Operation: Measure equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide. Simultaneously pour the hydrogen peroxide into both cups so that the liquid level is similar.Observation: Watch both cups immediately after pouring and continue observing for several seconds.Completion: After observation, dispose of the contents safely and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both cups are clear; potato pieces are solid and pale yellow or white.2. After Pouring: In the potato cup, rapid bubbling and white foam appear and rise quickly. In the empty cup, the liquid remains mostly unchanged with little or no bubbling.3. Comparison: The contrast between the two cups is obvious, with vigorous foam only in the potato cup.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRaw potato contains catalase, an enzyme widely present in living cells. Catalase rapidly catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen gas. The released oxygen forms bubbles, and when trapped by liquid, produces visible foam. The empty cup lacks catalase, so hydrogen peroxide decomposes very slowly, producing little observable change.Core Reaction: 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2 (catalyzed by catalase)

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Methylene Blue Staining of Human Cheek Epithelial CellsI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Methylene Blue Staining of Human Cheek Epithelial CellsSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Histology / Cell Biology)Experiment Objective: To observe the morphology of human cheek epithelial cells using methylene blue staining under a light microscope, and to understand basic cell staining principles and microscopic observation methods.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsClean glass microscope slide and coverslip; cotton swab or sterile toothpick; methylene blue solution (0.1%); dropper; light microscope with camera; distilled water; tissue paper or absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash hands. Place a clean microscope slide on a flat surface.2. Cell Collection: Gently swab the inner cheek with a cotton swab or toothpick.3. Smearing: Lightly smear the collected cheek cells onto the center of the slide to form a thin, even layer.4. Staining: Add 1–2 drops of methylene blue onto the smear and allow it to stain for about 1 minute.5. Rinsing (optional simplified step): Gently tilt the slide and use a small amount of distilled water to remove excess stain.6. Coverslip Placement: Carefully place a coverslip over the stained smear at an angle to avoid air bubbles.7. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the microscope stage, start with low magnification, then increase magnification. Adjust focus until cells are clear.8. Imaging: Fix the camera focus and record time-lapse or continuous observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitially, the slide appears light blue. Under the microscope, flat, irregularly shaped cheek epithelial cells are visible. The cytoplasm is lightly stained blue, while the nucleus appears darker blue and clearly defined. Cell boundaries can be distinguished.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMethylene blue is a basic dye that binds to acidic components of cells, especially nucleic acids in the nucleus. Cheek epithelial cells, when stained, show enhanced contrast between nucleus and cytoplasm, allowing clear observation of cell morphology under a light microscope.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate correct preparation and microscopic observation of methylene-blue-stained human cheek epithelial cells. Minimum assumptions include the presence of a human subject, standard lab tools, methylene blue dye, and a functional light microscope with camera.Phased Storyline: (1) Collection phase – inner cheek swabbing and transfer of cells to slide; (2) Preparation phase – thin smear, blue staining, and coverslip placement; (3) Observation phase – slide under microscope, focus adjustment, and stable time-lapse imaging. Visibility constraints require close-up views of slide preparation and microscope field of view for verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Posture and Balance Recovery After a Light Nudge While StandingI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Posture and Balance Recovery After a Light Nudge While StandingSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics (Human Functional Health)Objective: To observe and compare balance recovery responses between a young adult and an elderly adult after a light external perturbation, and to understand age-related differences in postural control.II. Experimental Participants and EquipmentParticipants: One healthy young man (20–30 years), one healthy elderly man (65+ years), one assistant acting as the nudger.Equipment: Flat non-slip floor, visual markers for standing position, camera capable of time-lapse recording, comfortable daily clothing, optional safety belt or spotter.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Mark two standing positions side by side, shoulder-width apart. Ask both participants to stand upright, feet parallel, arms relaxed, eyes forward.2. Recording Setup: Position the camera behind and slightly to the side, ensuring both bodies are fully visible from head to feet. Enable time-lapse or accelerated playback mode.3. Core Operation: The assistant delivers a light, brief push to the upper back (between shoulder blades) of both participants at the same time, using consistent force.4. Balance Recovery: Participants do not anticipate or resist the push; they recover balance naturally without stepping unless necessary.5. Completion: Stop recording once both participants regain stable standing posture.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both participants stand still with stable posture.During Push: Both bodies shift forward; center of mass moves beyond the base of support.Recovery Phase: The young man typically shows rapid ankle or hip adjustment with minimal sway; the elderly man shows slower correction, larger sway, or an extra step.Final State: Both regain balance, with visible differences in recovery speed and stability.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHuman balance relies on sensory input (vision, vestibular system, proprioception), neuromuscular response, and musculoskeletal strength. Aging is associated with reduced muscle strength, slower nerve conduction, and diminished sensory integration. Therefore, when subjected to the same light perturbation, elderly individuals generally exhibit delayed and less efficient balance recovery compared to young adults.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: age-related differences in postural control and balance recovery after external perturbation. Minimum assumptions: upright standing humans, light push to upper back, no anticipatory bracing, gravity-consistent motion.Phased storyline: (1) Stable side-by-side standing baseline; (2) simultaneous light push causing forward imbalance; (3) divergent recovery responses—young stabilizes quickly with small sway, elderly shows slower, larger correction; (4) both return to stable stance. Visibility requirements: full-body view from rear/side, clear view of feet and trunk, time-lapse acceleration without altering event order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Exhaled Breath Bubbling Through Limewater Demonstrates Carbon Dioxide DiffusionI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Exhaled Breath Bubbling Through Limewater Demonstrates Carbon Dioxide DiffusionSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Physiology / Respiratory Gas Exchange)Objective: To demonstrate that human exhaled breath contains carbon dioxide, which diffuses into limewater and causes a visible chemical change, using a control comparison.II. Materials and EquipmentClear limewater (calcium hydroxide solution), two identical transparent containers (e.g., beakers or test tubes), flexible plastic or glass tube, lab bench, camera with fixed focus (for continuous or time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical transparent containers side by side on a lab bench. Add an equal volume of clear, colorless limewater to each container.2. Control Setup: Leave one container undisturbed as a control throughout the experiment.3. Experimental Setup: Insert one end of the tube into the limewater of the experimental container, keeping the tube end submerged without touching the container walls.4. Core Operation: A person gently exhales through the free end of the tube, producing continuous bubbles in the limewater for several seconds.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and film continuously (or as time-lapse) during the bubbling process, ensuring both containers remain in frame.6. Completion: Stop exhaling, remove the tube from the limewater, and continue recording briefly to capture the final state.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial State: Both containers contain clear, colorless limewater.During Operation: In the experimental container, bubbles rise through the liquid and the limewater gradually becomes cloudy or milky. The control container remains clear with no visible change.Final State: A clear contrast is observed between the turbid experimental container and the unchanged control container.V. Experimental Principle SummaryHuman exhaled breath contains carbon dioxide. When CO2 diffuses into limewater, it reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, producing turbidity. The undisturbed control confirms that the change is caused by carbon dioxide in exhaled breath rather than environmental factors.Core reaction: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3↓ + H2O
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Human exhaled breath contains carbon dioxide that can diffuse into a liquid and be visually detected via a chemical reaction. Visibility constraints: both containers must stay in frame, camera focus fixed, and turbidity change clearly observable over time.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Salad Dressing Emulsion StabilityI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Emulsion Stability in Salad Dressing With and Without MustardSubject: Healthcare - Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To demonstrate how an emulsifier (mustard) affects the stability of an oil-and-vinegar salad dressing by observing whether the mixture stays mixed or separates into layers over time.II. Experimental MaterialsTwo identical clear glass bottles with lids; vegetable oil; vinegar; dried herbs; prepared mustard; measuring spoon; flat counter surface; fixed camera (or phone) on tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, dry clear glass bottles side by side on a counter. Ensure the camera is fixed, focused on both bottles, and will not move during the experiment.2. Ingredient Setup: Add equal amounts of oil, vinegar, and herbs into both bottles. Add one teaspoon of mustard only to the left bottle. Seal both bottles tightly.3. Mixing: Shake both bottles vigorously for the same duration (about 5 seconds) to fully mix the contents.4. Resting and Recording: Place both bottles back on the counter in their original positions. Start time-lapse recording with fixed focus and do not disturb the bottles.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Immediately after shaking, both bottles appear uniformly cloudy, indicating temporary mixing.Over Time: As the bottles rest, the right bottle (without mustard) gradually separates into two clear layers, with oil on top and vinegar at the bottom. The left bottle (with mustard) remains cloudy and mixed for a longer time, showing little or no clear layer separation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOil and vinegar naturally separate because oil is nonpolar and less dense than vinegar. Shaking creates a temporary emulsion. Mustard contains natural emulsifiers that stabilize the emulsion by reducing surface tension between oil and vinegar droplets, slowing separation. Therefore, the dressing with mustard stays mixed longer than the one without mustard.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Emulsion stability in nutrition, specifically how emulsifiers like mustard help oil-and-vinegar mixtures stay mixed. Minimum assumptions: oil and vinegar are immiscible; shaking creates a temporary emulsion; mustard provides emulsifying agents.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with two identical clear bottles, mustard only in the left. (2) Both bottles are shaken, becoming uniformly cloudy. (3) Bottles are set down and remain stationary under a fixed camera. (4) Over accelerated time-lapse, the right bottle visibly separates into oil and vinegar layers, while the left bottle remains cloudy and mixed. Visibility constraints: camera must stay fixed with consistent framing and focus so layer formation and contrast between bottles can be clearly verified.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Demonstration of Parkinsonian Movement During WalkingI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Demonstration of Delayed Initiation and Shuffling Gait in Parkinsonian MovementSubject: Healthcare – PhysiotherapyObjective: To visually demonstrate typical Parkinsonian walking characteristics, including delayed gait initiation, shuffling steps, and turning difficulty, for teaching and observation purposes.II. Experimental Environment and EquipmentQuiet indoor hallway with a flat, unobstructed floor; clear walking path of 6–8 meters; comfortable everyday clothing and flat shoes for the demonstrator; optional floor markers for distance reference.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The older adult stands still at one end of the hallway, feet shoulder-width apart, arms relaxed at the sides, eyes facing forward.2. Pause Phase: The subject remains motionless for several seconds, appearing ready to walk but not yet initiating movement.3. Gait Initiation: After the pause, the subject attempts to start walking, showing a clear delay before the first step is taken.4. Forward Walking: The subject walks forward several meters using short, shuffling steps with reduced foot clearance and minimal arm swing.5. Turning: At the marked point, the subject performs a cautious 180-degree turn using multiple small steps rather than a single pivot.6. Return Walking: The subject walks back toward the starting point with the same shuffling gait pattern.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject stands still, showing hesitation before movement.2. Delayed Initiation: A noticeable delay occurs between the intention to walk and the first step.3. Shuffling Gait: Steps are short, slow, and close to the floor, with reduced stride length.4. Turning Difficulty: The 180-degree turn is slow and segmented into several small steps.5. Consistency: The gait abnormalities persist during both forward and return walking.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesParkinsonian movement disorders are caused by impaired basal ganglia function, leading to bradykinesia, rigidity, and difficulty initiating movement. These deficits manifest as delayed gait initiation, reduced stride length, shuffling steps, and cautious turning. This demonstration visually links neurological impairment to observable gait characteristics commonly addressed in physiotherapy assessment and intervention.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Parkinsonian gait characterized by delayed initiation, shuffling steps, and turning difficulty in an older adult.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: The subject represents an older adult with Parkinsonian motor control deficits; the hallway is quiet and unobstructed; walking behavior follows physiotherapy knowledge of Parkinson’s disease.Phased Storyline: (1) Static pause indicating hesitation; (2) delayed initiation showing impaired motor start; (3) forward walking with sustained shuffling gait; (4) cautious 180-degree turn using multiple small steps; (5) return walk maintaining the same gait pattern. The camera should maintain a clear side or oblique view to verify step length, initiation delay, and turning behavior.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Microscope Focus Sweep of Compact Bone Cross-Section Showing Concentric LamellaeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Microscope Focus Sweep of Compact Bone Cross-Section2. Subject: Healthcare – Occupational Therapy (Histology Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the microstructure of compact bone under a light microscope by sweeping through focal planes, identify an osteon and its concentric lamellae, and practice fixing camera focus for time-lapse documentation.II. Experimental EquipmentLight microscope with fine and coarse focus knobs; prepared compact bone cross-section slide; glass slide holder; microscope-mounted camera or external camera adapter; computer or storage device for time-lapse capture; lens cleaning paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clean the objective lenses and place the compact bone slide securely on the microscope stage. Turn on the light source and adjust brightness to a moderate, even level.2. Initial Focusing: Using the low-power objective, adjust the coarse focus knob until the bone tissue comes into general focus. Center a single osteon in the field of view.3. Camera Setup: Attach the camera to the microscope eyepiece or phototube. Fix the camera focus and exposure settings so they do not change during the experiment.4. Focus Sweep Operation: Switch to a higher-power objective. Slowly rotate the fine focus knob to move through successive focal planes from the top to the bottom of the tissue section, maintaining a steady speed suitable for time-lapse recording.5. Recording: Capture continuous images or video during the focus sweep, ensuring the field of view remains stable.6. Completion: Stop recording after the full sweep. Return the objective to low power, remove the slide, and turn off the microscope.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The compact bone appears as a dense, pinkish or light-stained tissue with circular structures.2. During Focus Sweep: As the focal plane changes, different layers of the osteon become sharp. Concentric lamellae appear as alternating light and dark rings around a central Haversian canal.3. End State: After passing through all focal planes, lamellae gradually blur again as the focus moves beyond the tissue depth.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the principle of light microscopy and tissue sectioning. Compact bone is organized into osteons composed of concentric lamellae. Because the tissue section has depth, different structural layers lie at different focal planes. Adjusting the fine focus changes the focal plane of the objective lens, allowing sequential visualization of lamellae. Fixing the camera focus ensures that observed changes result solely from microscope focusing, not camera adjustment.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Adjust focus slowly to avoid losing the region of interest.2. Do not change camera focus or exposure during recording.3. Handle slides carefully to prevent damage or contamination.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Light microscope focus sweep revealing osteon concentric lamellae in compact bone. Minimum assumptions: a standard light microscope, a prepared compact bone cross-section slide, and fixed camera focus. Expected phenomena storyline: (1) microscope field shows compact bone with circular osteons; (2) fine focus adjustment begins, causing gradual sharpening of different tissue depths; (3) concentric lamellae appear sequentially as clear rings around a central canal; (4) continued focus movement causes earlier layers to blur. Visibility constraints: stable field of view, constant lighting, no camera refocusing; verification relies on clear causal linkage between focus adjustment and lamellar visibility.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Magnifying Glass Concentrating Sunlight onto PaperI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Magnifying Glass Concentrating Sunlight onto PaperSubject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision ScienceObjective: To observe how a convex lens focuses parallel sunlight to form a smallest, brightest spot at its focal region, and to understand light focusing and energy concentration.II. Experimental EquipmentMagnifying glass (convex lens), white paper sheet, flat table, direct sunlight (outdoors), optional ruler; safety note: avoid prolonged burning.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white paper flat on a table outdoors in direct sunlight. Ensure the sun is unobstructed.2. Alignment: Hold the magnifying glass above the paper with one hand. Tilt and adjust until sunlight passes through the lens and forms a visible bright spot on the paper.3. Core Operation: Slowly move the magnifying glass up and down (closer to and farther from the paper) while keeping it aligned with the sun.4. Observation: Watch the light spot change in size and brightness. Identify the position where the spot is smallest and brightest.5. Completion: Move the lens away after observation. Do not hold the brightest spot on the paper for long to prevent burning.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: A diffuse, relatively large bright patch appears on the paper.During movement: As the lens approaches the focal distance, the spot becomes smaller and brighter.At focus: The smallest spot is the brightest.Beyond focus: Moving closer or farther causes the spot to enlarge and dim.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSunlight reaching Earth is approximately parallel. A magnifying glass is a convex lens that refracts parallel rays toward a focal point. When the paper is near the focal plane, light energy is concentrated into the smallest area, producing the brightest spot. Away from the focus, rays spread, increasing spot size and reducing brightness.VI. PrecautionsAvoid eye exposure to focused sunlight. Do not maintain the brightest spot on paper for extended time. Perform under supervision.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Convex lens focusing parallel sunlight to a focal region, producing a smallest, brightest spot due to energy concentration. Minimum assumptions: outdoor direct sunlight, a hand-held convex magnifying glass, flat white paper on a table, gravity-stable hand motion.Phased storyline: (1) Setup—outdoor table with paper under direct sun; (2) Alignment—lens angled to catch sunlight, bright patch appears; (3) Transition—lens moves vertically, spot shrinks and brightens; (4) Peak—smallest, brightest spot at focus; (5) Exit—lens moves away, spot enlarges. Visibility constraints: camera must clearly show spot size and brightness changes and the hand-lens distance change relative to the paper.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Scrolling Axial CT Slices of a Water Phantom Showing Uniform Gray LevelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scrolling Axial CT Slices of a Water Phantom2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that axial CT grayscale slices of a cylindrical water phantom show uniform gray levels when scanned, and to understand the relationship between X-ray attenuation, CT numbers, and image uniformity.II. Experimental EquipmentCT scanner (or CT image dataset), cylindrical water phantom, image workstation with DICOM viewer, display monitor, fixed camera or screen-capture system for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the cylindrical water phantom at the isocenter of the CT scanner; ensure correct alignment and remove air bubbles. Set standard axial CT scan parameters for water imaging.Scanning and Data Acquisition: Perform an axial CT scan covering the full length of the phantom from top to bottom.Image Display: Load the axial CT images into the workstation. Set a standard grayscale window for water (soft-tissue window).Core Operation: Scroll through the axial slices smoothly from the superior end to the inferior end. Keep scrolling speed constant. Fix the camera focus or screen capture to avoid refocusing during scrolling.Completion: Stop scrolling after the last slice; save or record the scrolling sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: A single axial slice shows a circular cross-section of the water phantom with a uniform gray level.During Scrolling: As slices scroll from top to bottom, the circular shape remains consistent and the gray level remains uniform across slices, without sudden brightness changes.Final State: The last slice maintains the same uniform grayscale appearance as previous slices.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesWater has a nearly uniform X-ray attenuation coefficient. In CT imaging, this results in consistent CT numbers (approximately 0 HU) across the scanned volume. When axial slices are reconstructed and displayed sequentially, a homogeneous water phantom should appear with uniform gray levels across all slices. Smooth scrolling reflects correct reconstruction, stable scanner output, and proper image display settings.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct phantom positioning to avoid partial-volume effects; keep window/level settings constant; maintain fixed camera focus during recording to ensure visual consistency.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrate correct axial CT imaging of a cylindrical water phantom with uniform grayscale appearance. Minimum assumptions: water phantom has homogeneous composition; CT slices are reconstructed axially; camera or screen capture remains fixed.Phased storyline: (1) Display of an initial axial slice showing a circular, uniformly gray phantom; (2) smooth, continuous scrolling of slices from top to bottom with stable geometry and gray levels; (3) completion at the final slice without visual or temporal discontinuity. Visibility constraints: the entire frame should consistently show the CT image display, with no camera refocus or scene changes, enabling verification of uniform grayscale and smooth scrolling.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Relaxed Standing Posture and Anatomical Position TransitionSubject: Healthcare – Medicine (Anatomy)Objective: To visually compare relaxed standing posture with the anatomical position by observing torso alignment and forearm rotation, and to understand the standardized reference posture used in human anatomy.II. Experimental Materials and ConditionsAdult demonstrator (healthy adult), neutral clothing that reveals limb alignment, plain background, fixed camera on tripod, adequate lighting, time-lapse or accelerated recording setting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Position the camera at chest height directly in front of the subject; fix focus and exposure. Ensure the subject stands naturally on a marked floor position.2. Initial Posture (Relaxed Standing): The adult adopts a relaxed stance with slight slouching of the torso, shoulders naturally dropped, arms hanging loosely at the sides, and palms facing inward toward the thighs.3. Transition Operation: The subject slowly straightens the torso to an upright position, retracts shoulders slightly, and rotates the forearms laterally so that palms face forward while keeping arms at the sides.4. Anatomical Position: Hold the final posture briefly: body erect, head facing forward, arms at sides, palms forward, feet parallel.5. Camera Variation: Insert a brief side-angle cut during the transition to show torso straightening, then return to front view.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Curved or relaxed spinal alignment with inward-facing palms.2. During Transition: Visible extension of the spine and rotation of the forearms.3. Final State: Upright posture with symmetrical alignment and palms facing forward, representing the anatomical position.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe anatomical position is a standardized reference posture in medicine and anatomy. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Extracting Iron Particles from Fortified Breakfast Cereal Using a MagnetSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate that some fortified breakfast cereals contain elemental iron by extracting magnetic iron particles from a cereal slurry using a strong magnet.II. Experimental EquipmentFortified breakfast cereal (iron-fortified flakes or puffs), clear glass or plastic bowl, water, spoon or pestle for crushing, strong handheld magnet (e.g., neodymium magnet), paper towel (optional), safety gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a small amount of fortified cereal into a clear bowl. Add enough water to fully cover the cereal.2. Collection: Continue moving the magnet slowly for 1–2 minutes, tracing the bottom and sides to allow magnetic particles to gather.5. Completion: Stop moving the magnet and observe the areas where particles accumulate. Optionally remove the magnet and wipe collected particles with a paper towel.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMany fortified cereals contain elemental iron powder as a nutritional supplement. Elemental iron is ferromagnetic. A strong magnet placed near the slurry creates a magnetic field that attracts and concentrates these iron particles, making them visible. This demonstrates the presence of iron used for dietary fortification.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse a strong magnet for clear results; crush cereal thoroughly; use a clear bowl for visibility; do not ingest the slurry after the experiment; handle strong magnets carefully.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual: Milk Curdling When Lemon Juice Is AddedI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Milk Curdling When Lemon Juice Is Added at Room Temperature2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the curdling of milk protein when an acidic substance (lemon juice) is added at room temperature, and to visually demonstrate protein denaturation and coagulation through time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Fresh liquid milk (whole milk recommended, at room temperature)2. Fresh lemon juice (filtered to remove pulp)3. Clear glass bowl (transparent, medium size)4. Spoon or glass stirring rod5. Measuring spoon or dropper (for controlled addition of lemon juice)6. Camera or smartphone with stable stand (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass bowl on a stable, well-lit surface at room temperature. Ensure the camera is positioned directly in front or slightly above the bowl, with focus fixed and framing covering the entire bowl.2. Milk Addition: Pour fresh milk into the clear glass bowl until it reaches about half the bowl’s height. Observe and record the initial state of the milk (uniform white liquid).3. Lemon Juice Addition (Core Operation): While gently stirring the milk with a spoon, slowly add lemon juice drop by drop or in a thin stream using a measuring spoon or dropper.4. Observation and Recording: Continue gentle stirring for a short time, then stop stirring and allow the mixture to stand. Record the entire process using time-lapse photography to capture gradual changes.5. Completion: Once obvious curdling is observed, stop the recording. Dispose of the mixture properly and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The milk appears as a smooth, uniform, opaque white liquid with no visible particles.2. During Lemon Juice Addition: Small white clumps begin to appear in the milk, and the liquid gradually separates into solid curds and a pale yellow, translucent liquid (whey).3. Final State: The curds become more obvious and aggregate, while the whey becomes clearer, indicating clear separation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk contains casein protein, which is stable at near-neutral pH. Lemon juice contains citric acid, which lowers the pH of milk when added. At acidic pH, casein proteins lose their stable structure, denature, and aggregate to form solid curds. This process is known as acid-induced protein coagulation and is the scientific basis for yogurt and cheese making.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh milk at room temperature; cold milk may slow the reaction.2. Add lemon juice slowly to clearly observe the curdling process.3. Stir gently to avoid breaking formed curds into very fine particles.4. Ensure the camera remains fixed to maintain consistent time-lapse recording.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Acid-induced milk protein coagulation at room temperature. Minimum mechanistic assumption: lemon juice (acid) lowers milk pH, causing casein denaturation and aggregation. Phased storyline: (1) Initial uniform white milk in a clear glass bowl under fixed camera view; (2) Slow addition of lemon juice with gentle stirring as the causal trigger; (3) Emergence of small white curds and separation into curds and whey; (4) Final stabilized state with obvious solid-liquid separation. Visibility constraints: transparent bowl, clear lighting, fixed perspective to verify gradual change and causal order within a short, accelerated time-lapse.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Catalase Enzyme Activity Before and After Heat DenaturationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Catalase Enzyme Activity Before and After Heat Denaturation (Potato–Hydrogen Peroxide Foam Test)2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Biochemistry/Enzymology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that catalase in living tissues catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide, and that heating (boiling) denatures the enzyme, reducing or eliminating its activity, through visual observation of foam formation.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (same size), fresh raw potato, briefly boiled potato (boiled 2–3 minutes and cooled), knife and cutting board, hydrogen peroxide solution (3%), measuring cylinder or dropper, forceps, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse), lab gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut the raw potato and the boiled potato into similar-sized cubes. Label the left beaker as Raw Potato and the right beaker as Boiled Potato.2. Placement: Put equal amounts of raw potato into the left beaker and boiled potato into the right beaker. Place the two beakers side by side on a stable surface.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both beakers are clearly visible in the same frame for time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Measure equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide. Simultaneously pour the hydrogen peroxide into both beakers, fully covering the potato pieces.5. Observation: Record and observe changes in both beakers over time without moving the camera or beakers.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain potato pieces submerged in clear, colorless hydrogen peroxide with no foam.2. Raw Potato Beaker: Shortly after addition, abundant bubbles and white foam rapidly form and rise, indicating vigorous oxygen release.3. Boiled Potato Beaker: Very few or no bubbles appear; foam formation is minimal or absent.4. Over Time: The foam in the raw potato beaker increases noticeably, while the boiled potato beaker shows little change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCatalase is an enzyme widely present in living cells that catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2↑). The released oxygen forms visible bubbles and foam. Heating (boiling) denatures catalase by altering its protein structure, causing loss of enzymatic activity. Therefore, raw potato shows strong foam formation, while boiled potato shows weak or no reaction.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse equal potato sizes and hydrogen peroxide volumes; ensure boiled potato is cooled before use; avoid splashing hydrogen peroxide; keep camera fixed throughout observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Dialysis Tubing Membrane with CO2 Diffusion into Bromothymol Blue SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Dialysis Tubing Membrane with CO2 Diffusion into Bromothymol Blue Solution2. Subject: Healthcare – Nursing (Physiology / Basic Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate gas diffusion across a semi-permeable membrane and observe the effect of carbon dioxide on solution pH using bromothymol blue as an indicator.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass beaker (250–400 mL), bromothymol blue solution (initially blue, neutral to slightly basic), dialysis tubing (pre-soaked and tied at both ends), exhaled air source (human breath via straw or gentle blowing), string or clips for sealing tubing, distilled water (optional), camera or smartphone with tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Fill the clear beaker with bromothymol blue solution until it appears uniformly blue. Place the beaker on a stable surface with good lighting.2. Dialysis Tubing Setup: Soak dialysis tubing in water to soften it. Tie one end securely. Gently blow exhaled air into the tubing, then immediately tie the other end to seal the air inside.3. Core Operation: Submerge the sealed dialysis tubing completely into the bromothymol blue solution, ensuring the membrane is fully in contact with the surrounding liquid and not floating above the surface.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position. Begin time-lapse or continuous recording without moving the setup.5. Observation Period: Allow the setup to stand undisturbed while recording, accelerating time if necessary for demonstration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bromothymol blue solution in the beaker is blue and clear; dialysis tubing appears transparent with trapped air inside.2. During Diffusion: Over time, the solution near the dialysis tubing gradually changes color from blue to green and then toward yellow.3. Final State: A visible color gradient may form, with the strongest color change closest to the tubing.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesDialysis tubing acts as a semi-permeable membrane that allows small gas molecules such as CO2 to diffuse through. Exhaled air inside the tubing contains a high concentration of CO2, which diffuses into the surrounding solution. CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, lowering the pH. Bromothymol blue is a pH indicator that changes from blue (basic) to green and yellow (acidic), visually demonstrating CO2 diffusion and acid-base balance.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure tubing is tightly sealed to prevent air leakage. Do not shake or move the beaker during observation. Maintain fixed camera focus and stable lighting for clear time-lapse recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Acetic Acid–Sodium Acetate Buffer Resists pH ChangeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Resistance of pH Change by Acetic Acid–Sodium Acetate Buffer2. Subject: Healthcare - Medicine (Acid–Base Balance)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the buffering effect of an acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer by comparing its pH change with plain water when vinegar is added, and to understand the principle of buffer systems in maintaining pH stability.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo clear glass beakers (100–150 mL), acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer solution (about 50 mL), distilled water (about 50 mL), universal pH indicator or bromothymol blue, vinegar (5% acetic acid), two droppers, stirring rods or gentle swirling by hand, camera or phone fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Label one Buffer and the other Water.2. Solution Addition: Pour equal volumes (about 50 mL) of acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer into the Buffer beaker and distilled water into the Water beaker.3. Indicator Addition: Add the same number of drops of pH indicator to each beaker and gently swirl until the color is uniform. Record the initial colors.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and framing so both beakers remain fully visible throughout the experiment.5. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add vinegar dropwise to each beaker alternately or simultaneously, gently swirling after each drop.6. Observation: Continue adding vinegar for several drops while observing and recording the color changes in both beakers.7. Completion: Stop adding vinegar once a clear contrast in color change is observed. End recording and clean up materials.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both solutions show similar initial indicator color, indicating comparable starting pH.2. During Vinegar Addition: The water beaker shows a rapid and obvious color change after only a few drops of vinegar, indicating a sharp pH decrease.3. Buffer Response: The buffer beaker shows little or much slower color change over the same number of vinegar drops, indicating resistance to pH change.4. Final State: A clear contrast is visible: water is significantly more acidic than the buffer.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAn acetic acid–sodium acetate buffer consists of a weak acid (CH3COOH) and its conjugate base (CH3COO−). When acid (vinegar) is added, acetate ions consume added H+ to form acetic acid, minimizing pH change. In plain water, no such equilibrium exists, so added acid directly increases H+ concentration, causing rapid pH decrease. This demonstrates how buffer systems help maintain stable pH, a key concept in medical and physiological acid–base balance.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plant Cell Plasmolysis and Recovery under Salt-to-Water Osmotic Stress (Onion Epidermis)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Plasmolysis and Recovery in Onion Epidermal Cells2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Cell Biology / Physiology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe plasmolysis and subsequent recovery of plant cells under a light microscope by applying concentrated salt solution and then replacing it with pure water, and to understand osmotic principles in plant cells.II. Experimental EquipmentLight microscope; glass slide and cover slip; fresh onion bulb; forceps; scalpel or blade; dropper or pipette; concentrated salt solution (e.g., 10% NaCl); pure water (distilled water); absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Peel a thin, transparent epidermal layer from the inner side of an onion scale using forceps. Place it flat on a clean glass slide.2. Initial Observation: Add a drop of pure water, gently place a cover slip, and observe the onion epidermis cells under low to medium magnification. Identify clear cell walls and cytoplasm.3. Plasmolysis Induction: While keeping the same field of view, add a drop of concentrated salt solution to one side of the cover slip and use absorbent paper on the opposite side to draw the solution under the cover slip. Continuously observe the same cells.4. Recovery (Deplasmolysis): After plasmolysis is evident, add pure water in the same manner to replace the salt solution, again maintaining the same field of view.5. Ending: Observe until recovery is clear, then remove the slide and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In pure water, onion epidermis cells appear turgid; the cell membrane is closely pressed against the cell wall.2. After Salt Addition: The cytoplasm and cell membrane shrink inward and separate from the cell wall, forming clear gaps; this is plasmolysis.3. After Water Replacement: The shrunken protoplast gradually expands and reattaches to the cell wall, restoring the original shape; this is recovery (deplasmolysis).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on osmosis across a semi-permeable cell membrane. In a hypertonic salt solution, water exits the plant cell, causing plasmolysis. When the external solution is replaced with hypotonic pure water, water re-enters the cell, leading to recovery. The rigid cell wall maintains overall cell shape, making plasmolysis and recovery observable under a microscope.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Osmosis-driven plasmolysis and recovery in plant cells, assuming a semi-permeable membrane, rigid cell wall, and visible protoplast changes under light microscopy. Expected phased storyline: (1) initial turgid onion epidermis cells in water with membrane appressed to the wall; (2) addition of concentrated salt causes water efflux and visible protoplast shrinkage away from the wall; (3) replacement with pure water causes water influx and gradual re-expansion of the protoplast. Verification requires a stable microscope perspective on the same cells, clear visibility of cell walls and membrane position, and a chronological, causally linked transition between phases.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Acid-Induced Denaturation of Milk Proteins Forming CurdsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Acid-Induced Denaturation of Milk Proteins Forming Curds2. Subject: Healthcare - Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how acids denature milk proteins (casein), leading to curd formation and whey separation through direct visual observation.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass bowl; warm milk (40-50°C, about 300 mL); white vinegar (5% acetic acid); spoon; measuring cup; optional thermometer; camera on tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the clear glass bowl on a stable surface. Pour warm milk into the bowl. Fix the camera on a tripod, set focus on the milk surface, and start time-lapse recording.Core Operation: While gently stirring the milk with a spoon, slowly pour vinegar into the milk in a thin stream (about 10-20 mL total).Observation: Continue gentle stirring for 10-20 seconds, then stop stirring and observe changes.Conclusion and Cleanup: Stop recording after clear curd formation and separation appear. Dispose of contents appropriately and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Milk appears white, opaque, and uniform.During Addition: As vinegar is added, small white clumps begin to appear.After Mixing: White curds aggregate and separate from a more translucent yellowish liquid (whey).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMilk contains casein proteins dispersed as micelles. Adding acid lowers the pH toward casein isoelectric point (~4.6), neutralizing charges and destabilizing micelles. Proteins denature and aggregate into curds, separating from liquid whey.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse warm, not hot, milk to avoid boiling effects. Add vinegar slowly to control curd formation. Maintain gentle stirring to avoid breaking curds excessively. Ensure camera remains fixed for clear time-lapse.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Comparison of Swollen Ankle Versus Normal Ankle Under PressureI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Swollen Ankle Versus Normal Ankle Under Pressure (Pitting Edema Demonstration)Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsExperiment Objective: To visually compare tissue response to pressure between a swollen ankle and a normal ankle, and to understand the basic principle of pitting edema related to fluid retention.II. Experimental EquipmentChair for seated subject, adult participant with one swollen ankle and one normal ankle, clinician or demonstrator, clean hands or gloves, camera with tripod, stable lighting, optional skin-safe marker for pressure point.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the adult comfortably with both ankles exposed and placed side by side at the same height. Ensure lighting is even. Fix the camera on a tripod, frame both ankles clearly, and lock focus for time-lapse photography.2. Positioning: Identify the same anatomical location on both ankles (medial lower shin above the ankle). Mark lightly if needed.3. Core Operation: The clinician presses a thumb vertically into the marked spot on the swollen ankle for about 5 seconds, then releases. Repeat the same pressure, duration, and thumb position on the normal ankle.4. Recording: Maintain fixed camera focus and angle throughout. Allow a short observation period after each release to capture tissue recovery.5. Completion: End recording after both ankles have been pressed and released once.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The swollen ankle appears visibly larger and tighter than the normal ankle.During Pressure: Thumb pressure creates an indentation on both ankles.After Release: On the swollen ankle, the indentation persists for several seconds (pitting). On the normal ankle, the skin rebounds quickly and returns to its original shape.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSwollen ankles often involve excess interstitial fluid accumulation. When external pressure is applied, fluid is displaced, creating a temporary pit. Due to impaired fluid return, the pit persists (pitting edema). In normal tissue, elastic recoil and effective circulation allow rapid recovery after pressure release.

Minimum assumptions: adult seated, one ankle swollen, clinician applies equal thumb pressure, fixed camera focus. manual: Experiment Title: Single-Leg Balance with Arm Movement Demonstrating Whole-Body StabilizationI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Healthcare - PhysiotherapyObjective: To demonstrate how whole-body stabilization and postural control are maintained during a single-leg stance while performing controlled arm movements, and to observe balance strategies under increasing postural challenge.II. Experimental EquipmentFlat, non-slip floor; neutral indoor environment; camera or smartphone mounted on tripod; timer or time-lapse function; comfortable clothing; barefoot participant.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the camera on a tripod facing the participant. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Ensure the floor is flat and free of obstacles. The participant removes footwear and stands upright facing the camera.2. Starting Position: The participant stands barefoot on both feet, arms relaxed at sides, gaze forward.3. Single-Leg Stance: The participant lifts one foot off the ground and maintains balance on the supporting leg.4. Arm Movements: While maintaining single-leg balance, the participant slowly moves both arms forward to shoulder height, then slowly moves them sideways to shoulder height, and finally raises them overhead. Movements should be continuous and controlled.5. Recording: The camera remains fixed throughout. The sequence may be recorded in real time or using time-lapse to condense duration.6. Completion: The participant lowers arms, places the raised foot back on the floor, and relaxes posture.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Stable upright posture on one leg with minimal sway.2. During Arm Movement: As arms move forward, sideways, and overhead, subtle adjustments occur at the ankle, knee, hip, and trunk; center of mass shifts and is corrected.3. Overall Outcome: Balance is maintained through coordinated whole-body stabilization; no stepping or foot touchdown occurs if balance is successful.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSingle-leg stance reduces the base of support, increasing balance demand. Arm movements shift the body’s center of mass and create rotational moments. The nervous system responds through anticipatory and reactive postural adjustments, engaging core muscles, hip stabilizers, and ankle strategies to maintain equilibrium. This demonstrates principles of postural control, proprioception, and whole-body coordination central to physiotherapy balance training.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the environment is safe; stop immediately if loss of balance occurs; keep camera fixed to avoid visual interference; movements should be slow and controlled.
