manual: Instructions for the Experiment Benedict’s Test on Glucose Solution Heated in a Water BathI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Benedict’s Test on Glucose Solution Heated in a Water Bath2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Biochemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the reducing sugar reaction of glucose using Benedict’s reagent, compare experimental and control groups, and visually observe reaction results under heating in a water bath.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tubes (2, identical size), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, glucose solution, distilled water, Benedict’s reagent (blue), beaker or water bath container, heat source (hot plate), thermometer (optional), test tube holder, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on a rack. Label one as Glucose and the other as Water (control). Put on safety goggles.2. Sample Addition: Add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of glucose solution to the Glucose tube. Add the same volume of distilled water to the Water tube.3. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of Benedict’s reagent to each test tube. Gently mix by tapping.4. Heating: Place both test tubes simultaneously into a hot water bath (about 80–100 °C). Ensure the liquid levels are below the tube mouths and the tubes are upright.5. Observation: Heat for 2–5 minutes. Keep the camera focus fixed and record using time-lapse photography to capture gradual color changes.6. Completion: Remove the test tubes using a holder, place them back on the rack, and allow them to cool before disposal and cleaning.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both test tubes contain a blue solution due to the presence of copper(II) ions in Benedict’s reagent.2. During Heating: The glucose solution gradually changes color from blue to green, yellow, orange, or brick-red, forming a precipitate. The water control remains blue with no precipitate.3. Final State: A distinct color difference is observed between the glucose tube and the control tube.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBenedict’s test is used to detect reducing sugars. Glucose, a reducing sugar, reduces Cu²⁺ ions in Benedict’s reagent to Cu₂O under heating, forming a colored precipitate. The color intensity reflects the presence of reducing sugar. Distilled water lacks reducing sugars and therefore shows no reaction.Core Reaction: Reducing sugar + Cu²⁺ → Cu₂O↓ (brick-red precipitate) + oxidized sugar.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal volumes of solutions and reagent for valid comparison.2. Heating must be done in a water bath to avoid direct flame hazards.3. Do not seal test tubes during heating.4. Dispose of chemical waste according to laboratory safety guidelines.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of Benedict’s test identifying glucose as a reducing sugar using a controlled water-bath heating setup. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: Benedict’s reagent contains Cu²⁺ ions; heating enables redox reaction; glucose reduces Cu²⁺ to Cu₂O while water does not react.Phased storyline for verification:Phase 1 (Setup): Two clearly visible test tubes with equal liquid volumes; one identified as glucose solution, the other as water; both initially blue after Benedict’s reagent addition.Phase 2 (Action): Both test tubes are placed together into a hot water bath; camera remains fixed, enabling time-lapse capture; heating is the only applied stimulus.Phase 3 (Causal Transition): As heating continues, only the glucose tube shows progressive color change and precipitate formation, while the control remains unchanged.Phase 4 (Outcome): Final contrast is clearly visible—colored precipitate in glucose tube versus blue solution in control—allowing unambiguous confirmation of the reducing sugar reaction.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Smooth Pursuit Eye Movement During Slow Target TrackingSubject Area: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision ScienceObjective: To observe and understand smooth pursuit eye movements by having a seated subject visually track a slowly moving object across the field of view.II. Experimental Equipment1. Colored ball (approximately 3–5 cm diameter, bright color such as red or green)2. Chair for the subject3. Neutral background4. Camera positioned at eye level, facing the subject5. Adequate, even lightingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the subject comfortably on a chair facing the camera. Ensure the head is upright and the eyes are at the same height as the camera lens.2. Target Setup: Hold the colored ball at the subject’s eye level, approximately 50–70 cm in front of the face.3. Instruction to Subject: Ask the subject to keep their head still and follow the ball only with their eyes.4. Core Operation: Move the ball slowly and smoothly from the subject’s left side to the right side at a constant speed, remaining at eye level.5. Recording: The camera focuses on the subject’s face, especially the eyes, during the entire tracking process.6. Completion: Stop the ball movement after it reaches the right side and allow the subject to relax.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject’s eyes look straight ahead with a neutral facial expression.2. During Tracking: As the ball moves left to right, the subject’s eyes move smoothly in the same direction, maintaining fixation on the ball with minimal head movement.3. End State: When the ball stops, eye movement ceases and gaze stabilizes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates smooth pursuit eye movements, a fundamental function of the visual system. Smooth pursuit allows the eyes to closely follow a slowly moving object so that its image remains on the fovea, enabling clear vision. The movement is controlled by cortical and subcortical visual pathways that process motion information and generate continuous, coordinated eye movement. Slow, predictable target motion is essential for eliciting smooth pursuit rather than rapid saccadic eye movements.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: smooth pursuit eye movement in optometry, defined as continuous ocular tracking of a slow, predictable moving target, assuming normal vision and basic neuromuscular control. Expected phenomena follow a clear storyline: (1) a stationary seated subject faces the camera; (2) a colored ball appears at eye level on the left; (3) the ball moves slowly and smoothly to the right; (4) the subject’s eyes and subtle facial cues track the ball continuously without abrupt jumps; (5) motion stops and gaze stabilizes. Verification requires a frontal camera perspective focused on the eyes, stable lighting, and unobstructed visibility of both the ball and ocular motion.

manual: Experiment Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ripple Tank Demonstration of Water Waves Crossing a Water–Oil Boundary2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences (Wave Physics and Imaging Analogy)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and record the behavior of surface water waves as they cross a straight boundary between water and oil, and to understand wave refraction and wavelength change due to differences in wave speed in different media. Time-lapse photography is used to clearly visualize wave propagation.II. Experimental Equipment1. Ripple tank with transparent base2. Shallow water (clear, uniform depth)3. Light-colored oil (e.g., mineral oil) with higher viscosity than water4. Straight divider or guide (for initial separation, removable)5. Point wave source (vibrating pin or dipper driven by motor)6. Overhead light source or stroboscopic lamp7. Camera mounted vertically above the tank, with fixed focus and fixed position8. Dark background screen or projection screen beneath the tankIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the ripple tank on a stable horizontal surface. Pour water into one side of the tank to a shallow, uniform depth. Gently pour oil into the other side, using a straight divider to maintain a clear, straight boundary between water and oil. Remove the divider carefully to preserve the boundary.2. Optical Setup: Turn on the overhead light so that surface waves can be clearly projected onto the screen below. Adjust brightness to obtain sharp wave patterns.3. Camera Setup: Mount the camera directly above the tank. Fix the focus, exposure, and frame so that the entire boundary region is visible. Do not change focus during recording.4. Wave Generation: Place the point source in the water region, several centimeters away from the boundary. Switch on the vibrator to generate continuous circular water waves propagating toward the oil boundary.5. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording. Allow waves to reach and cross the boundary between water and oil.6. Completion: Stop the wave source and recording after clear boundary-crossing behavior is captured. Turn off the light source and clean the tank.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Circular wavefronts propagate uniformly in the water region toward the straight boundary.2. At the Boundary: When wavefronts reach the water–oil interface, their direction changes.3. After Crossing: In the oil region, the wavelength and wave speed are different from those in water, causing refraction. Wavefront spacing changes and the circular pattern becomes distorted compared with the original water waves.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Surface water waves travel at different speeds in different media due to differences in density and viscosity.2. When waves cross a boundary at an angle, a change in speed causes refraction, analogous to light refraction in imaging sciences.3. The frequency of the wave source remains constant, so a change in wave speed leads to a change in wavelength.4. This experiment models wave behavior relevant to medical imaging, such as ultrasound refraction at tissue boundaries.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Maintain a straight and stable boundary between water and oil.2. Avoid vibrations of the table that may disturb wave patterns.3. Ensure the camera focus remains fixed throughout recording.4. Clean oil and water thoroughly after the experiment to avoid contamination.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate refraction of surface water waves at a water–oil boundary using a ripple tank, assuming constant wave source frequency and different wave speeds in different media.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Surface waves propagate outward from a point source; wave speed depends on medium properties; crossing a boundary changes wave speed and wavelength but not frequency.Phased Storyline:Phase 1 – Setup Visibility: Overhead view shows ripple tank with a straight water–oil boundary and fixed camera perspective.Phase 2 – Wave Generation: Circular waves originate from a point source in water and travel toward the boundary.Phase 3 – Boundary Interaction: Wavefronts reach the boundary and begin to change direction.Phase 4 – Refraction Outcome: In the oil region, waves show altered spacing and direction, verifying refraction.Visibility Constraints: Boundary line and wavefront spacing must be clearly visible; camera must remain fixed to allow temporal comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Refraction of a Laser Beam at the Air–Water BoundaryI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Refraction of a Laser Beam at the Air–Water Boundary2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the refraction of light when a laser beam passes from air into water, understand how changes in refractive index alter light direction, and observe the dynamic change in the beam path as the water level rises.II. Experimental EquipmentRed laser pointer (continuous beam), clear rectangular glass or acrylic water tank, water source (beaker or bottle), stable stand or clamps for laser alignment, white background or screen (optional), camera or smartphone on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the empty clear rectangular tank on a stable surface. Position the camera in front of the tank and lock focus and exposure.2. Laser Alignment: Secure the red laser so that it enters one side wall of the tank at an oblique angle relative to the normal. Turn on the laser and ensure the beam path is clearly visible.3. Initial Observation: With the tank empty (air only), observe and record the straight-line path of the laser through air.4. Core Operation: Slowly pour water into the tank. Allow the water level to rise gradually until it crosses the laser beam.5. Recording: Maintain a fixed camera position and focus while continuously recording or capturing time-lapse images.6. Completion: Stop pouring when the beam is fully passing through water. Turn off the laser and end recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In air, the red laser travels in a straight line without bending.2. At the Air–Water Boundary: When the rising water surface intersects the beam, the laser bends at the interface.3. In Water: Below the water surface, the beam follows a new straight path at a different angle, bending toward the normal compared with its path in air.4. Dynamic Change: As the water level continues to rise, the refraction point moves upward with the surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates refraction, which occurs when light passes between media with different refractive indices. Water has a higher refractive index than air, so the laser beam slows down and bends toward the normal at the air–water boundary. The relationship between incident angle and refracted angle is described by Snell’s law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂. The changing water level shifts the interface, making the refraction point move while the physical law remains constant.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct eye exposure to the laser beam.2. Ensure the tank walls are clean to reduce scattering.3. Keep the camera focus fixed to maintain consistent observation.4. Pour water slowly to keep the refraction process clearly visible.

Experimental Equipment1. Two transparent chambers connected side-by-side2. Semipermeable membrane fixed between the chambers3. Clear water with a faint, uniform dye (same initial concentration in both chambers)4. Concentrated salt (NaCl) solution5. Dropper or pipette6. Stable support platform7. Camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the two connected transparent chambers on a stable surface. Ensure the semipermeable membrane is securely positioned between them with no leaks.2. Filling Chambers: Add equal volumes of clear, faintly dyed water to both chambers. Confirm that the initial liquid levels and dye intensity are identical.3. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the chambers. Fix the focus, framing both chambers clearly, and begin time-lapse recording.4. Core Operation: Using a dropper, slowly add a measured amount of concentrated salt solution only to the left chamber. Do not disturb the right chamber.5. Observation Period: Allow the system to stand undisturbed while recording continues, enabling accelerated visualization of changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both chambers show equal liquid levels and uniform faint dye coloration.2. After Salt Addition: The left chamber becomes more concentrated with ions, while the right chamber remains unchanged.3. Over Time: Water gradually moves from the right chamber to the left chamber across the semipermeable membrane. The liquid level on the left side increases slightly, and the dye appears more diluted on the right and relatively more concentrated on the left.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates osmosis driven by an ion concentration gradient. The semipermeable membrane allows water molecules to pass but restricts ions. When a concentrated salt solution is added to the left chamber, an osmotic gradient forms. Water moves from the lower ion concentration side (right chamber) to the higher ion concentration side (left chamber) to reduce the gradient. This principle underlies fluid movement in many biological systems, including aqueous humor dynamics and corneal hydration in vision science.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the membrane is intact and properly sealed.2. Use equal initial volumes and dye concentrations for accurate comparison.3. Avoid shaking or moving the chambers during observation.4. Keep the camera focus fixed to maintain valid time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Emulsification of Oil by Soap (Simulation of Bile Salts)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Emulsification of Oil by Soap in WaterSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsExperiment Objective: To demonstrate how bile salts or soap act as emulsifiers, helping oil disperse in water, and to visually compare emulsified and non-emulsified systems.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers, water, edible oil, liquid soap (or detergent), stirring rod or gentle hand swirling, stable flat surface, camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Pour equal volumes of water into each beaker.2. Formation of Oil Layer: Gently add an equal amount of oil to each beaker, allowing the oil to form a clear layer above the water. Do not stir.3. Control Setup: Leave the left beaker unchanged as the control.4. Experimental Operation: Add a small amount of liquid soap to the right beaker only.5. Swirling: Gently and simultaneously swirl both beakers using the same motion and intensity.6. Recording: Keep the camera focus fixed and record the process using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: In both beakers, oil floats clearly above the water, forming two distinct layers.After Swirling Without Soap (Left Beaker): Oil and water quickly separate again, maintaining clear layers.After Swirling With Soap (Right Beaker): The mixture becomes cloudy and uniform, with oil dispersed as fine droplets throughout the water, forming a stable emulsion.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesOil and water do not mix due to differences in polarity. Soap molecules, similar to bile salts in the human digestive system, have hydrophilic (water-attracting) and hydrophobic (oil-attracting) ends. When soap is added and the mixture is swirled, soap molecules surround oil droplets and prevent them from coalescing, forming an emulsion. This demonstrates how bile salts aid fat digestion by increasing the surface area of fats for enzyme action.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse identical beakers and equal volumes to ensure fair comparison. Swirl gently to avoid splashing. Do not adjust camera focus during recording to maintain consistent observation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Color Retention in Green Beans After Blanching vs RawI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Blanching on Color Retention of Green BeansSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To demonstrate that blanching green vegetables before cooking improves green color retention by inactivating enzymes.II. Equipment and MaterialsFresh green beans (uniform size), pot with boiling water, bowl of ice water, stove or hot plate, tongs, timer, two heat-safe containers, kitchen counter, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash and trim green beans. Divide into two equal piles placed left and right on the counter. Fix camera focus and framing; do not move camera during recording.2. Blanching (Left Pile): Place left pile into boiling water for 1–2 minutes until bright green. Immediately transfer to ice bath for 1 minute, then drain and return to left position.3. Control (Right Pile): Keep right pile raw on the counter.4. Final Cooking: Place both left (blanched) and right (raw) piles into boiling water side by side at the same time. Cook for the same short duration (e.g., 2–3 minutes).5. Observation: Remove both piles and place them back in their original left/right positions for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Both piles are raw green beans with similar color.After blanching: Left pile becomes brighter green.After final cooking: Left pile remains vivid green; right pile appears duller or olive-green.V. Experimental Principle SummaryGreen vegetables contain chlorophyll, which degrades and dulls in color due to heat-activated enzymes and acidic conditions. Blanching briefly in boiling water inactivates these enzymes, and rapid cooling in an ice bath stops further cooking. As a result, blanched green beans retain a brighter green color during subsequent cooking compared with raw beans.VI. PrecautionsUse equal bean sizes and cooking times; ensure rapid transfer to ice bath; maintain fixed camera position for accurate time-lapse comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Blanching improves color retention in green vegetables by enzyme inactivation. Minimum assumptions: green beans contain chlorophyll; heat activates enzymes; blanching plus ice bath halts enzyme action.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup on a counter with two equal piles, fixed camera. (2) Left pile briefly boiled then shocked in ice bath, becoming brighter green. (3) Right pile remains raw. (4) Both piles boiled together in final cook. (5) End comparison shows left pile greener than right. Visibility constraints: left/right positions must remain constant; color differences must be clearly visible in time-lapse.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Bile-Assisted Fat EmulsificationI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Bile-Assisted Fat Emulsification Using Oil, Water, and Bile-Salt SubstituteSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To demonstrate how bile salts emulsify dietary fats, increasing dispersion stability and surface area for digestion.II. MaterialsTwo identical clear glass beakers; water (equal volumes); cooking oil (equal volumes); bile-salt substitute or mild emulsifier; dropper or spatula; stirring rod (optional); camera with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear beakers side by side on a lab bench. Add equal volumes of water to each beaker, then gently add equal volumes of cooking oil, forming a visible oil layer on top of the water.2. Addition of Emulsifier: Add a measured amount of bile-salt substitute to the left beaker only. Do not add anything to the right beaker (control).3. Shaking: Seal or cover both beakers and shake them with equal force and duration.4. Observation Setup: Place both beakers back on the bench. Fix the camera focus and begin time-lapse recording to capture separation over time.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial State: In both beakers, oil and water are clearly separated into two layers.After Shaking: Both beakers appear cloudy, but the left beaker shows finer, more uniform oil droplets.Standing Over Time: The right (control) beaker rapidly separates into a clear oil layer and water layer. The left beaker remains cloudy longer, with slower and incomplete separation, indicating a stable emulsion.V. Experimental Principle SummaryBile salts are amphipathic molecules with hydrophilic and hydrophobic ends. During shaking, they adsorb at the oil–water interface, reducing surface tension and breaking large fat globules into many small droplets. This emulsification stabilizes fat dispersion in water, delaying separation and increasing surface area, which in human digestion facilitates lipase action and fat absorption.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: bile-assisted fat emulsification in human digestion, requiring only the assumptions that oil and water are immiscible and bile salts act as emulsifiers.Minimum mechanistic assumptions: shaking provides mechanical energy; bile-salt substitute has amphipathic properties; emulsification increases droplet dispersion stability.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup showing layered oil and water in two clear beakers; (2) causal intervention where bile-salt substitute is added only to the left beaker; (3) equal shaking of both beakers; (4) post-shake settling under fixed-focus time-lapse; (5) divergence of outcomes—rapid separation in control versus persistent cloudiness in emulsified beaker.Visibility and perspective constraints: camera must clearly show both beakers simultaneously, maintain fixed focus, and allow comparison of droplet cloudiness and separation over accelerated time.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Standing Leg Swings Forward and Backward Before RunningI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Standing Leg Swings Forward and Backward Before Running2. Subject: Healthcare – Physiotherapy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate a common dynamic warm-up technique used before running, observe balance control and hip joint mobility, and understand how controlled leg swings prepare the lower limb muscles and joints for running.II. Experimental EquipmentOutdoor running track with visible lane markings; sportswear and running shoes; tripod-mounted camera or fixed-position camera capable of time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Choose an outdoor running track. Place the camera on a tripod beside the lane, fixing focus and angle to capture the full body of the athlete from the side.Starting Position: The athlete stands beside the lane, feet together, torso upright, eyes facing forward.Balance Setup: Shift body weight onto the standing leg, keeping the pelvis level and the stance knee slightly flexed for stability.Core Operation: Lift the free leg with the knee extended and swing it straight forward from the hip, then smoothly swing it backward from the hip. Maintain a controlled, rhythmic forward–backward motion.Repetition and Recording: Continue swinging for several cycles while maintaining balance. Record using time-lapse photography to compress repeated motion into a short sequence.Completion: Gradually stop the swing, return the free leg to the ground, and relax posture.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Athlete is stationary, balanced on one leg with stable posture.During Motion: The free leg swings forward and backward in a straight line from the hip; the torso remains mostly upright; the standing leg provides balance with small corrective movements.Time-lapse Effect: Repeated swings appear as a smooth, rhythmic oscillation, emphasizing range of motion and balance control.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on physiotherapy and sports biomechanics principles. Standing leg swings are a dynamic warm-up that mobilizes the hip joint, gently stretches the hamstrings and hip flexors, and activates balance-related muscles in the standing leg. Controlled hip flexion and extension increase joint range of motion and neuromuscular readiness, reducing injury risk before running.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Plant Phototropism in SeedlingsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Plant Phototropism in Seedlings2. Subject: Healthcare – Nursing (Basic Biology for Nursing)3. Knowledge Point: Plant phototropism – seedlings bend toward a unilateral light source via photoreceptors.4. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that plant seedlings show directional growth toward a unilateral light source; to compare growth direction under unilateral light versus uniform light or darkness; to understand the biological principle of phototropism; to practice basic experimental observation and time-lapse recording methods.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Identical seedling trays (2 trays) with the same plant species (e.g., wheat, mung bean, or radish seedlings).2. Growth medium (soil or moist paper towel), same type and amount for both trays.3. Desk lamp or LED lamp (single directional light source).4. Dark box or evenly lit environment (for control group).5. Camera or mobile phone with time-lapse photography function.6. Tripod or fixed stand to hold the camera.7. Ruler or scale (optional, for measuring bending angle).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Prepare two identical seedling trays with the same number, size, and growth stage of seedlings.   (2) Ensure both trays have equal water, soil, and environmental conditions at the start.2. Experimental Setup:   (1) Place Tray A (experimental group) near a lamp so that light comes clearly from only one side.   (2) Place Tray B (control group) under evenly distributed light or in darkness, ensuring no unilateral light source.   (3) Adjust the distance and brightness of the lamp so seedlings receive visible but non-damaging light.3. Camera and Recording:   (1) Fix the camera on a tripod facing both trays or separately facing each tray.   (2) Fix the focus, angle, and framing of the camera; do not change them during the experiment.   (3) Turn on time-lapse mode to record growth over time (hours to days). For demonstration video, compress or accelerate the process while keeping the growth sequence.4. Observation and Maintenance:   (1) Observe seedlings at regular intervals without moving trays or light sources.   (2) Keep water and temperature conditions consistent throughout the experiment.5. Completion:   (1) Stop recording after clear bending differences are observed.   (2) Save and review the time-lapse footage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Seedlings in both trays grow upright with no obvious bending.2. Experimental Group (Unilateral Light): Over time, seedlings gradually bend toward the lamp; stems curve in the direction of the light source.3. Control Group (Uniform Light or Dark): Seedlings grow mostly straight upward or show no consistent bending toward one side.4. Final Comparison: The bending angle and growth direction in Tray A are明显 toward the light source, while Tray B shows no directional growth.V. Summary of Experimental Principle1. Plants exhibit phototropism, a directional growth response to light.2. When light comes from one side, photoreceptors (such as phototropins) in the plant detect light direction.3. Auxin, a plant growth hormone, redistributes to the shaded side of the stem.4. Cells on the shaded side elongate faster than those on the illuminated side, causing the stem to bend toward the light.5. Under uniform light or darkness, auxin distribution remains relatively even, so no directional bending occurs.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical seedlings to reduce experimental error.2. Ensure the light source is clearly unilateral for the experimental group.3. Do not move trays or camera during recording.4. Avoid overheating or drying seedlings with the lamp.5. Focus on growth direction rather than exact growth time during accelerated demonstrations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Plant phototropism, defined as directional growth of seedlings toward a unilateral light source, assuming basic plant growth, light perception, and hormone redistribution mechanisms. Minimum assumptions: seedlings are alive, light direction is stable, and growth can be visually accelerated.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase: two identical upright seedling trays under different lighting conditions; (2) Exposure phase: unilateral light applied to one tray while control remains uniform or dark; (3) Transition phase: gradual curvature of stems toward the light source; (4) Outcome phase: clear directional bending in experimental group and straight growth in control. Visibility constraints: camera must remain fixed with consistent framing and lighting so directional growth and causal contrast are verifiable.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Foot-to-Foot BIA Scale DemonstrationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Foot-to-Foot Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) Scale Demonstration2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a foot-to-foot BIA scale measures body composition-related impedance through barefoot contact and posture changes, and to observe corresponding numerical pointer fluctuations.II. Experimental EquipmentFoot-to-foot BIA scale with metal foot pads and visible numerical pointer/display; flat floor surface; camera capable of time-lapse recording.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the BIA scale on a flat, stable surface. Ensure the metal foot pads are clean and dry. Set the camera to a fixed position, framing both the feet and the numerical pointer.Step-On Operation: A barefoot person steps onto the scale, placing both feet fully on the metal pads. Core Operation: Starting near the bolus end, apply a ring-like squeeze around the tube, then sequentially move the squeeze forward along the tube toward the far end, releasing behind as you progress. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Observation of Cosmic Ray Particle Tracks in a Classroom Cloud ChamberI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Cosmic Ray Particle Tracks Using a Cloud ChamberSubject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging SciencesExperiment Objective: To observe and record visible tracks produced by cosmic ray particles in a supersaturated alcohol vapor environment, and to understand the imaging principle of ionizing radiation interactions with matter.II. Experimental EquipmentClear cloud chamber (transparent walls and sealed lid), metal base plate, dry ice, isopropyl alcohol (90% or higher), absorbent felt or sponge lining, insulating tray, protective gloves, fixed-focus camera mounted above or to the side of the chamber interior, dim ambient lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on protective gloves. Place dry ice in the insulating tray and position the metal base plate directly on top to ensure strong cooling.2. Chamber Setup: Line the inner top rim of the chamber with felt or sponge. Evenly soak it with isopropyl alcohol until saturated but not dripping.3. Assembly: Place the clear chamber body onto the cooled metal base, forming a sealed environment. Ensure the chamber remains undisturbed.4. Camera Setup: Fix the camera so it focuses on the interior volume just above the base plate. Lock focus and exposure settings for time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Observation: Allow 2–5 minutes for the bottom region to cool and the alcohol vapor to become supersaturated. Observe the chamber without movement.6. Recording: Capture continuous or time-lapse images of the interior for several minutes, focusing on the appearance of particle tracks.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: A clear chamber with faint mist near the cold base, no visible tracks.During Observation: Thin, straight, brief streaks appear suddenly and disappear (cosmic ray muons). Occasional thicker, shorter, or curved tracks may appear (alpha particles or secondary particles).Stable State: Repeated appearance of transient tracks against a dark, misty background near the base plate.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe cloud chamber operates on the principle of supersaturated vapor condensation. Dry ice cools the base, creating a temperature gradient that supersaturates alcohol vapor near the bottom. When cosmic ray particles pass through the chamber, they ionize air molecules along their paths. Alcohol vapor condenses on these ions, forming visible droplets that trace the particle trajectories. This provides a direct imaging demonstration of ionizing radiation, analogous to track formation concepts used in radiographic and imaging sciences.

manual: Experimental Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescence Time-Lapse Observation of Macrophage Phagocytosis of Green Fluorescent Bacteria2. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the dynamic process of phagocytosis by cultured human macrophages when exposed to green fluorescent bacteria using fluorescence time-lapse microscopy, and to identify key cellular behaviors during macrophage–bacteria interactions.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Cultured human macrophages (adherent cells in glass-bottom culture dish)2. Green fluorescent protein (GFP)-labeled bacteria (heat-killed or attenuated, suspended in culture medium)3. Cell culture medium (phenol red-free for fluorescence imaging)4. Micropipette and sterile tipsIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the macrophage culture dish into the live-cell imaging chamber on the fluorescence microscope. Baseline Imaging: Switch to fluorescence mode and capture initial images to confirm absence or minimal presence of green fluorescent bacteria in the field of view.3. Bacterial Exposure: Gently add a small volume of green fluorescent bacterial suspension to the culture dish using a micropipette, avoiding disturbance of the cells.4. Time-Lapse Acquisition: Immediately begin time-lapse fluorescence imaging, capturing images at regular short intervals (for example, every 10–20 seconds) over several minutes. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Dissolution Characteristics of Tablet, Capsule, and Liquid Medication in Water2. Subject: Healthcare – Nursing (Medication Administration Basics)3. Experiment Objective: To visually compare the dissolution speed and behavior of three common medication forms (tablet, capsule, liquid) in water through time-lapse observation, helping learners understand how dosage form influences drug dissolution and onset of action.II. Experimental Equipment1. Three identical clear glass cups (transparent, cylindrical, same size)2. Clean drinking water (room temperature, same volume in each glass, e.g., 200 mL)3. One solid tablet (uncoated or film-coated, simulated medication allowed)4. One capsule (gelatin capsule, simulated medication allowed)5. One liquid medication (colored or clear, water-soluble)6. Camera or smartphone with tripod7. Timer or time-lapse recording functionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Place three identical clear glasses side by side on a flat, well-lit surface.   b. Pour the same volume of clear water into each glass, ensuring water levels are equal.   c. Label the glasses visually from left to right as: Tablet, Capsule, Liquid.   d. Fix the camera position directly in front of the glasses; ensure all three glasses are fully in frame and in focus.2. Core Operation:   a. Start video or time-lapse recording without changing camera focus.   b. Drop one tablet vertically into the left glass.   c. Drop one capsule vertically into the center glass.   d. Slowly pour a measured amount of liquid medication into the right glass.3. Observation Stage:   a. Continue recording as the substances interact with the water.   b. Do not stir or disturb the water.   c. Observe changes in shape, color diffusion, sinking or floating, and dissolution speed.4. Completion:   a. Stop recording after the main dissolution behaviors are clearly visible.   b. Dispose of the solutions safely and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Tablet:   - Initially sinks to the bottom.   - Gradually breaks apart, forming cloudy particles.   - Dissolves slowly, with visible sediment dispersing over time.2. Capsule:   - May float briefly or sink slowly.   - Outer gelatin shell softens and dissolves first.   - Contents are released, causing gradual cloudiness.3. Liquid Medication:   - Immediately disperses upon pouring.   - Rapid and uniform color diffusion in water.   - No solid residue remains.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDifferent medication dosage forms dissolve differently in water due to their physical structure and formulation. Tablets require disintegration before dissolution, capsules must first dissolve their gelatin shell, while liquid medications are already in dissolved form and therefore disperse immediately. This principle explains differences in onset of action and is critical for nursing practice in medication administration and patient education.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use identical glasses and equal water volumes to ensure fairness.2. Avoid stirring to preserve natural dissolution behavior.3. Fix camera focus and position to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.4. Use simulated or non-active medications for safety.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Geiger–Müller Tube Responding to a Nearby Radiation Source with Flashing IndicatorI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Geiger–Müller Tube Responding to a Nearby Radiation Source with Flashing Indicator2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how a Geiger–Müller (GM) tube detects ionizing radiation and converts it into visible signals, by observing changes in LED flashing frequency as a sealed radioactive check source is moved from far away to very close and then back again. The experiment helps learners understand radiation detection principles and the inverse relationship between radiation intensity and distance.II. Experimental Equipment1. Powered tabletop Geiger–Müller tube with built-in electronics and a visible LED indicator (and optional audible clicker).2. Sealed handheld radioactive check source (low-activity, laboratory-approved, safely encapsulated).3. Stable laboratory table or bench.4. Camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod, with focus fixed for time-lapse or continuous recording.5. Power supply for the GM tube.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Place the Geiger–Müller tube flat and stable on the tabletop.   b. Connect the GM tube to its power supply and switch it on.   c. Confirm that the LED flashes occasionally, indicating background radiation.   d. Position the camera facing the GM tube so that the LED is clearly visible; fix the focus and do not change camera settings during the experiment.2. Initial Observation (Source Far Away):   a. Hold the sealed radioactive check source at a position far from the GM tube (e.g., more than 50 cm).   b. Observe and record the LED flashing rate for several seconds; it should be slow and similar to background radiation.3. Approaching the Radiation Source:   a. Slowly move the radioactive check source toward the GM tube in a straight, controlled motion.   b. Continue to observe the LED as the distance decreases.   c. When the source is very close to the GM tube (a few centimeters away), hold it steady briefly.4. Withdrawing the Radiation Source:   a. Slowly move the radioactive check source away from the GM tube, retracing the path back to the far position.   b. Continue observing the LED flashing rate until it returns to near-background levels.5. Completion:   a. Place the radioactive check source back into its shielded storage container.   b. Switch off the GM tube and power supply.   c. Stop recording and safely store all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: With the radioactive source far away, the GM tube LED flashes infrequently, representing detection of natural background radiation.2. During Approach: As the radioactive check source moves closer to the GM tube, the LED flashes become progressively more frequent, clearly visible as an increase in blinking rate.3. Closest Position: When the source is very close, the LED flashes rapidly and almost continuously, indicating a high detection rate of ionizing radiation.4. During Withdrawal: As the source is moved away, the LED flashing rate gradually decreases.5. Final State: When the source is again far away, the LED returns to a low, background-level flashing rate.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Detection Principle: A Geiger–Müller tube is filled with low-pressure gas and operates at high voltage. When ionizing radiation enters the tube, it ionizes gas molecules, creating charged particles that trigger a brief electrical discharge.2. Signal Conversion: Each discharge is converted by the electronics into a visible LED flash (and sometimes an audible click), representing one detected radiation event.3. Distance Effect: The intensity of detected radiation depends on the distance between the source and the detector. As the radioactive source moves closer, more radiation reaches the GM tube per unit time, increasing the count rate; as it moves away, the count rate decreases.4. Educational Significance: This experiment visually demonstrates radiation detection, count rate variation, and the basic operating principle of radiation monitoring devices used in radiography and healthcare settings.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only sealed, approved low-activity radioactive check sources.2. Do not open or damage the radioactive source.3. Minimize handling time and follow laboratory radiation safety guidelines.4. Ensure the GM tube remains powered and stationary throughout the observation.5. Keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent visual comparison of LED flashing rates.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visual demonstration of radiation detection using a Geiger–Müller tube, assuming only that ionizing radiation events produce detectable electrical pulses converted into LED flashes. Minimum assumptions include a functioning GM tube, a low-activity sealed radioactive source, and a stable observation setup.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase – GM tube powered on, LED flashes slowly due to background radiation; camera is fixed. (2) Approach phase – the handheld radioactive source moves steadily closer, causing a clear, stepwise increase in LED flashing frequency. (3) Peak phase – source held very close, LED flashes rapidly and almost continuously. (4) Withdrawal phase – source moves away, LED flashing rate decreases back toward background. Visibility constraints: the LED must remain clearly visible throughout, and the relative distance change between source and detector must be obvious from the camera perspective to verify causal transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Freezing and Thawing Strawberries to Observe Ice-Crystal Texture DamageI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Freezing and Thawing Strawberries Showing Ice-Crystal Texture Damage2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To observe how freezing and subsequent thawing affect the texture of strawberries, and to understand how ice-crystal formation damages plant cell structure, leading to texture degradation.II. Experimental EquipmentFresh whole strawberries (3–5, ripe and undamaged), freezer (household freezer at approximately −18°C), plate or shallow container, room-temperature surface for thawing, knife (optional, for slicing), clean cutting board, camera or smartphone with fixed focus and tripod (for close-up and time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select whole strawberries, rinse briefly with clean water, and gently pat dry. Place them on a clean plate in a single layer.2. Freezing: Put the plate with whole strawberries into the freezer. Freeze until the strawberries are completely solid.3. Thawing: Remove the frozen strawberries from the freezer and place them on a plate at room temperature. Do not apply heat or water. Allow them to thaw naturally.4. Camera Setup: Position the camera close to the strawberries, fix the focus and angle, and keep the camera stable. If possible, record the thawing process using time-lapse.5. Core Demonstration: After thawing is complete, gently press one strawberry with a finger or slice it with a knife. Record a close-up of the action.6. End of Experiment: Observe the strawberry’s texture and juice release. Clean up the workspace and dispose of the strawberries appropriately.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Frozen State: Strawberries appear hard and opaque, often with frost on the surface.2. During Thawing: As temperature rises, strawberries lose structural rigidity; moisture appears on the surface.3. After Thawing: The strawberry becomes soft and mushy. When gently pressed or sliced, the flesh collapses easily and releases juice.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesStrawberries are composed of plant cells filled with water. During freezing, water inside the cells forms ice crystals, which expand and puncture cell walls. Upon thawing, the damaged cells cannot retain their original structure or water, resulting in a soft, watery texture. This experiment demonstrates ice-crystal-induced texture damage, a key concept in food freezing and nutrition science.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use whole strawberries to ensure clear comparison before and after freezing.2. Avoid rapid heating during thawing, as it may introduce additional variables.3. Handle knives carefully during slicing to ensure safety.4. Ensure the camera focus remains fixed to clearly capture texture changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salt Added to Water Completes a Simple LED CircuitI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salt Added to Water Completes a Simple LED Circuit2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics (basic electrolyte and conductivity concept)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that adding table salt (sodium chloride) to water increases its electrical conductivity, allowing a simple circuit to be completed and an LED to light.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass or beaker (1), clean tap or distilled water, table salt (sodium chloride), two metal electrodes (e.g., iron or copper nails), battery (e.g., 3–9 V), LED light, connecting wires, stirring rod or spoon.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear glass on a tabletop and fill it with clean water. Ensure the water is clear and colorless.2. Circuit Setup: Connect the battery, LED, and two metal electrodes in series using wires, leaving the two electrodes as free ends.3. Electrode Placement: Insert the two metal electrodes into the water in the glass, keeping them separated and not touching each other.4. Initial Observation: Observe the LED state before adding salt (typically off or very dim).5. Core Operation: Use a hand to add a small amount of table salt into the water while the circuit remains connected. Stir gently until the salt dissolves.6. Final Observation: Continue observing the LED as the salt dissolves and the solution is stirred.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The water is clear; the LED does not light or is very dim because pure water conducts electricity poorly.2. During Salt Addition and Stirring: As salt dissolves, the LED gradually lights up or becomes noticeably brighter.3. Final State: After sufficient salt has dissolved, the LED lights steadily, indicating that the circuit is completed.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePure water has very low electrical conductivity. Table salt (sodium chloride) dissolves in water to form sodium ions (Na+) and chloride ions (Cl−). These ions move freely in the solution and carry electric charge, increasing the conductivity of the water. When the conductivity becomes sufficient, electric current can flow between the electrodes, completing the circuit and causing the LED to light.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the electrodes do not touch directly in the water to avoid short-circuiting.2. Use low-voltage batteries for safety.3. Add salt gradually to clearly observe the change in LED brightness.4. Dry hands after the experiment and disconnect the battery when finished.

Experiment Title: Oxygen Generation in a Hydrogen Peroxide Contact Lens Case2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the neutralization process of hydrogen peroxide in a soft contact lens disinfection system by observing oxygen bubble formation from a built-in catalytic disc, and to understand the working principle of peroxide-based lens care.II. Experimental EquipmentHydrogen peroxide contact lens case with built-in catalytic disc (platinum-coated), soft contact lenses (one pair), hydrogen peroxide lens care solution (3%), clean tabletop, camera or smartphone mounted on a fixed stand for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean hydrogen peroxide lens case upright on a stable tabletop. Ensure the catalytic disc at the bottom of the case is intact and visible.2. Lens Placement: Put each soft contact lens into its respective lens basket, ensuring correct orientation (concave side up) and that lenses are fully seated.3. Filling with Solution: Slowly pour hydrogen peroxide solution into the case until the fill line is reached and the lenses are fully submerged.4. Closure: Securely close the lens case lid to activate contact between the solution and the catalytic disc.5. Observation Period: Allow the case to remain undisturbed on the tabletop while recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. This reaction neutralizes the peroxide over time, making the solution safe for contact with the eyes. The core reaction is: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂↑.VI. Enable time-lapse capture.3. Framing Calibration: Adjust camera position to frame the object tightly at macro scale. Mark the rail or table to guide forward/backward motion while keeping framing similar.4. Core Operation: Start time-lapse recording. Fixed Focus Plane: With manual focus locked, only subjects at the focus plane appear sharp; changing distance causes defocus blur, exaggerated in macro due to shallow depth-of-field.2. Depth-of-Field in Macro: Macro lenses have very shallow depth-of-field, making small distance changes visually significant.3. Lighting Geometry: With a fixed lamp, illuminance on the subject changes with distance, altering brightness and shadow contrast.VI. Precautions1. Do not refocus during the experiment.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Knee Flexion and Extension During Seated Leg BendI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Knee Flexion and Extension During Seated Leg Bend2. Subject: Healthcare – Physiotherapy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe controlled knee flexion and extension in a seated position, understand basic knee joint biomechanics, and provide a standard visual record using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentBench or treatment table with flat surface; chair-height support allowing thighs to rest fully; camera or smartphone with tripod; timer or time-lapse function; comfortable clothing allowing knee visibility.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the bench on stable ground. Set up the camera on a tripod facing the side of the participant, ensuring the knee joint is centered in the frame. Fix focus and exposure; enable time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Starting Position: The participant sits upright on the bench with hips flexed about 90 degrees. Thighs are fully supported on the bench, feet are off the ground, and the lower leg hangs freely. Hands rest on the bench for balance.3. Core Operation: Slowly straighten the knee from a relaxed flexed position to a comfortable extension range without locking the joint. Then slowly bend the knee back to the starting position. Maintain smooth, controlled motion.4. Repetition: Repeat the bending and straightening cycle several times at a steady, slow pace suitable for therapeutic exercise.5. Completion: Stop the recording, ensure the participant returns to a resting position, and power off the camera.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The thigh remains stable and supported on the bench; the lower leg hangs vertically under gravity.2. During Extension: The lower leg moves upward as the knee extends, forming a larger angle between thigh and lower leg; movement is smooth and controlled.3. During Flexion: The lower leg moves downward as the knee bends, returning toward the initial hanging position without sudden drops or jerks.4. Throughout: The thigh stays relatively still, and motion is isolated mainly to the knee joint.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe knee is a hinge joint primarily allowing flexion and extension. In a seated leg bend, knee extension is mainly produced by contraction of the quadriceps femoris, while knee flexion is controlled by the hamstrings and gravity. Supporting the thigh isolates knee motion, reduces load on the joint, and allows safe observation of joint range, muscle control, and movement quality. Fixed-focus time-lapse recording provides a clear visual record of joint kinematics over repeated cycles.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the range of motion remains pain-free; avoid rapid or forceful movement; keep the camera fixed to maintain consistent observation; stop the experiment if discomfort occurs.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstration of seated knee flexion and extension as a basic physiotherapy exercise with isolated knee motion and stable visual documentation. Minimum assumptions include a human subject seated on a bench, thigh supported, lower leg free, and a fixed camera capturing side-view knee motion.Expected Phenomena Storyline: Phase 1 – Static setup: subject seated, thigh supported, lower leg hanging freely, camera fixed. Phase 2 – Extension: quadriceps activation causes the lower leg to lift smoothly, increasing knee angle. Phase 3 – Flexion: controlled relaxation and hamstring action allow the lower leg to lower smoothly back to start. Phase 4 – Repetition: cycles repeat smoothly with consistent posture. Visibility constraints: the knee joint, thigh, and lower leg must remain in frame from a stable side perspective to verify motion, range, and continuity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Laser Passing from Air into a Rectangular Acrylic or Glass BlockI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Laser Passing from Air into a Rectangular Acrylic or Glass Block2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences (Optical Physics Foundation)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the refraction of light when a visible laser beam passes from air into a rectangular glass or acrylic block; to visualize the incident, refracted, and emergent beams; and to relate angle changes to the law of refraction. The experiment also demonstrates stable optical imaging conditions suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentVisible laser pointer (red or green, continuous beam), rectangular glass or acrylic block with polished faces, rotatable laser mount or adjustable stand, white paper or protractor sheet (for angle reference), darkened room or low ambient light environment, camera or smartphone mounted on a tripod with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography), safety goggles suitable for laser use.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the rectangular glass/acrylic block flat on a table covered with white paper. Draw a baseline along one face of the block and mark a normal line at the point of incidence. Mount the camera on a tripod facing the block and fix the focus; do not adjust focus during the experiment.2. Alignment: Position the laser pointer so that the beam travels horizontally in air and strikes one flat face of the block at a chosen point. Ensure the beam is clearly visible in air and inside the block (using low ambient light).3. Initial Observation: Turn on the laser and observe the straight-line propagation of the incident beam in air, the bent path inside the block, and the emergent beam exiting the opposite face.4. Angle Variation: Slowly rotate the laser source around the point of incidence to change the incident angle while keeping the block stationary. Record the changing beam paths using time-lapse photography, maintaining constant camera focus.5. Completion: After observing several incident angles, turn off the laser, stop recording, and safely store the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The laser beam travels in a straight line through air before reaching the block.2. At the Air–Block Interface: Upon entering the glass/acrylic block, the laser beam bends toward the normal.3. Inside the Block: The beam travels in a straight line at a new angle determined by the refractive index of the material.4. Exiting the Block: When the beam leaves the block and re-enters air, it bends away from the normal and emerges parallel to the incident beam (for parallel faces).5. Angle Dependence: As the incident angle increases, the refracted angle inside the block and the emergent angle change correspondingly.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates light refraction at the boundary between two media with different refractive indices. According to Snell’s law (n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂), when light passes from air (lower refractive index) into glass or acrylic (higher refractive index), its speed decreases and its direction changes, bending toward the normal. When the light exits back into air, it bends away from the normal. The relationship between incident and refracted angles is deterministic and forms the physical basis of image formation and beam behavior in radiographic and optical imaging systems.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Do not look directly into the laser beam or point it at others.2. Use a low-power visible laser suitable for educational demonstrations.3. Keep the block stationary while varying the laser angle to ensure valid observations.4. Maintain fixed camera focus throughout recording to ensure consistent imaging conditions.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: optical refraction of a laser beam at an air–glass/acrylic interface, demonstrating angle-dependent bending governed by Snell’s law. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: light travels in straight lines in uniform media; speed and direction change at media boundaries with different refractive indices; rectangular block has parallel faces.Expected phased storyline: (1) A visible laser propagates straight in air toward a stationary rectangular transparent block. (2) At the first interface, the beam bends toward the normal and becomes visible inside the block. (3) The laser source rotates, increasing or decreasing the incident angle, causing systematic changes in the internal beam angle. (4) The beam exits the opposite face, bending away from the normal and remaining parallel to the incident beam. Visibility constraints: low ambient light to see the beam path, fixed camera position and focus to verify smooth temporal changes and spatial consistency.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Antacids Neutralizing Stomach Acid Demonstrated by pH Indicator Color ChangeI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Antacids Neutralizing Acid Demonstrated with Universal pH IndicatorSubject: Healthcare – NursingExperiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how antacids neutralize stomach acid by observing the color change of a universal pH indicator, and to understand the basic principle of acid–base neutralization relevant to nursing practice.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear glass beakers (2 identical beakers)Dilute acidic solution simulating stomach acid (e.g., dilute hydrochloric acid or vinegar)Universal pH indicator solutionCrushed antacid tablet (e.g., calcium carbonate–based)Glass stirring rodCamera or smartphone with fixed focus (for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a stable surface and label them as Left Beaker and Right Beaker.2. Solution Setup: Pour equal volumes of the acidic solution into each beaker. Add the same number of drops of universal pH indicator to both beakers and gently swirl to mix. Observe and confirm that both beakers show the same acidic indicator color.3. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both beakers are clearly visible in the frame. Begin time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Core Operation: Add a measured amount of crushed antacid into the Left Beaker only. Use a glass rod to gently stir the solution to ensure contact between the antacid and the acid.5. Control Condition: Do not add anything to the Right Beaker. Do not stir it.6. Observation Period: Allow the reaction to proceed while recording. Continue gentle stirring in the Left Beaker if needed, then stop and observe.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain acidic liquid with the same indicator color.During Reaction: In the Left Beaker, after adding crushed antacid, the indicator color gradually changes toward green or a neutral color, indicating a rise in pH. The Right Beaker shows no noticeable color change and remains acidic.Final State: A clear color contrast is visible between the Left Beaker (less acidic or neutral) and the Right Beaker (still acidic).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAntacids are basic substances, commonly containing compounds such as calcium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide. When added to an acidic solution, they react with hydrogen ions in the acid, reducing acidity. This acid–base neutralization increases the pH of the solution, which is visually represented by the color change of the universal pH indicator. This principle explains how antacids relieve gastric discomfort caused by excess stomach acid in clinical nursing practice.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse dilute acid to ensure safety.Add antacid slowly to prevent excessive bubbling or splashing.Ensure both beakers start with identical conditions for clear comparison.Handle glassware carefully and clean all equipment after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstrating acid–base neutralization of stomach acid by antacids using a universal pH indicator in a controlled, comparative setup relevant to nursing education. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: acidic solution represents gastric acid; antacid is a basic substance; universal indicator reliably changes color with pH; no other reactions interfere.Phased storyline: (1) Initial phase – two identical clear beakers with the same acidic indicator color are shown side by side under a fixed camera. (2) Intervention phase – crushed antacid is added and gently stirred only in the left beaker while the right remains untouched. (3) Reaction phase – the left beaker shows a gradual, smooth color shift toward neutral, causally following antacid addition, while the right beaker shows no change. (4) Comparison phase – a stable final contrast between beakers is visible. Visibility constraints: both beakers must remain in frame, color changes must be clearly discernible, and camera perspective must remain fixed to verify temporal progression.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Yeast Fermentation Balloons: Lactose Solution vs. Lactose Plus Lactase EnzymeSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition & DieteticsObjective: To demonstrate that yeast cannot directly ferment lactose, and that the addition of lactase enables fermentation by hydrolyzing lactose into fermentable monosaccharides, observed through carbon dioxide production inflating a balloon.II. Experimental MaterialsClear flasks (2 identical flasks, 250–500 mL), active dry yeast (equal amounts), lactose solution (same concentration and volume in both flasks), liquid lactase enzyme, balloons (2 identical), measuring cylinder or dropper, labels (Left: Lactose only; Right: Lactose + Lactase), camera or smartphone on tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear flasks side by side on a stable surface. Label the left flask ‘Lactose’ and the right flask ‘Lactose + Lactase’.2. Solution Setup: Pour equal volumes of lactose solution into both flasks. Add the same amount of yeast to each flask and gently swirl to mix.3. Balloon Attachment: Stretch and securely attach identical balloons over the mouths of both flasks, ensuring an airtight seal.4. Enzyme Addition (Core Operation): Using a dropper, add a measured amount of liquid lactase only into the right flask. Do not add anything to the left flask.5. Filming: Set the camera directly in front of the two flasks. Fix the focus, ensure both balloons are fully in frame, and start time-lapse or continuous recording. Leave the setup undisturbed.6. Completion: After sufficient recording time, stop filming and compare the balloon sizes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both balloons are deflated; solutions appear similar.During Reaction: The balloon on the right flask gradually inflates, while the left balloon shows little or no inflation.Final State: A clear difference in balloon size is observed, with the right balloon noticeably larger.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleYeast cannot ferment lactose directly because it lacks sufficient lactase. Lactase enzyme hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, which yeast can ferment anaerobically. Fermentation produces carbon dioxide gas, which accumulates and inflates the balloon. Therefore, only the flask with added lactase shows significant balloon inflation.VI. PrecautionsEnsure equal yeast and lactose amounts in both flasks; keep temperature consistent; do not disturb the setup during filming; balloons must be identical and securely attached.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Enzyme-enabled digestion and fermentation of lactose. Minimum assumptions: yeast produces CO2 only when fermentable sugars are available; lactase hydrolyzes lactose into fermentable sugars; balloon inflation reflects gas production. Phased storyline: (1) Two identical flasks with yeast and lactose are shown side by side, balloons deflated; (2) lactase is added only to the right flask; (3) time-lapse shows gradual inflation of the right balloon while the left remains mostly unchanged; (4) final comparison highlights causal link. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear view of both balloons and flasks, labels or spatial cues distinguishing left and right.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Starch–Iodine Color Change During Amylase Digestion of StarchI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Starch–Iodine Color Change During Amylase Digestion of Starch2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Biochemistry / Physiology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that amylase enzymatically digests starch, leading to the loss of the characteristic blue-black color formed by the starch–iodine reaction, and to understand enzyme specificity through comparative observation.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clear beakers (2, identical)2. Starch suspension (cloudy starch solution, equal volume for each beaker)3. Amylase solution (e.g., salivary amylase or commercial amylase)4. Iodine solution (iodine–potassium iodide)5. Droppers or pipettes (at least 2)6. Glass stirring rods or gentle swirling by hand7. Lab bench, labels, and camera fixed for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear beakers side by side on a lab bench. Label the left beaker as Amylase and the right as Control. Pour equal volumes of cloudy starch solution into each beaker.2. Enzyme Addition: Add a measured amount of amylase solution only to the left beaker. Do not add amylase to the right beaker. Gently swirl both beakers to ensure uniform mixing.3. Initial Test: Using a dropper, add a few drops of iodine solution to each beaker while gently swirling. Observe and record the immediate color change.4. Time-Lapse Observation: Keep the camera focus fixed. At regular intervals, continue to drip iodine into both beakers and swirl gently. Record changes over time.5. Completion: Stop the experiment once a clear difference between the two beakers is observed. Dispose of solutions properly and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain cloudy, colorless starch suspension.2. After Iodine Addition: Both beakers initially turn blue-black, indicating the presence of starch.3. Over Time: In the amylase-treated beaker, the blue-black color becomes lighter and eventually disappears or turns yellow-brown with iodine addition. In the control beaker, the blue-black color remains stable.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine forms a blue-black complex with intact starch molecules. Amylase catalyzes the hydrolysis of starch into smaller sugars (such as maltose and dextrins) that no longer form the blue-black complex with iodine. Therefore, as starch is digested by amylase, the iodine color reaction weakens or disappears. The untreated control confirms that the color change is due to enzymatic digestion rather than time or iodine instability.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Amylase specifically digests starch, which can be visualized by the loss of the iodine–starch blue-black color. Minimum mechanistic assumption: iodine indicates intact starch; amylase hydrolyzes starch over time. Phased storyline: (1) two identical beakers of cloudy starch are presented side by side; (2) amylase is added only to the left beaker; (3) iodine initially turns both solutions blue-black; (4) with time, only the amylase-treated beaker loses the blue-black color while the control remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: fixed camera, clear beaker labeling, and strong color contrast to allow direct visual comparison in a short time-lapse.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Observation of Neutrophil Chemotaxis Using a MicropipetteSubject: Healthcare – Veterinary MedicineObjective: To observe and record the directed migration of live neutrophils toward a chemoattractant source under a light microscope using fixed-focus time-lapse imaging.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Add neutrophil suspension to the fluid chamber and allow cells to settle and adhere lightly. Place the chamber on the microscope stage.2. Core Operation: Begin releasing chemoattractant by diffusion from the micropipette tip and start time-lapse recording.6. Experiment Title: Sit-to-Stand Training from a Chair Using Lower-Body Strength2. Subject: Healthcare – Physiotherapy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and practice the standard sit-to-stand movement using lower-limb muscle strength and balance control, and to understand the biomechanical principles of functional mobility training in rehabilitation.II. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place the chair on a flat surface. The participant sits in the middle of the chair, back upright, feet flat on the floor and shoulder-width apart, knees bent about 90 degrees, hands resting on thighs.Starting Position: Ensure the participant is seated steadily with weight evenly distributed and eyes looking forward.Core Operation: The participant leans the trunk slightly forward, presses both feet firmly into the floor, and uses lower-body strength to rise from the chair to a full standing position with hips and knees fully extended.Return Movement: After standing steadily for a brief moment, the participant bends hips and knees in a controlled manner and slowly sits back down until fully seated.Repetition: Repeat the sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit cycle several times at a steady and safe pace.IV. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSit-to-stand training is a fundamental functional movement in physiotherapy. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Basophil Detection (Toluidine Blue Staining Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Basophil Detection by Toluidine Blue StainingSubject: Healthcare – Basic ImmunologyObjective: To prepare a peripheral blood smear, perform toluidine blue staining, and identify basophils under oil immersion microscopy.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClean glass slides, sterile lancet, capillary blood sample, methanol, toluidine blue stain, distilled water, dropper, staining rack, light microscope with oil immersion objective, immersion oil.III. Experimental Procedure1. Blood Smear Preparation: Place a small drop of peripheral blood near one end of a clean slide. Use a spreader slide to push forward smoothly, forming a thin, even smear.2. Air-Drying: Place the slide horizontally and allow the smear to air-dry completely.3. Fixation: Flood the dried smear with methanol for about 1–2 minutes to fix the cells. Drain and air-dry.4. Staining: Add toluidine blue stain to cover the smear and stain for a short time (about 1–3 minutes).5. Rinsing: Gently rinse the slide with distilled water to remove excess stain without disturbing the smear.6. Drying: Place the slide upright or flat and allow it to dry completely.7. Microscopic Observation: Add a drop of immersion oil, observe under a light microscope using the oil immersion objective, adjust focus, and record images if required.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaRed blood cells appear pale, while basophils are rare and show large, coarse, dark blue to purple granules in the cytoplasm, often obscuring the nucleus.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesToluidine blue is a basic dye that binds to acidic substances such as heparin and histamine in basophil granules. Due to metachromasia, basophil granules stain blue-purple, allowing differentiation from other leukocytes after proper fixation and staining.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Visualization of basophils using toluidine blue metachromatic staining after correct smear preparation and fixation. Minimum assumptions: existence of a thin blood smear, intact cells after methanol fixation, and proper dye-cell interaction. Phased storyline: (1) blood smear creation and air-drying; (2) methanol fixation stabilizing cells; (3) brief toluidine blue staining and gentle rinsing; (4) oil immersion microscopy revealing rare basophils with blue-purple granules. Visibility constraints: close-up view of slide during staining and high-magnification microscopic field during observation to verify basophil identification.
