manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Dissolution Comparison of Powdered Tablet vs Intact Tablet in Water2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how increasing surface area affects the dissolution rate of a tablet by comparing a powdered tablet with an intact tablet under identical conditions.II. Experimental Equipment- Two identical clear glass beakers- Still water (same volume in each beaker, room temperature)- One tablet of the same type, divided into powdered form and intact form- Camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass beakers side by side on a stable surface; add equal volumes of still water to each beaker. Ensure the water is not stirred and remains motionless.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus to cover both beakers simultaneously; do not change focus or angle during recording.3. Core Operation: At the same time, gently add the powdered tablet to the left beaker and the intact tablet to the right beaker. Do not stir either beaker.4. Observation: Record the dissolution process using time-lapse photography until clear differences in dissolution are visible.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both beakers contain clear, still water.2. Early Stage: The powdered tablet disperses quickly, forming a cloudy region in the left beaker; the intact tablet sinks or remains whole with minimal surface change.3. Later Stage: The left beaker shows rapid and widespread dissolution; the right beaker shows slow dissolution occurring mainly at the tablet surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates the pharmaceutical principle that increasing surface area increases dissolution rate. Powdering a tablet greatly increases its contact area with water, enhancing solvent interaction and mass transfer, leading to faster dissolution compared with an intact tablet under the same conditions.VI. Experimental Precautions- Use identical beakers and equal water volumes to ensure fairness.- Add tablets simultaneously and avoid stirring.- Maintain fixed camera focus for accurate time-lapse comparison.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Quadriceps Group Extending the Knee During a Seated Leg RaiseSubject: Healthcare – PhysiotherapyObjective: To demonstrate and observe knee extension produced by quadriceps contraction during a seated leg raise, suitable for visual analysis and time-lapse recording.II. Equipment and Setup1. Flat bench or examination table.2. Adult subject wearing shorts to expose the thigh and knee.3. Camera placed at a fixed side view, perpendicular to the sagittal plane of the subject; focus locked for time-lapse photography.4. Stable lighting to avoid visual fluctuation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits upright on the bench with hips flexed at approximately 90 degrees. One thigh is fully supported on the bench; the lower leg hangs freely over the edge.2. Positioning: Ensure the thigh is exposed, the knee joint is clearly visible, and the foot is relaxed. The camera framing includes the thigh, knee, and lower leg from the side.3. Core Operation: The subject slowly contracts the quadriceps to extend the knee, raising the lower leg until near full knee extension.4. Holding Phase (brief): Pause momentarily at the top to show the extended knee position.5. Lowering Phase: The subject slowly relaxes the quadriceps, allowing the lower leg to lower under control back to the hanging position.6. Repetition: Perform 1–2 controlled repetitions to clearly demonstrate the motion within a short recording duration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The lower leg hangs vertically with the knee flexed.2. During Extension: The lower leg moves upward in an arc as the knee extends smoothly.3. End Position: The knee approaches full extension, and the lower leg aligns more horizontally.4. During Lowering: The lower leg descends smoothly back to the initial hanging position.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe quadriceps femoris group is the primary extensor of the knee joint. During a seated leg raise, concentric contraction of the quadriceps produces knee extension, lifting the lower leg against gravity. Controlled relaxation (eccentric contraction) allows smooth lowering of the leg. This demonstration visualizes the functional role of the quadriceps in knee extension under open-chain conditions.VI. manual: Pepsin Activity Detection (Protein Digestion Method)I. Basic InformationSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: Demonstrate that pepsin digests protein under acidic and warm conditions by comparing an experimental tube with a control tube.II. MaterialsTwo identical test tubes, test tube rack, equal-sized protein samples (e.g., egg white or gelatin cubes), pepsin solution, dilute acidic solution (e.g., HCl, pH≈2), distilled water, warm water bath (≈37°C).III. Experimental Procedure1. Place one equal protein sample into each of two clean test tubes.2. To Tube A (experimental), add pepsin solution followed by acidic solution until the protein is just submerged.3. To Tube B (control), add an equal volume of distilled water.4. Place both tubes into a warm water bath and keep them warm.5. Gently shake both tubes intermittently.6. After heating for a period (shown by time-lapse), remove and compare the two tubes side by side.IV. Observation of PhenomenaInitial: Both tubes contain intact, solid protein pieces.After warming: Tube A shows protein softening, fragmentation, or partial dissolution; Tube B shows little or no change.V. Experimental PrinciplePepsin is a digestive enzyme that breaks down proteins into smaller peptides. It is active only in acidic conditions and works more efficiently at body temperature. Therefore, protein digestion occurs in the tube containing pepsin and acid when warmed, while the control tube without pepsin shows no significant digestion.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Tablet Disintegrant Effect (Starch vs No Disintegrant)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tablet Disintegrant Effect in Water2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of a starch disintegrant in promoting tablet disintegration in water by visually comparing a tablet containing starch disintegrant with a tablet without disintegrant.II. Experimental EquipmentClear glass bowls (2 identical), still water (room temperature), identical white tablets (one containing starch disintegrant, one without disintegrant), tweezers, flat stable table, camera or smartphone with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear bowls on a flat table and add the same volume of still water to each bowl. Allow the water to stand until completely motionless.2. Placement: Using tweezers, place the tablet containing starch disintegrant gently onto the water surface in the left bowl. Place the tablet without disintegrant gently onto the water surface in the right bowl at the same time.3. Recording: Fix the camera directly above or in front of the bowls, ensure both bowls are in frame, lock focus and exposure, and start time-lapse recording.4. Observation Period: Allow the tablets to remain undisturbed in water while recording until clear differences in tablet state are observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tablets are intact, white, and solid, resting in still water.2. During Experiment: The tablet with starch disintegrant absorbs water, swells, cracks, and gradually breaks into smaller fragments, dispersing into the water. The tablet without disintegrant shows minimal swelling and remains largely intact.3. Final State: The left bowl contains dispersed tablet fragments or cloudy suspension, while the right bowl still contains a mostly intact tablet.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesTablet disintegrants such as starch promote rapid tablet breakup by absorbing water and swelling. When exposed to water, starch particles expand, creating internal stress that causes the tablet to crack and disintegrate, increasing surface area for dissolution. Tablets without disintegrants lack this mechanism, so water penetration is slower and the tablet remains intact for a longer time.

Visibility constraints: both bowls must remain in frame with stable focus to verify left-right comparison and causal progression.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Phase-Contrast Time-Lapse Observation of Apoptosis in a Cultured Animal CellI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Phase-Contrast Time-Lapse Observation of Single-Cell Apoptosis2. Subject: Healthcare - Veterinary Medicine - Cell Biology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the morphological characteristics of apoptosis in an animal cell by continuously imaging a single isolated cell in a cultured monolayer under phase-contrast microscopy after apoptosis-inducing treatment.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsPhase-contrast inverted microscope with time-lapse imaging system, CO2 cell culture incubator, animal cell line (e.g., canine or murine fibroblasts), cell culture dishes suitable for microscopy, complete culture medium, apoptosis-inducing agent (e.g., staurosporine), micropipettes and sterile tips, biosafety cabinet.III. Experimental Procedure1. Cell Preparation: Culture animal cells in a microscopy-compatible dish until a subconfluent monolayer forms. Select a field containing a single well-isolated cell within the monolayer.2. Treatment: Add apoptosis-inducing agent to the culture medium at the recommended concentration, gently mixing to avoid disturbing cell position.3. Imaging Setup: Place the dish on the phase-contrast microscope equipped with environmental control. Focus on the selected isolated cell and fix the field of view.4. Time-Lapse Imaging: Start continuous phase-contrast imaging immediately after treatment. Acquire images at regular intervals, using accelerated playback to fit the total process within a short observation time.5. Completion: Stop imaging once the target cell has fully fragmented into apoptotic bodies. Save image sequences for analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The isolated cell appears flat and adherent with a clear outline under phase-contrast, similar to neighboring cells.2. Early Apoptosis: After treatment, the cell gradually shrinks, becomes more refractile, and shows membrane blebbing.3. Late Apoptosis: The cell fragments into multiple small, round, membrane-bound apoptotic bodies while neighboring cells remain largely unchanged.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesApoptosis is a programmed cell death process regulated by intracellular signaling pathways, including caspase activation. Upon exposure to apoptosis-inducing agents, cells undergo characteristic morphological changes: cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, and fragmentation into apoptotic bodies. Phase-contrast microscopy enhances visualization of these structural changes without staining, enabling continuous live-cell observation in veterinary cell biology research.VI. Experimental PrecautionsMaintain sterile conditions, avoid mechanical disturbance during imaging, and ensure constant environmental control to prevent non-apoptotic cell death.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: apoptosis observed as orderly morphological changes in a single cultured animal cell under phase-contrast microscopy. Minimum assumptions: cells are viable at start, apoptosis is chemically induced, and phase-contrast imaging is used without labeling. Phased storyline: baseline adherent cell in monolayer; post-treatment onset of shrinkage and increased refractivity; membrane blebbing; final fragmentation into apoptotic bodies. Verification requires a fixed field of view, continuous time-lapse, and clear visualization of one isolated cell distinct from neighbors.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Diffusion Comparison of Liposome-Encapsulated Dye and Free Dye in WaterSubject: Healthcare – PharmacyObjective: To visually compare diffusion behaviors of liposome-encapsulated blue dye and free blue dye in water, and understand how liposomal membranes modulate molecular diffusion.II. Materials and EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers (250 mL); distilled water (200 mL per beaker, still); liposome-encapsulated blue dye solution; free blue dye solution (same dye concentration); two droppers or micropipettes; stable flat surface; camera or smartphone with tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass beakers side by side on a flat surface. Add equal volumes of still distilled water to each beaker and allow the water to settle completely.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers, ensuring both beakers are fully in frame. Fix focus, exposure, and framing. Enable time-lapse recording.3. Simultaneous Addition: Using separate droppers, add an equal volume of liposome-encapsulated blue dye to the center of the left beaker and free blue dye to the center of the right beaker at the same time, without stirring.4. Recording: Continue time-lapse recording as the dyes diffuse naturally in the still water.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear diffusion differences are observed. Dispose of solutions according to laboratory guidelines and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless, still water.Early Stage: The free blue dye in the right beaker rapidly spreads outward and downward, forming diffuse blue gradients. The encapsulated dye in the left beaker remains more localized.Later Stage: The right beaker becomes uniformly blue relatively quickly, while the left beaker shows slower, limited diffusion with visible concentrated regions.V. Experimental Principle SummaryFree dye molecules diffuse rapidly in water due to direct molecular motion driven by concentration gradients. In contrast, liposome-encapsulated dye is enclosed within phospholipid bilayer vesicles, which restrict immediate dye release and slow effective diffusion. This demonstrates how liposomes act as controlled-release carriers in pharmaceutical drug delivery.VI. PrecautionsEnsure water remains still; avoid shaking or stirring. Use identical volumes and concentrations. Maintain fixed camera focus to ensure valid time-lapse comparison.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Dissolution Comparison of Sustained-Release vs Immediate-Release TabletsSubject: Healthcare – PharmacyObjective: To visually compare the dissolution behaviors of sustained-release and immediate-release tablets using blue food dye in water, and to understand controlled drug release principles.II. Experimental EquipmentTwo identical clear glass beakers; still water at room temperature; one blue-dye sustained-release tablet; one blue-dye immediate-release tablet; tweezers; camera or smartphone with tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear glass beakers side by side on a stable surface. Add equal volumes of still water to each beaker. Label the left beaker as sustained-release and the right as immediate-release.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing both beakers. Lock focus and exposure to avoid changes during recording. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.3. Core Operation: Using tweezers, simultaneously drop the sustained-release tablet into the left beaker and the immediate-release tablet into the right beaker. Do not stir.4. Observation: Observe the tablets and water over several minutes (or accelerated time-lapse), focusing on the rate and pattern of blue dye release.5. Completion: Stop recording after clear differences are visible. Dispose of solutions properly and clean equipment.IV. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Dissolution of Crystalline Sugar vs. Amorphous Sugar Glass in WaterI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Comparison of Dissolution Behavior of Crystalline Sugar and Sugar Glass in WaterSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Physical Pharmacy / Solid-State Properties)Experiment Objective: To visually compare the dissolution rates of crystalline sugar and amorphous sugar glass in water, and to understand how solid-state structure affects dissolution behavior.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsClear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 250 mL each), room-temperature distilled water, crystalline sugar (granulated sucrose), sugar glass shards (amorphous sucrose), glass stirring rods (2), camera with fixed focus and tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat surface. Add an equal volume of room-temperature water to each beaker.2. Camera Setup: Position the camera directly in front of the beakers, ensure both beakers are fully in frame, fix the focus, and start time-lapse recording.3. Addition of Solids: Simultaneously add an equal mass of crystalline sugar into the left beaker and sugar glass shards into the right beaker.4. Stirring: Gently stir each beaker with identical motion and speed using separate stirring rods for a short, equal duration.5. Observation: Stop stirring and allow dissolution to proceed while continuing time-lapse recording until a clear difference is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both beakers contain clear, colorless water with visible solid sugar at the bottom.During Dissolution: Sugar glass shards in the right beaker rapidly soften and dissolve, dispersing into solution; crystalline sugar in the left beaker dissolves more slowly, with granules remaining visible for a longer time.Final State: The solution containing sugar glass becomes uniform earlier than the solution containing crystalline sugar.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCrystalline sugar has an ordered lattice structure with lower free energy, requiring more time for water molecules to disrupt the crystal lattice. Sugar glass is an amorphous solid with a disordered structure and higher free energy, allowing water to penetrate and dissolve it more rapidly. This experiment demonstrates the influence of solid-state form on dissolution behavior, a key concept in physical pharmacy.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Gastric Acid pH Detection (Simulated Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Objective: To understand the acidity of gastric acid by using a pH test strip method, learn how to operate pH indicator strips correctly, and interpret acidity by comparing color changes with a standard pH chart.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean pH test strip flat on a clean, dry surface. Ensure the pH color chart is visible nearby.2. Liquid Application: Use a dropper to draw a small amount of simulated gastric juice.3. Core Operation: Hold the dropper above the test strip and gently release one drop of simulated gastric juice onto the center of the strip.4. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Immune Cell Apoptosis Detection (Annexin V Staining Simulation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology2. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the standard procedure and principle of detecting immune cell apoptosis using Annexin V staining and flow cytometry, and to recognize typical dot plot results.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentCultured immune cells (e.g., lymphocytes), centrifuge tubes, binding buffer, Annexin V staining reagent (fluorophore-labeled), pipettes and tips, flow cytometer with analysis software, timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Cell Preparation: Collect cultured immune cells into centrifuge tubes and centrifuge gently. Discard supernatant.2. Washing: Resuspend cells in binding buffer and centrifuge again to remove residual culture medium. Repeat once to ensure cells are in binding buffer.3. Staining: Resuspend cells in an appropriate volume of binding buffer. Add the recommended amount of Annexin V reagent.4. Mixing and Incubation: Gently mix by pipetting or flicking the tube. Incubate for a short time (about 10 minutes) at room temperature, protected from light.5. Data Acquisition: Load the stained cell suspension into the flow cytometer. Acquire data and generate dot plots showing fluorescence intensity.6. Imaging Note: Focus the image on the sample tube and cytometer interface; use time-lapse photography to compress incubation and acquisition steps.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before staining: Cells show no specific fluorescence signal.2. After Annexin V staining: A subset of cells displays increased fluorescence.3. Flow cytometry results: Dot plots separate cells into populations, with Annexin V-positive cells indicating apoptotic cells.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDuring early apoptosis, phosphatidylserine translocates from the inner to the outer leaflet of the cell membrane. Annexin V specifically binds to exposed phosphatidylserine in the presence of calcium. When Annexin V is conjugated to a fluorophore, apoptotic cells can be detected and quantified by flow cytometry based on fluorescence signals, allowing differentiation between viable and apoptotic immune cells.VI. PrecautionsHandle cells gently to avoid artificial apoptosis. Protect fluorescent reagents from light. Follow instrument operation guidelines.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pancreatic Juice pH Detection (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pancreatic Juice pH Detection Using pH Test Strips2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To determine the pH of pancreatic juice using a pH test strip, understand the alkaline nature of pancreatic juice, and master the standard操作流程 of pH detection by test strip comparison.II. Experimental EquipmentClean test tube (1), test tube rack, pancreatic juice sample (small volume), pH test strips (wide-range or alkaline range), standard pH color comparison chart, gloves and lab tissue.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the test tube rack. Wear gloves to ensure hygiene.2. Sample Addition: Pour a small volume (about 1–2 mL) of pancreatic juice into the test tube, ensuring the liquid is clear and uncontaminated.3. pH Strip Testing: Take one pH test strip and briefly dip its reactive end into the pancreatic juice for about 1 second. Do not soak for a long time.4. Removal: Remove the pH strip and gently shake off excess liquid without touching the reactive area.5. Comparison: Immediately compare the color of the pH strip with the standard pH color chart under good lighting.6. Recording: Identify and record the corresponding pH value. Dispose of used strips properly and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The pancreatic juice appears as a clear or slightly opalescent liquid in the test tube.2. After Dipping: The reactive area of the pH test strip changes color rapidly.3. Comparison Result: The color corresponds to a pH value typically around 7.5–8.5, indicating weak alkalinity.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPancreatic juice contains bicarbonate ions (HCO3−), which neutralize gastric acid entering the duodenum. The pH test strip contains acid–base indicators that change color depending on hydrogen ion concentration. When the strip contacts pancreatic juice, its alkaline pH causes the indicator to shift color, allowing pH estimation by comparison with a standard color chart.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh and uncontaminated pancreatic juice samples.2. Do not immerse the pH strip for too long to avoid inaccurate readings.3. Compare colors immediately after removal to prevent drying effects.4. Maintain cleanliness and proper disposal of biological materials.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Flame Test of Sodium Salt Producing Bright Yellow EmissionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Flame Test of Sodium Salt Producing Bright Yellow Emission2. Subject: Healthcare - Pharmacy3. Experiment Objective: To identify sodium ions by observing the characteristic bright yellow flame produced during a flame test, and to master the standard operation of flame testing using a Bunsen burner.II. Experimental EquipmentBunsen burner (with gas supply), platinum or nichrome wire loop, sodium salt solution (e.g., sodium chloride aqueous solution), concentrated hydrochloric acid (for cleaning the wire loop), beaker, dropper, safety goggles, camera mounted on a fixed stand for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Put on safety goggles. Ignite the Bunsen burner and adjust it to obtain a steady, non-luminous blue flame. Fix the camera focus and position to clearly capture the flame area.Cleaning the Wire Loop: Dip the wire loop into concentrated hydrochloric acid, then place it into the blue flame until no color is observed, ensuring the loop is clean.Dipping the Sample: Use a dropper to place a small amount of sodium salt solution into a beaker. Dip the cleaned wire loop into the sodium salt solution so that a thin film adheres to the loop.Flame Test Operation: Place the wire loop with sodium salt into the hottest part of the blue Bunsen burner flame while keeping the loop steady.Completion: After observing the flame color, remove the wire loop from the flame, turn off the burner, and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The Bunsen burner flame is steady and blue, and the clean wire loop produces no color.2. During the Flame Test: When the sodium-dipped wire loop is introduced into the flame, the flame immediately turns a bright, intense yellow.3. After Removal: The yellow color disappears once the wire loop is removed from the flame.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSodium ions, when heated in a flame, have their outer electrons excited to higher energy levels. As these electrons return to their ground state, they emit light at a characteristic wavelength (~589 nm), which appears as a bright yellow color. This emission is highly distinctive and forms the basis of the flame test for sodium identification.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the wire loop is thoroughly cleaned before testing to avoid contamination. Use a steady blue flame for accurate color observation. Keep flammable materials away from the burner and maintain a fixed camera focus throughout the experiment.

Minimum assumptions include a clean wire loop, presence of sodium salt, and a steady blue Bunsen burner flame.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 shows a stable blue flame and a clean wire loop with no color effect. Phase 2 shows the wire loop dipped into sodium salt solution. Phase 3 shows insertion into the flame, immediately causing a bright yellow emission. Phase 4 shows removal of the loop and disappearance of the yellow color. The camera remains fixed, with clear visibility of the flame region to verify causal transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lymphocyte Proliferation Assay (Simplified MTT Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lymphocyte Proliferation Assay (Simplified MTT Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate lymphocyte proliferation in response to a mitogen using the MTT colorimetric method; to master the basic operational sequence and understand the experimental principle.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents96-well culture plate; adjustable micropipettes with sterile tips; isolated lymphocyte suspension; complete culture medium; mitogen (e.g., PHA or ConA); MTT reagent; solubilization solution (e.g., DMSO or acidified isopropanol); CO2 incubator (37°C); plate shaker or gentle manual mixing.III. Experimental Procedure1. Cell Seeding: Using a pipette, add an equal volume of isolated lymphocyte suspension into designated wells of the culture plate.2. Mitogen Stimulation: Add mitogen solution to experimental wells; add medium only to control wells. Gently tap to mix.3. Incubation: Place the culture plate into a 37°C CO2 incubator and incubate briefly (time-lapse accelerated for demonstration).4. MTT Addition: Remove the plate and add MTT reagent to each well using a clean pipette.5. Second Incubation: Return the plate to the incubator to allow viable proliferating cells to reduce MTT to formazan.6. Solubilization: Add solubilization solution to each well; gently mix until the purple formazan crystals dissolve uniformly.7. Preparation for Measurement: Ensure homogeneous color in wells, ready for absorbance measurement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Cell suspension appears light and translucent in wells.2. After Mitogen and Incubation: No obvious color change; cells remain viable.3. After MTT Incubation: Purple precipitate appears in wells with proliferating lymphocytes; weaker color in controls.4. After Solubilization: Purple color becomes uniform and clear, suitable for optical density reading.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMTT is reduced by mitochondrial dehydrogenases in metabolically active lymphocytes to form insoluble purple formazan. Mitogen-stimulated lymphocyte proliferation increases metabolic activity, producing more formazan. After solubilization, the color intensity correlates with the degree of lymphocyte proliferation.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Magnetic Nanoparticle Dye Guided by External Magnet in Clear GelSubject: Healthcare - PharmacyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the magnetic responsiveness of magnetic nanoparticles and visualize how an external magnetic field can guide and concentrate drug-like carriers in a gel model simulating biological tissue.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent shallow dish or Petri dish; clear gel (agar or gelatin-based, colorless and transparent); magnetic nanoparticle dye (dark-colored, evenly dispersible); handheld permanent magnet; dropper or pipette; gloves and lab wipes.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the transparent dish on a stable, well-lit surface. Pour clear gel into the dish and allow it to set fully, ensuring transparency and a smooth surface.Dye Dispersion: Using a dropper, add several small drops of magnetic nanoparticle dye onto the gel surface. Gently spread or allow diffusion until the dye is evenly dispersed within or on the gel, forming a uniform light coloration.Core Operation: Hold the handheld magnet close to one outer side of the dish without touching the gel. Slowly move the magnet along that side in a horizontal direction, maintaining a constant distance from the dish wall.Observation: Continuously observe the gel from above or the side as the magnet moves. Track changes in dye distribution near the magnet-facing region.Completion: Stop magnet movement after clear aggregation is observed. Remove the magnet and note whether the dye remains localized or slowly redistributes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The gel is clear and transparent, with magnetic nanoparticle dye evenly dispersed and no visible clustering.During Magnet Movement: As the magnet approaches and moves along one side of the dish, the dye gradually migrates toward that side, forming a darker, concentrated band or region closest to the magnet.After Movement: The region near the magnet shows明显 enrichment of dye, while areas farther away become lighter.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMagnetic nanoparticle dyes contain particles that respond to external magnetic fields. manual: Complement-Mediated Hemolysis (Simulation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Complement-Mediated Hemolysis of Sheep Red Blood Cells (Simulation)2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the classical complement pathway by showing antibody-dependent hemolysis of sheep red blood cells, and to understand the role of antigen–antibody complexes and complement in immune-mediated cell lysis.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (3, clean, labeled), test tube rack, adjustable pipettes with tips, sheep red blood cell (SRBC) suspension (washed, 2–5%), specific anti-sheep RBC antibody (hemolysin), fresh serum as a complement source, physiological saline (optional control), timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place labeled test tubes on a rack and focus the camera on the tubes. Gently resuspend the sheep RBC suspension to ensure uniformity.2. Addition of Sheep RBCs: Using a pipette, add an equal volume of sheep RBC suspension to each test tube.3. Addition of Specific Antibody: Add the appropriate amount of anti-sheep RBC antibody to the test tube. Gently mix by tapping or slow pipette aspiration to avoid mechanical hemolysis.4. Addition of Complement: Add fresh serum to the mixture as the complement source. Mix gently and evenly.5. Incubation: Incubate the tube briefly at room temperature or 37°C. For demonstration purposes, use time-lapse or accelerated visualization.6. Observation Setup: Keep the tubes stationary in frame, ensuring clear visibility of color and clarity changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sheep RBC suspension appears uniformly turbid and red.2. After Antibody Addition: No obvious visual change; RBCs remain intact but sensitized by antibody binding.3. After Complement Addition and Incubation: The suspension becomes clearer, and the supernatant turns pink or red due to released hemoglobin, indicating hemolysis.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment demonstrates complement-mediated hemolysis via the classical pathway. Specific antibodies bind antigens on the surface of sheep RBCs, forming antigen–antibody complexes. Fresh serum provides active complement proteins, which are sequentially activated, leading to formation of the membrane attack complex (MAC). The MAC disrupts the RBC membrane, causing cell lysis and release of hemoglobin, producing visible hemolysis.VI. PrecautionsUse fresh serum to ensure complement activity; avoid vigorous mixing to prevent mechanical hemolysis; maintain clear labeling and correct sequence of reagent addition.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lactase Activity Detection (Lactose Fermentation Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lactase Activity Detection by Benedict Test2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Objective: To demonstrate lactase activity by comparing lactose breakdown in the presence and absence of lactase enzyme using Benedict reagent.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2), test tube rack, droppers, lactose solution, lactase enzyme solution, Benedict reagent, warm water bath (about 37°C), heating source (hot plate or alcohol lamp), test tube holder, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the rack. Use a dropper to add equal volumes of lactose solution into each tube.2. Enzyme Addition: Add several drops of lactase enzyme to Tube A (experimental tube). Do not add enzyme to Tube B (control).3. Incubation: Place both tubes into a warm water bath and incubate for a short time (time-lapse shown).4. Benedict Test: Remove tubes, add equal volumes of Benedict reagent to each tube using a dropper, and mix gently.5. Heating: Heat both tubes gently in a water bath or over a heating source until color changes appear.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both tubes are blue due to Benedict reagent.After Heating: Tube A changes from blue to green/yellow/orange or brick-red precipitate; Tube B remains blue or shows minimal change.V. PrecautionsEnsure equal volumes in both tubes; maintain moderate heating; handle hot test tubes with holders; dispose of waste properly.

Straight narrow channel molded or cut into the gelatin4. Small absorbent pad (e.g., filter paper or sponge piece)5. Food coloring (any bright color, e.g., red or blue)6. Dropper or pipette7. Paper towels (for cleanup)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage: Place the shallow tray containing the fully set, clear gelatin on a stable, well-lit surface. Ensure the gelatin channel is continuous from one end to the other and clearly visible. Confirm that a small absorbent pad is embedded midway along the channel and is in contact with the channel base.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record that the gelatin is transparent, the channel is empty of liquid, and the absorbent pad is dry and unchanged.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, carefully draw up a small amount of food coloring. Hold the dropper vertically above one end of the gelatin channel. Gently release a single drop of food coloring into the channel without disturbing the gelatin structure.4. Flow and Absorption: Allow the food coloring to move naturally along the channel under capillary action and diffusion. Do not tilt or shake the tray.5. Completion: Continue observing until the colored liquid reaches the absorbent pad and visible absorption occurs. Stop the experiment once the main phenomena are clearly observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The gelatin channel is clear and colorless; the absorbent pad appears dry and unchanged.2. During Flow: After the dye drop is released, the colored liquid slowly moves along the gelatin channel, forming a visible colored front.3. At the Absorbent Pad: When the dye reaches the embedded pad, the pad gradually takes up the color, becoming visibly stained. The flow of dye slows down or partially stops at the pad location, and the color intensity beyond the pad is reduced or delayed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates basic principles of diffusion and absorption relevant to pharmacy and healthcare. The gelatin simulates soft biological tissue or a delivery medium, allowing liquid to move through a confined pathway. The food coloring represents a dissolved substance (such as a drug solution). As the liquid moves through the channel, it spreads by diffusion and capillary action. When it encounters the absorbent pad, the pad acts as an absorption site, removing part of the liquid from the flow. This models how drugs or fluids can be absorbed by tissues or materials during delivery processes.VI. Experimental Notes and Precautions1. Ensure the gelatin is fully set before starting; soft gelatin may collapse and alter results.2. Use only a small drop of food coloring to maintain clear observation of flow and absorption.3. Avoid moving the tray during the experiment to prevent forced flow.4. Dispose of gelatin and absorbent materials according to local waste guidelines after the experiment.

Phase 2 – Action initiation: a single drop of colored dye is released at one end of the channel. Phase 3 – Transport: dye slowly advances along the channel in a continuous front. Phase 4 – Absorption: upon reaching the pad, dye visibly spreads into the pad, with flow slowing or diminishing beyond it. Visibility constraints: camera should clearly show the channel path and pad location from a top or slight oblique view to verify flow direction and absorption behavior.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Biceps Brachii ReflexI. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Biceps Brachii Tendon Reflex TestSubject: Healthcare – Human PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the biceps brachii reflex by eliciting forearm movement through tendon percussion and to understand the neural reflex arc involved.II. EquipmentReflex hammer; examination chair or stool; examiner’s thumb; adequate lighting for close-up observation.III. Experimental Procedure1. Subject Preparation: Seat the subject comfortably. Ask the subject to relax the upper limb.2. Positioning: Place the subject’s forearm on the thigh with the elbow flexed about 90 degrees, palm facing upward.3. Tendon Localization: The examiner palpates the biceps tendon in the elbow crease (antecubital fossa).4. Thumb Placement: Place the examiner’s thumb firmly over the biceps tendon.5. Stimulation: Using a reflex hammer, strike the examiner’s thumb once with a quick, controlled tap.6. Recording: Focus the camera on the elbow and forearm; use time-lapse or slow-motion emphasis to capture the immediate response.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Forearm relaxed, no visible movement.After Stimulation: Immediately after the hammer strike, the biceps muscle contracts, producing visible forearm flexion and/or slight supination.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe biceps brachii reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex. Percussion of the biceps tendon stretches muscle spindles, activating Ia afferent fibers that enter the spinal cord (C5–C6). These fibers synapse directly with alpha motor neurons, causing rapid contraction of the biceps muscle and resulting forearm movement.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the subject is relaxed; use a single, moderate strike; avoid repeated or excessive force; maintain clear visual focus on the tendon and forearm.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pupil Light Reflex (Bright Light)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Pupil Light Reflex under Bright LightSubject: Healthcare – Human PhysiologyObjective: To observe the pupil light reflex by examining pupil size changes when bright light is applied and removed, and to understand the neural regulation of pupil constriction and dilation.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld flashlight (steady white light), chair, neutral indoor lighting environment, camera or imaging device capable of focusing on one eye and capturing time-lapse images.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: The subject sits upright on a chair facing forward in a normally lit room. The observer positions the camera to focus clearly on one eye, ensuring the pupil is visible.Initial Observation: Observe and record the initial pupil size under normal lighting for a short period.Light Stimulation: Hold the flashlight to the side of the observed eye (not directly in front) and briefly shine bright light into the eye.Observation During Stimulation: Continuously observe and record the change in pupil size as the light is applied.Light Removal: Remove the flashlight and continue observing and recording the pupil as lighting returns to normal.Completion: Stop recording after the pupil size stabilizes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The pupil has a moderate diameter under normal lighting.During Bright Light: The pupil rapidly constricts, becoming noticeably smaller.After Light Removal: The pupil gradually dilates and returns toward its original size.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe pupil light reflex is an involuntary physiological response that regulates the amount of light entering the eye. Bright light stimulates photoreceptors in the retina, sending signals via the optic nerve to the midbrain. Motor signals then travel through the oculomotor nerve to the iris sphincter muscle, causing pupil constriction. When the light is removed, reduced stimulation leads to relaxation of the sphincter muscle and pupil dilation. This reflex protects the retina and optimizes visual sensitivity.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: the human pupil light reflex, requiring the assumptions that pupil size is controlled by involuntary neural pathways responding to light intensity and that bright light causes constriction. Phased storyline: (1) baseline observation of a stable pupil under normal light; (2) side-directed bright light applied causing rapid pupil constriction; (3) light removed leading to gradual pupil dilation. Verification requires a clear close-up of one eye, stable camera focus, visible timing of light application and removal, and unobstructed view of pupil size changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Salivary Amylase Activity Detection (Starch–Iodine Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Salivary Amylase Activity Detection (Starch–Iodine Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that salivary amylase can digest starch, and to understand the role of salivary amylase in carbohydrate digestion through a simple color-change reaction using iodine.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment- Test tubes (2, clean and dry)- Test tube rack- Dropper (several, or one cleaned between uses)- Starch solution (freshly prepared, colorless)- Fresh saliva (collected just before the experiment)- Distilled water- Iodine solution (yellow-brown)- Warm water bath or hand warming (approximately body temperature, 37°C)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes upright in a test tube rack. Using a dropper, add an equal volume (about 2 mL) of starch solution into each test tube.2. Labeling: Designate one test tube as Tube A (saliva) and the other as Tube B (control).3. Addition of Samples: Use a clean dropper to add a small amount of fresh saliva into Tube A. Use another clean dropper to add the same volume of distilled water into Tube B.4. Mixing and Incubation: Gently shake both test tubes to mix. Incubate the tubes briefly at approximately body temperature by placing them in a warm water bath or holding them in the hand for about 1–2 minutes.5. Iodine Test: After incubation, use a dropper to add iodine solution dropwise into Tube A and observe the color. Then add iodine solution dropwise into Tube B and observe the color.6. Observation and Recording: Compare the color changes in the two test tubes and record the results.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before adding iodine, both test tubes contain a colorless starch solution.2. Tube A (Starch + Saliva): After adding iodine, the solution shows little to no blue-black color and may remain yellow-brown or light in color.3. Tube B (Starch + Distilled Water): After adding iodine, the solution turns blue-black, indicating the presence of starch.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSalivary amylase is an enzyme that breaks down starch into smaller sugar molecules. In Tube A, salivary amylase digests the starch during incubation, so little or no starch remains to react with iodine. Therefore, no blue-black color appears. In Tube B, distilled water contains no enzyme, so starch is not digested and reacts with iodine to produce a blue-black color. This color difference demonstrates the digestive function of salivary amylase.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh saliva to ensure enzyme activity.2. Keep the temperature close to body temperature for optimal enzyme function.3. Do not mix droppers between solutions to avoid contamination.4. Observe color changes promptly after adding iodine.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Inactivated Vaccine Antigenicity Detection (Immunofluorescence Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Inactivated Vaccine Antigenicity Detection by Immunofluorescence2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To detect whether antigens in an inactivated vaccine retain antigenicity by observing specific antigen–antibody reactions using the immunofluorescence method, and to master the basic operation of slide handling, antibody addition, washing, and fluorescence microscope observation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsAntigen-coated glass slides (inactivated vaccine antigen fixed on slides), humidified incubation box, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), specific primary antibody against vaccine antigen, fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody (e.g., FITC-labeled anti-IgG), droppers or micropipettes, wash bottle, absorbent paper, fluorescence microscope, gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the antigen-coated glass slide on a clean, flat surface or slide rack. Label the slide clearly. Wear gloves.2. Primary Antibody Addition: Use a dropper to add an appropriate volume of specific primary antibody onto the antigen-coated area, ensuring even coverage. Place the slide in a humidified box and incubate for the required time.3. Washing: Remove the slide and gently rinse with PBS 2–3 times to remove unbound primary antibody. Blot excess liquid from the slide edge with absorbent paper.4. Secondary Antibody Addition: Add fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody onto the slide using a clean dropper. Incubate in the dark to protect fluorescence.5. Second Washing: Wash the slide again with PBS 2–3 times to remove unbound secondary antibody. Keep the slide protected from strong light.6. Observation: Place the slide on the fluorescence microscope stage. Turn on the light source, select the appropriate filter, focus gradually, and observe the fluorescence signal. Time-lapse or accelerated observation can be used to demonstrate focusing and signal appearance.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The slide appears non-fluorescent under the microscope before antibody reactions.2. After Immunoreaction: Under the fluorescence microscope, specific bright fluorescence is observed in areas where vaccine antigen is present.3. Control of Background: After proper washing, background fluorescence is weak or absent, and fluorescence is localized and clear.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe immunofluorescence method is based on the specific binding between antigen and antibody. The primary antibody specifically binds to the antigen in the inactivated vaccine fixed on the slide. A fluorescent-labeled secondary antibody then binds to the primary antibody. When excited by light of a specific wavelength in a fluorescence microscope, the fluorophore emits visible fluorescence. The presence and distribution of fluorescence indicate that the inactivated vaccine antigen retains antigenicity.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Paper Chromatography of Food Coloring DyesSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Analytical Methods)Objective: To demonstrate the separation of mixed food coloring dyes by paper chromatography, observe capillary-driven solvent movement and dye separation, and understand the principle of differential partition and adsorption.II. Experimental EquipmentFilter paper strips (rectangular, clean, dry), food coloring dyes (two or more colors), dropper or micropipette, pencil, transparent container or beaker, water (as mobile phase), clip or rod for suspension, camera fixed on tripod (for time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Cut a filter paper strip. Using a pencil, draw a light baseline about 1.5–2 cm from the bottom edge.2. Sample Application: Place small drops of different food coloring dyes on the baseline, spacing them apart. Allow drops to dry; repeat once if color is too light.3. Solvent Setup: Pour a small amount of water into the container so the depth is shallow (below the baseline level).4. Chromatography Development: Suspend the filter paper vertically in the container so the bottom edge touches the water while the dye spots remain above the water surface.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position; start time-lapse photography to capture the separation process.6. Completion: When the solvent front approaches the top, remove the paper and allow it to dry.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Colored spots remain at the baseline; filter paper is dry above the water.During Development: Water rises upward along the paper; dye spots move upward and gradually separate into different colored bands.Final State: Distinct color bands appear at different heights, with a visible solvent front above the bands.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPaper chromatography separates components of a mixture based on differential interactions between a stationary phase (filter paper) and a mobile phase (water). Water rises by capillary action, carrying dye molecules upward. Different dyes move at different rates due to varying solubility in the solvent and different adsorption strengths to the paper, resulting in spatial separation into colored bands.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Tollens’ Silver Mirror Reaction with an Aldehyde SolutionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tollens’ Silver Mirror Reaction with an Aldehyde Solution2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Pharmaceutical Chemistry)3. Experiment Objective: To verify the characteristic oxidation reaction of aldehydes using Tollens’ reagent through visual observation of the silver mirror phenomenon; to understand the redox principle of aldehydes reducing silver ions; to master correct handling of Tollens’ reagent, gentle water-bath heating, and standardized observation suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, dry, preferably new or well-polished), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, beaker (for water bath), hot plate or thermostatic water bath, thermometer (optional), glass rod or slow manual rotation by hand, Tollens’ reagent (freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution), colorless aldehyde solution (e.g., glucose or ethanal solution), distilled water, safety goggles, laboratory gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear safety goggles and gloves. Ensure the test tube is thoroughly cleaned and free of grease, as any contamination may prevent silver deposition. Place the test tube on the rack.2. Addition of Reagent: Using a dropper, add 2–3 mL of freshly prepared Tollens’ reagent into the test tube. The solution should be clear and colorless.3. Addition of Aldehyde: Add 1–2 mL of the colorless aldehyde solution into the same test tube. Gently swirl once to mix, avoiding splashing.4. Heating Operation: Place the test tube into a beaker containing warm water (approximately 50–60 °C). Gently warm the mixture; do not heat directly with a flame.5. Core Demonstration Operation: While warming, slowly and continuously rotate the test tube so that the solution evenly contacts the inner wall. Keep the camera focus fixed and stable for time-lapse photography.6. Completion: When a visible silver mirror or gray-black silver coating appears on the inner wall, remove the test tube from the water bath. Place it back on the rack for observation.7. Post-experiment Handling: Dispose of the reaction mixture according to silver-containing waste regulations. Clean the test tube promptly to avoid permanent silver staining.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The mixed solution in the test tube is colorless and transparent, with no precipitate or turbidity.2. During Heating: As the test tube is gently warmed and rotated, a shiny metallic silver layer gradually forms on the inner wall of the test tube.3. Final State: A continuous silver mirror or evenly distributed silver coating is clearly visible, while the solution may remain mostly clear or slightly darkened.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the redox reaction between aldehydes and Tollens’ reagent. Tollens’ reagent contains the diamminesilver(I) complex [Ag(NH3)2]+, which acts as a mild oxidizing agent. Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylates under alkaline conditions, while silver(I) ions are reduced to metallic silver.Core reaction principle: R–CHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3OH− → R–COO− + 2Ag↓ + 4NH3 + 2H2OThe reduced metallic silver deposits on the inner surface of the test tube, forming the characteristic silver mirror. This reaction is a classic qualitative test for aldehyde functional groups and is widely used in pharmaceutical and organic chemistry analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Tollens’ reagent must be freshly prepared and should not be stored, as it may form explosive by-products upon standing.2. The test tube must be clean and grease-free to ensure uniform silver deposition.3. Heating should be gentle and carried out in a water bath to prevent decomposition of the reagent.4. Silver-containing waste must be collected and disposed of according to laboratory safety regulations.

(2) Activation phase: test tube placed in warm water bath, gently rotated; no immediate visual change. (3) Reaction phase: gradual appearance of gray to shiny metallic silver on inner wall, spreading evenly due to rotation. (4) Completion phase: stable silver mirror visible; camera remains fixed to allow time-lapse verification. Visibility constraints: inner wall of test tube must remain in focus; lighting should allow reflection of metallic silver for clear verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Immune Complex Detection (PEG Precipitation Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Immune Complex Detection by Polyethylene Glycol (PEG) Precipitation Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the standard operational procedure for detecting immune complexes in patient serum using the PEG precipitation method. Emphasis is placed on correct labeling of test tubes, accurate pipetting, gentle mixing, and orderly procedural flow. The demonstration focuses on operation only and does not present final diagnostic results.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Clean test tubes (2–3, 10–15 mL capacity)2. Test tube rack3. Micropipettes (100–1000 µL) with sterile tips4. Patient serum sample (clear, non-hemolyzed)5. Specific antigen solution (corresponding to suspected immune complex)6. Polyethylene glycol (PEG) solution (commonly 3–5% PEG 6000 or PEG 8000, prepared in buffer)7. Dropper or micropipette for PEG addition8. Disposable gloves and lab coatIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation and Labeling: Place clean test tubes on the test tube rack and label them clearly according to sample identity. Put on gloves and ensure the work area is clean and organized.2. Addition of Patient Serum: Using a micropipette, aspirate the required volume of patient serum (e.g., 200 µL) and dispense it into the labeled test tube. Avoid creating bubbles and keep the pipette tip from touching the tube wall.3. Addition of Specific Antigen Solution: Using a fresh pipette tip, add an equal or specified volume of the specific antigen solution into the same test tube containing the serum.4. Gentle Mixing: Mix the serum and antigen solution by gently tapping the tube or slowly inverting it once or twice. Do not vortex or shake vigorously.5. Addition of PEG Solution: Using a dropper or micropipette, add PEG solution dropwise along the inner wall of the test tube while holding the tube at a slight angle.6. Secondary Mixing: After PEG addition, gently invert the test tube several times to ensure uniform mixing.7. Standing Period: Place the test tube upright in the rack and allow it to stand undisturbed for a short, defined time (e.g., a few minutes) to allow immune complex precipitation to occur.8. Demonstration Endpoint: End the demonstration without showing or interpreting the final precipitation result. Maintain focus on tube handling, pipetting accuracy, and procedural order.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena (Descriptive, Not Displayed)1. Initial State: Serum and antigen solutions are clear and transparent liquids.2. During PEG Addition and Standing: PEG promotes aggregation of immune complexes. In a real test, turbidity or fine precipitate may gradually appear, but this demonstration does not emphasize or display final outcomes.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe PEG precipitation method is based on immunological antigen–antibody reactions. When specific antigens bind to corresponding antibodies in patient serum, immune complexes are formed. Polyethylene glycol reduces protein solubility by excluding solvent, thereby promoting aggregation and precipitation of immune complexes. The presence of precipitable complexes reflects antigen–antibody interaction, which forms the theoretical basis of immune complex detection.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use clear, non-hemolyzed serum to avoid interference.2. Add PEG solution slowly and mix gently to prevent false aggregation.3. Maintain consistent volumes and standardized timing.4. Dispose of biological materials according to biosafety regulations.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Salivary Amylase Activity Detection (Starch-Iodine Method)Subject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate that salivary amylase can digest starch by comparing the iodine reaction of starch with saliva versus a control, and to understand the role of enzymes in digestion.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2), test tube rack, droppers, starch solution (1%), fresh saliva, distilled water, iodine solution, warm water bath or body-temperature environment (about 37°C).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes in a rack. Using a dropper, add an equal volume (about 2–3 mL) of starch solution into each test tube.2. Experimental Setup: Add fresh saliva (about 1 mL) to the first test tube using a dropper. Add the same volume of distilled water to the second test tube as a control.3. Incubation: Gently mix both tubes and incubate them briefly at body temperature (approximately 1–2 minutes) to allow enzymatic reaction.4. Detection: Using a clean dropper, add iodine solution dropwise to each test tube.5. Observation: Place the tubes side by side and observe the color changes.6. Cleanup: Dispose of solutions properly and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both tubes contain colorless, transparent starch solution.After Iodine Addition:- Control tube (starch + distilled water): turns blue-black, indicating the presence of starch.- Experimental tube (starch + saliva): remains yellow-brown or shows a much lighter color, indicating starch has been digested.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSalivary amylase is a digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into smaller sugar molecules such as maltose. Iodine reacts specifically with intact starch to produce a blue-black color. In the control tube, starch remains intact and reacts with iodine. In the saliva tube, salivary amylase digests the starch during incubation, so iodine cannot produce the blue-black color. This color difference demonstrates the activity of salivary amylase in carbohydrate digestion.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse fresh saliva for reliable enzyme activity. Ensure equal volumes in both tubes. Do not add iodine before incubation. Observe color changes promptly under good lighting.

manual: Intestinal Lipase Activity Detection (Fat Hydrolysis Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Intestinal Lipase Activity Detection by Fat Hydrolysis2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the hydrolytic activity of intestinal lipase on lipids by comparing an active enzyme tube with an inactivated enzyme control under near-physiological temperature conditions.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tubes (2), test tube rack, lipid substrate (milk or lipid emulsion), buffer solution (pH ~8), intestinal lipase solution, heat-inactivated lipase solution, pH indicator (phenolphthalein), warm water bath (approximately 37°C), dropper, timer.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Label two test tubes as Experimental and Control. Add equal volumes of lipid substrate and buffer to each tube. Add 1–2 drops of phenolphthalein indicator; solutions appear light pink.2. Enzyme Addition: Add intestinal lipase solution to the Experimental tube. Add an equal volume of inactivated lipase to the Control tube.3. Incubation: Place both tubes in a warm water bath near body temperature (about 37°C).4. Mixing: Gently remove and mix the tubes at regular intervals to ensure uniform reaction, then return them to the water bath.5. Reaction Termination and Comparison: After a short, accelerated incubation (for demonstration), remove tubes and visually compare the color changes.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both tubes show a uniform pink color due to alkaline buffer and indicator.During Incubation: The Experimental tube gradually loses pink color, becoming colorless as fatty acids are released; the Control tube remains pink.Final Comparison: A clear contrast is visible between the colorless Experimental tube and unchanged Control tube.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIntestinal lipase catalyzes the hydrolysis of triglycerides into fatty acids and glycerol. The released fatty acids lower the pH of the solution, causing phenolphthalein to change from pink (alkaline) to colorless. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Pupillary Accommodation Reflex (Near Object)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of the Pupillary Accommodation Reflex During Near Focusing2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology3. Knowledge Point: Pupillary accommodation reflex (near object)4. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the pupillary accommodation reflex when shifting gaze from a distant object to a near object, and to relate pupil size changes to the physiological mechanism of near vision.II. Experimental Equipment and Conditions1. Subject: One healthy adult with normal vision2. Objects: One distant visual target (e.g., mark on wall) and one finger or small object held near the eyes (about 10–15 cm)3. Recording Equipment: Camera capable of focusing on the eyes, preferably with time-lapse or high-frame-rate recording4. Environment: Quiet indoor setting, neutral lighting, no distracting backgroundIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits upright, head stable, eyes open naturally. Ensure lighting is even and the camera is focused clearly on both eyes.2. Distant Gaze: The subject is instructed to look steadily at the distant target for 2–3 seconds, keeping the eyes relaxed.3. Gaze Shift: On cue, the subject quickly shifts gaze from the distant target to the finger held close to the eyes.4. Near Focusing: The subject maintains fixation on the near finger for 2–3 seconds while the camera continuously records eye movement and pupil size.5. Completion: Recording stops after the pupil response is clearly observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: While looking at the distant target, the pupils appear relatively larger and stable.2. During Gaze Shift: The eyeballs move inward toward the near object (convergence).3. Near Focus State: Shortly after focusing on the near finger, the pupils visibly constrict (become smaller).4. Stability: The constricted pupil size remains relatively stable while near fixation is maintained.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe pupillary accommodation reflex is part of the near response triad, which includes lens accommodation, pupillary constriction, and ocular convergence. When viewing a near object, parasympathetic fibers from the oculomotor nerve stimulate the sphincter pupillae muscle, causing pupil constriction. This reduces light scattering and increases depth of focus, allowing clearer near vision. The observed pupil constriction following the gaze shift demonstrates this reflex and reflects normal autonomic control of the eye.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Pupillary accommodation reflex during near vision, requiring only the assumption that near focusing activates parasympathetic pathways causing pupil constriction and eye convergence.Mechanistic Assumptions: The subject has normal autonomic eye control; shifting gaze from far to near triggers the near response triad.Phased Storyline: Phase 1 – Stable distant fixation with relatively larger pupils. Phase 2 – Rapid gaze shift toward a nearby finger with visible eye convergence. Phase 3 – Observable pupil constriction shortly after near fixation. Visibility Constraint: Camera must remain tightly focused on the eyes to verify pupil size change and gaze direction within a short, continuous time window.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pepsin Activity Detection (Protein Digestion Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pepsin Activity Detection by Protein Digestion2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that pepsin can digest protein effectively only under acidic and warm conditions by comparing a pepsin-treated sample with a control sample.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTwo test tubes with rack; equal-sized protein samples (e.g., egg white or gelatin cubes); pepsin solution; dilute acidic solution (e.g., hydrochloric acid, weak acid level); distilled water; dropper; warm water bath or constant warm environment (about 37°C).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the rack. Put equal-sized protein samples into each test tube.2. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add pepsin solution together with the acidic solution into the first test tube until the protein is submerged. Add an equal volume of water into the second test tube as a control.3. Heating: Place both test tubes into a warm water bath or warm environment and keep them at approximately body temperature.4. Shaking: During heating, gently shake both test tubes occasionally to ensure even contact between the protein and the liquid.5. Comparison: After heating for a period (time-lapse observation), remove the test tubes and place them side by side for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Protein samples in both test tubes are solid and similar in size and appearance.2. After Heating and Shaking: In the pepsin–acid test tube, the protein becomes softer, smaller, or partially dissolved, and the liquid may turn cloudy. In the water control tube, the protein shows little or no change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplePepsin is a digestive enzyme that breaks down proteins into smaller peptides. It is active only in an acidic environment and at warm temperatures similar to those in the human stomach. In this experiment, protein in the pepsin–acid tube is digested due to enzyme activity, while protein in the water tube remains mostly unchanged, demonstrating the specific conditions required for pepsin activity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Enteric-Coated Tablet vs Regular Tablet in Acidic LiquidI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Comparison of Enteric-Coated Tablet and Regular Tablet in Acidic Liquid2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the different behaviors of an enteric-coated tablet and a regular tablet in an acidic environment, and to understand the protective function of enteric coatings against gastric acid.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear glass beakers (2 identical beakers, 100–150 mL capacity)2. Colorless acidic liquid (simulated gastric acid, e.g., dilute hydrochloric acid or vinegar)3. Enteric-coated tablet (smooth, glossy surface)4. Regular tablet (chalky, matte surface)5. Camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording)6. Labels or marker (optional, to distinguish beakers)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear beakers side by side on a flat, well-lit surface. Pour equal volumes of colorless acidic liquid into each beaker.2. Tablet Placement: Gently place the smooth glossy enteric-coated tablet into the left beaker and the chalky matte regular tablet into the right beaker at the same time.3. Recording Setup: Fix the camera position and focus so that both beakers are fully visible. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.4. Soaking Observation: Allow both tablets to soak without disturbance. Do not stir or move the beakers.5. Completion: After clear differences are observed, stop recording and document the final states of both tablets.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both liquids are colorless and transparent; tablets are intact at the bottom of each beaker.2. During Soaking: The regular tablet gradually absorbs liquid, swells, and disintegrates, causing cloudiness or particles in the solution. The enteric-coated tablet remains intact with little to no visible change.3. Final State: The beaker with the regular tablet shows significant dissolution or dispersion, while the enteric-coated tablet largely maintains its original shape and smooth surface.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesEnteric-coated tablets are designed with a polymer coating that resists dissolution in acidic environments like the stomach but dissolves in neutral or alkaline conditions in the intestine. Regular tablets lack this protective coating and therefore dissolve readily in acid. This experiment visually demonstrates how enteric coatings protect drugs from gastric acid and prevent premature release.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both beakers and liquid volumes are identical to maintain experimental fairness.2. Use a mild, safe acidic liquid for demonstration purposes.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Plexus ReflexI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Plexus Reflex by Light Mechanical Stimulation2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe a plexus reflex by lightly tapping the skin over a nerve plexus area, understand reflex characteristics (rapid, involuntary), and master correct hand position, tapping technique, and observation of immediate limb response.II. Experimental EquipmentReflex hammer (standard rubber head), chair for subject, clear exposure of the tested area (e.g., supraclavicular/brachial plexus region), camera for focused time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits comfortably and relaxed on a chair with the tested limb naturally supported. Expose the skin over the selected nerve plexus area. Hand Position: The examiner holds the reflex hammer loosely between thumb and fingers, allowing the hammer head to swing freely by wrist motion.3. Core Operation: Lightly tap the skin over the nerve plexus area once using a quick, controlled wrist movement. Avoid excessive force.4. Observation: Immediately observe the tested limb for involuntary movement (brief contraction, twitch, or slight lift). manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Scratch Reflex (Frog Simulation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Scratch Reflex in a Spinal Frog2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology (Neurophysiology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the spinal scratch reflex by applying a tactile stimulus to a spinal frog’s flank and observing the hind limb scratching movement toward the stimulated site, thereby understanding basic spinal reflex mechanisms.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentSpinal frog (brain destroyed, spinal cord intact), flat experimental board, blunt probe (rounded tip), forceps or gloves (for handling), adequate lighting, camera for focused time-lapse recording (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the spinal frog in a prone position on a flat board, ensuring the body is stable and limbs are relaxed.2. Positioning: Adjust lighting and camera to focus on the frog’s trunk and hind limbs; ensure the operator’s hand is visible.3. Stimulation: Using a blunt probe, lightly touch the skin of the frog’s flank on one side without causing injury.4. Observation: Maintain the stimulus briefly and observe the hind limb on the same side.5. Recording: Use time-lapse or accelerated recording to clearly show stimulus application followed by limb movement.6. Completion: Remove the probe and continue observing until the scratching movement ceases.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The frog remains still with no voluntary movement.2. After Stimulation: The hind limb on the stimulated side lifts and performs a scratching movement directed toward the touched flank.3. Repeatability: Reapplication of the stimulus produces a similar scratching response.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe scratch reflex is a spinal reflex mediated by sensory receptors in the skin, afferent neurons, interneurons in the spinal cord, and efferent motor neurons. In a spinal frog, the brain is not involved; the tactile stimulus to the flank activates sensory neurons, which transmit impulses to the spinal cord. Through interneuronal processing, motor neurons are activated, causing coordinated contraction of hind limb muscles to scratch toward the stimulus. This demonstrates that basic reflexes can be integrated at the spinal level.VI. Precautions1. Use only a blunt probe and apply light touch to avoid tissue damage.2. Ensure the frog is a proper spinal preparation.3. Keep the frog moist and the environment calm to avoid confounding movements.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: B Lymphocyte Detection by Surface Antibody Staining MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of B Lymphocytes by Surface Antibody Staining2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To identify B lymphocytes in a cell suspension by using fluorescently labeled antibodies against B-cell surface markers, and to understand the basic principle and procedure of immunofluorescent surface staining.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Equipment: Micropipettes and tips, centrifuge, centrifuge tubes, vortex mixer (or gentle manual mixing), fluorescence microscope or flow cytometer.2. Reagents: Prepared single-cell suspension (e.g., peripheral blood mononuclear cells), fluorescently labeled anti-B-cell surface antibody (e.g., anti-CD19 or anti-CD20), staining buffer (PBS with serum or BSA).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a fixed volume of prepared cell suspension into a clean centrifuge tube.2. Antibody Staining: Add an appropriate amount of fluorescently labeled anti-B-cell surface antibody to the cell suspension.3. Mixing: Gently mix the tube by tapping or brief low-speed vortexing to ensure even antibody distribution.4. Incubation: Incubate the mixture for a short, defined period at room temperature or 4°C, protected from light.5. Washing: Add staining buffer, centrifuge to pellet cells, discard supernatant, and resuspend cells to remove unbound antibodies.6. Observation: Place the stained cells on a slide or into a flow cytometer sample tube and observe under a fluorescence microscope or analyze by flow cytometry.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The unstained cell suspension shows no specific fluorescence.2. After Staining and Washing: Under fluorescence observation, a subset of cells displays distinct fluorescent signals on their surface, while other cells remain non-fluorescent.3. Interpretation: Fluorescent cells correspond to B lymphocytes expressing the target surface antigen.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the specific binding of antibodies to antigens on the surface of B lymphocytes. Fluorescently labeled antibodies recognize B-cell surface markers and bind selectively. After washing away unbound antibodies, only B lymphocytes retain fluorescence, allowing their detection and identification using a fluorescence microscope or flow cytometer.VI. Precautions1. Protect fluorescent antibodies from light throughout the experiment.2. Mix gently to avoid cell damage.3. Ensure adequate washing to reduce background fluorescence.
