manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sucrase Activity Detection (Sucrose Hydrolysis Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sucrase Activity Detection by Sucrose Hydrolysis2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the enzymatic activity of sucrase by comparing sucrose hydrolysis in the presence of active sucrase versus heat-inactivated sucrase, and to detect the production of reducing sugars using Benedict reagent.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTwo clean test tubes and rack; sucrose solution; active sucrase solution; heat-inactivated sucrase solution; Benedict reagent; dropper or pipette; water bath maintained at 37°C; beaker or heating device for gentle heating; marker or labels; safety gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Label two test tubes as Tube A (active enzyme) and Tube B (control). Add equal volumes of sucrose solution to each tube.2. Enzyme Addition: Add active sucrase solution to Tube A. Add the same volume of heat-inactivated sucrase solution to Tube B.3. Incubation: Place both tubes into a 37°C water bath and incubate for a short, equal time (time-lapse may be used to accelerate this step).4. Detection Reaction: Remove the tubes and add an equal volume of Benedict reagent to each tube. Mix gently.5. Heating: Heat both tubes gently in a hot water bath or over a heating device until a color change is observed.6. Completion: Place tubes back on the rack for observation and comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: Both tubes appear blue after Benedict reagent addition.After heating: Tube A (active sucrase) changes color from blue to green, yellow, or orange, indicating the presence of reducing sugars. Tube B (control) remains blue or shows minimal change.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSucrase catalyzes the hydrolysis of sucrose into glucose and fructose, both reducing sugars. Benedict reagent reacts with reducing sugars under heating conditions to produce a color change. Active sucrase enables sucrose hydrolysis, resulting in a positive Benedict reaction, while heat-inactivated sucrase lacks enzymatic activity and does not produce reducing sugars.VI. PrecautionsEnsure equal volumes and consistent conditions for both tubes; maintain the water bath at approximately 37°C; heat Benedict reagent gently to avoid splashing; handle hot equipment with care.

Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect the presence and relative level of cholecystokinin (CCK) in a digestive fluid sample using a rapid test strip method, and to master standardized strip handling, timing, and result comparison.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Clearly label the sample tube with sample ID. Place the tube upright in the center of the frame.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper to add an appropriate volume of digestive fluid into the labeled tube. Avoid bubbles and splashing.3. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe CCK test strip is based on immunochromatographic principles. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Pupil Light Reflex in Dim LightI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pupil Light Reflex in Dim Light2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe the pupil light reflex under reduced lighting conditions, understand how ambient light intensity affects pupil size, and recognize the autonomic regulation of the eye.II. Experimental EquipmentCamera capable of close-up or macro recording, stable tripod, controllable room lighting (dimmer or switchable lights), chair for subject, neutral background.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Seat the subject comfortably facing forward. Ensure the subject remains relaxed and keeps one eye open throughout the experiment. Position the camera on a tripod and focus tightly on one eye, ensuring the pupil is clearly visible.Initial State: Set the room to normal lighting. Begin recording with the camera fixed and the subject maintaining a stable head and eye position.Core Operation: Gradually and smoothly reduce the room light intensity. Do not introduce any sudden flashes or external light sources. Maintain continuous recording as lighting decreases.Observation Phase: Continue recording as the lighting becomes dim. Ensure the eye remains open and the camera focus remains stable. Use time-lapse or accelerated capture if needed to fit within a short recording duration.Conclusion: Stop recording once pupil size stabilizes under dim light conditions. Restore normal lighting after recording ends.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Under normal lighting, the pupil appears relatively small.2. During Light Reduction: As the room light gradually dims, the pupil slowly and smoothly dilates.3. Final State: In dim light, the pupil reaches a noticeably larger diameter and stabilizes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe pupil light reflex is an involuntary physiological response controlled by the autonomic nervous system. When ambient light intensity decreases, fewer photons stimulate the retina. This response increases the amount of light entering the eye, helping maintain visual sensitivity in low-light conditions.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Effect of Cold Stimulation on VasoconstrictionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Effect of Cold Stimulation on Vasoconstriction in Human SkinSubject: Healthcare – Human PhysiologyObjective: To observe the effect of cold stimulation on peripheral blood vessels by comparing skin surface changes of a hand immersed in cold water with a hand kept at room temperature.II. Experimental MaterialsTransparent container, cold water (5–10°C), room-temperature environment, towel, camera or phone for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the container with cold water on a stable surface. Ensure both hands are dry and at room temperature. Start camera recording with a fixed focus on both hands.2. Initial Observation (Before): Hold both hands side by side above the container for several seconds. Observe and record normal skin color and surface appearance.3. Cold Stimulation (During): Slowly immerse one hand into the cold water while keeping the other hand exposed to room temperature. Maintain immersion for a short period (about 5–10 seconds).4. Removal and Recovery (After): Remove the immersed hand from the water and place it next to the control hand. Continue recording as skin color and surface gradually change.5. End: Stop recording, dry the immersed hand with a towel.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaBefore immersion: Both hands show similar skin color and surface appearance.During cold exposure: The immersed hand becomes paler or less red, with reduced surface blood flow; the control hand remains unchanged.After removal: The immersed hand gradually regains normal color as blood flow returns.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCold stimulation activates the sympathetic nervous system, causing peripheral blood vessels in the skin to constrict (vasoconstriction). manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Righting Reflex in CatsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Cat Righting Reflex2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology (Comparative Physiology)3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the righting reflex in cats by observing how a cat reorients its body during free fall to land on its feet, and to understand the neural and biomechanical principles underlying this reflex.II. Experimental Equipment1. Healthy, calm domestic cat accustomed to handling2. Soft padded landing surface (thick mat or mattress)3. Low platform or handler’s arms (height sufficient for brief descent, not exceeding safe limits)4. Video recording device with slow-motion capability5. Adequate lighting and unobstructed backgroundIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a soft padded mat on the ground. Ensure the environment is quiet and the cat is calm. Set the camera to record continuously, with an option for brief slow-motion playback.2. Initial Positioning: Gently hold the cat so that it is lying on its back (belly up), with the body relaxed and limbs free.3. Core Operation: Lift the cat to a safe, low height above the padded surface. Release support smoothly and simultaneously, allowing the cat to move naturally during descent.4. Recording: Capture the entire process in one continuous take. Apply brief slow motion or time-lapse emphasis during playback to highlight posture changes from descent to landing.5. Completion: Ensure the cat lands on the padded surface and immediately regains a stable standing posture. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Cat begins in a belly-up orientation.2. During Descent: The cat rotates its head first, followed by twisting of the spine; forelimbs and hindlimbs reposition to reorient the body.3. Landing: The cat completes reorientation and lands on its feet, absorbing impact with flexed limbs.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe righting reflex is an innate motor reflex in cats. Sensory input from the vestibular system and vision allows the cat to detect body orientation. Through rapid neural processing, the cat rotates its head, then uses spinal flexibility and angular momentum redistribution to realign the torso and limbs independently of overall body rotation. This enables a feet-first landing without violating conservation of angular momentum.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Perform only at a safe, low height with a soft landing surface.2. Handle the cat gently; stop immediately if the cat shows stress.3. Do not restrain limb movement during release.4. This experiment is for demonstration only and should not be repeated excessively.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Precipitation Caused by pH Shift (Acidification Method)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Precipitation of a Dissolved Compound Induced by pH ShiftSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Physical Pharmacy)Objective: To demonstrate that a dissolved compound can precipitate as a solid when environmental pH changes, and to observe precipitation induced by gradual acidification.II. Materials and ReagentsBeaker (100 mL), glass rod, dropper, camera or smartphone with fixed focus; sodium benzoate aqueous solution (clear and colorless); dilute hydrochloric acid solution (colorless).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean beaker on a stable surface. Pour an appropriate volume of clear sodium benzoate solution into the beaker. Ensure the solution is colorless and transparent.2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera focus and position directly facing the beaker to allow continuous time-lapse recording throughout the experiment.3. Core Operation: Insert a glass rod into the beaker and gently stir at a constant speed. Using a dropper, add dilute hydrochloric acid drop by drop into the solution while continuously stirring.4. Observation: Continue dropwise addition until visible changes occur. Maintain gentle stirring to ensure uniform pH distribution.5. Completion: Stop adding acid once a clear precipitation phenomenon is observed. Allow the mixture to stand briefly for observation, then stop recording.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial state: The solution in the beaker is clear, colorless, and transparent.During acid addition: Fine colorless solid particles gradually appear in the solution, increasing in number and forming a visible precipitate.Final state: A suspension or sediment of colorless solid is observed at the bottom or throughout the liquid.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment demonstrates precipitation caused by a pH shift. Sodium benzoate is soluble in water under neutral or slightly basic conditions. When acid is added, the pH decreases, converting benzoate ions into benzoic acid, which has low water solubility. Once the solution becomes supersaturated with benzoic acid, it precipitates as a solid. This principle is widely applied in pharmaceutical crystallization and drug purification processes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Leptin Detection by Colorimetric Method (ELISA)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Leptin Detection by Colorimetric Method (ELISA)2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic procedure of serum leptin detection using a colorimetric ELISA method, observe color development, and understand the immunological and enzymatic principles behind leptin quantification.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents96-well microplate pre-coated with anti-leptin capture antibody (or labeled reaction tubes), micropipettes with disposable tips, serum samples, leptin detection antibody (enzyme-linked), wash buffer, colorimetric substrate solution (e.g., TMB), stop solution (acidic), waste container, absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the labeled microplate on a flat surface; ensure all reagents are at room temperature.2. Sample Addition: Using a pipette, add a fixed volume of serum sample into the designated wells.3. Antibody Reaction: Add leptin detection antibody reagent into each well; gently tap to mix and allow binding.4. Washing: Discard liquid and wash wells with wash buffer several times to remove unbound substances.5. Substrate Addition: Add colorimetric substrate to each well; incubate briefly as color begins to develop.6. Reaction Termination: Add stop solution to each well to halt the enzymatic reaction.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Wells are colorless after washing.2. After Substrate Addition: Wells containing leptin gradually develop a blue color.3. After Stopping Reaction: The color changes to yellow and stabilizes, with deeper color indicating higher leptin concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Leptin in the serum specifically binds to antibodies immobilized on the microplate. An enzyme-linked detection antibody forms an immune complex. After washing away unbound components, the enzyme reacts with the added substrate to produce a colored product. The reaction is stopped chemically, and the final color intensity is proportional to the leptin concentration in the sample.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lactase Activity Detection (Lactose Fermentation Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lactase Activity Detection by Benedict Test2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the role of lactase in lactose digestion by comparing reducing sugar formation in lactose solutions with and without lactase enzyme, and to understand enzyme specificity and digestive physiology.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents- Test tubes (2, identical size), test tube rack- Droppers or pipettes (2–3)- Lactose solution (approximately 5%)- Lactase enzyme solution- Benedict reagent- Warm water bath (37–40°C)- Beaker or heating bath- Alcohol lamp or electric heater- Test tube holder or clampIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes on the rack and label them Tube A (Lactose + Lactase) and Tube B (Control: Lactose only).2. Add lactose solution: Using a dropper, add equal volumes (about 2–3 mL) of lactose solution to both test tubes.3. Enzyme addition: Add several drops of lactase enzyme to Tube A only. Do not add enzyme to Tube B.4. Mixing: Gently shake both tubes to mix contents evenly.5. Incubation: Place both test tubes into a warm water bath at approximately 37–40°C and incubate for a short time (time-lapse demonstration).6. Benedict test preparation: Remove the tubes from the water bath and add an equal volume of Benedict reagent to each tube.7. Heating: Gently heat both tubes in a hot water bath or over a heater, using a test tube holder, until color change occurs.8. Completion: Remove tubes from heat and place them back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial state: Both test tubes contain clear, colorless lactose solution.2. After incubation: No obvious visual difference is observed before Benedict reagent is added.3. After heating with Benedict reagent: Tube A (with lactase) changes color from blue to green, yellow, or orange with possible precipitate formation; Tube B (control) remains blue or shows minimal change.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLactose is a disaccharide that is not a reducing sugar detectable by Benedict reagent unless it is hydrolyzed. Lactase specifically catalyzes the hydrolysis of lactose into glucose and galactose, both of which are reducing sugars. During heating with Benedict reagent, these reducing sugars reduce Cu²⁺ ions to Cu₂O, producing a color change. The control tube lacks lactase, so lactose remains largely undigested and does not produce a significant Benedict-positive reaction. This experiment demonstrates enzyme specificity and the physiological role of lactase in digestion.VI. Experimental Precautions- Ensure equal volumes of solutions in both tubes for fair comparison.- Maintain warm, not boiling, conditions during incubation.- Heat gently during the Benedict test to avoid splashing or breakage.- Handle hot test tubes with a holder and follow laboratory safety rules.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescence of Quinine in Tonic Water under UV and Visible Light2. Subject: Healthcare - Pharmacy3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and compare the fluorescence behavior of quinine in tonic water when illuminated by ultraviolet (UV) light versus visible white light, and to understand the photophysical principle of fluorescence relevant to pharmaceutical analysis.II. Experimental Equipment1. Clear glass (transparent, colorless)2. Commercial tonic water containing quinine (fill glass to about 2/3 volume)3. Dark, non-reflective table or surface4. UV flashlight (long-wave UV, approximately 365 nm)5. White-light flashlight (ordinary LED flashlight)6. Camera or smartphone mounted on a fixed position (tripod recommended)7. Darkened room (or reduced ambient light)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   (1) Place the dark table in a room with low ambient light.   (2) Position the clear glass at the center of the table and pour tonic water until it is about 2/3 full.   (3) Fix the camera so that the glass and tabletop are fully visible and remain stationary throughout the experiment.2. UV Illumination:   (1) Turn off or minimize ambient lighting.   (2) Switch on the UV flashlight.   (3) Shine the UV flashlight steadily onto the glass of tonic water from the side or slightly above, avoiding camera movement.   (4) Maintain illumination for several seconds to allow clear observation.3. Visible Light Illumination:   (1) Turn off the UV flashlight.   (2) Without moving the camera or the glass, switch on the white-light flashlight.   (3) Shine the white-light flashlight onto the glass from a similar angle as the UV light.   (4) Observe and record the appearance of the tonic water.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Under low ambient light without illumination, the tonic water appears colorless and transparent.2. Under UV Light: When illuminated by the UV flashlight, the tonic water emits a clear blue to blue-white glow throughout the liquid, appearing significantly brighter than the surroundings.3. Under White Light: When illuminated by the white-light flashlight, the tonic water does not glow; it appears similar to ordinary clear liquid, only reflecting the white light without emission.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Quinine molecules dissolved in tonic water can absorb ultraviolet light and enter an excited electronic state.2. After excitation, quinine releases part of the absorbed energy as visible blue fluorescence when returning to the ground state.3. White visible light does not effectively excite quinine to produce fluorescence; therefore, no glow is observed under white-light illumination.4. This fluorescence phenomenon is widely applied in pharmacy and analytical chemistry for substance identification and qualitative analysis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the glass is clean and transparent to avoid interference with observation.2. Do not look directly into the UV flashlight to protect eyes.3. Keep camera position fixed to ensure valid visual comparison.4. Use tonic water that explicitly contains quinine, as non-quinine beverages will not fluoresce.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pancreatic Juice pH Detection (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pancreatic Juice pH Detection Using pH Test Strips2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To determine the pH of pancreatic juice using a pH test strip, observe its alkaline property, and understand the physiological significance of pancreatic secretion in digestion.II. Experimental EquipmentClean test tube (1), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, pancreatic juice sample (or simulated pancreatic juice), pH test strips (wide-range), standard pH color comparison chart, gloves (optional for hygiene).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Ensure the pH color chart is laid flat and clearly visible.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, transfer a small volume (about 2–3 mL) of pancreatic juice into the test tube.3. pH Testing: Hold a pH test strip and briefly dip one end into the pancreatic juice for 1–2 seconds.4. Removal: Remove the strip immediately and avoid shaking or wiping it.5. Comparison: Hold the reacted test strip next to the standard pH color chart and compare the color.6. Recording: Identify and note the corresponding pH value.7. Completion: Dispose of the used strip properly and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Comparing this color with a standard chart reveals the alkaline nature of pancreatic juice, reflecting its role in maintaining optimal pH for intestinal enzyme activity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Achilles Tendon Reflex (Standing Position)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Achilles Tendon Reflex Examination (Standing Position)2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe the Achilles tendon reflex in a standing subject, understand the basic operation of tendon reflex testing, and relate the observed movement to spinal reflex physiology.II. Experimental EquipmentReflex hammer (1); flat, stable floor surface; optional support (examiner hands or nearby support) to ensure subject safety.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ask the subject to stand upright with both feet flat on the floor. The subject slightly leans forward to relax the calf muscles. The examiner stands beside or behind the subject to provide support if needed.2. Positioning: Clearly expose and visually locate the Achilles tendon just above the heel at the back of the ankle. Ensure the lower legs and feet are fully visible.3. Core Operation: Using a reflex hammer, tap the Achilles tendon once with a quick, controlled motion. Avoid repeated or excessive force.4. Observation: Immediately observe the ankle and foot response following the tap.5. Completion: Allow the subject to return to a neutral standing posture and ensure balance is maintained.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject stands with feet flat and ankles relaxed, showing no movement.2. After Tapping: Immediately after the tendon is tapped, the foot shows a brief plantar flexion (downward movement) of the ankle.3. End State: The ankle quickly returns to its resting position after the reflex movement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Achilles tendon reflex is a stretch reflex mediated by the spinal cord. Tapping the Achilles tendon stretches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, activating muscle spindle receptors. Sensory impulses travel via afferent nerves to the spinal cord (primarily S1–S2 segments), where they synapse directly with motor neurons. The resulting efferent signal causes the calf muscles to contract, producing plantar flexion of the foot. This reflex demonstrates the integrity of the peripheral nerves, spinal cord segment, and neuromuscular junction.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the subject is supported to prevent loss of balance.2. Use a single, moderate tap to avoid discomfort or injury.3. The subject should remain relaxed; voluntary muscle contraction may reduce the reflex response.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Leptin Detection by Colorimetric MethodSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the basic procedure of leptin detection in serum using a colorimetric ELISA method, and to understand antigen–antibody specific binding and enzyme-catalyzed color development.II. Sample Addition: Use a pipette to add a fixed volume of serum sample into the labeled wells or tubes.3. Antibody Reaction: Add leptin antibody reagent into each well. Gently tap or briefly incubate to allow antigen–antibody binding.4. Washing: Discard liquid and wash wells several times with wash buffer to remove unbound substances.5. Color Development: Add colorimetric substrate to each well. Allow color to develop briefly (time-lapse accelerated).6. Stop Reaction: Add stop solution to each well to terminate the reaction.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Wells are colorless after washing.During Reaction: After adding substrate, wells gradually develop a blue color.After Stopping: Color changes to yellow after stop solution; deeper color indicates higher leptin concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the ELISA principle. Leptin in the serum specifically binds to immobilized anti-leptin antibodies. An enzyme-labeled antibody forms a complex with leptin. After washing, the added substrate is catalyzed by the enzyme to produce a colored product. PrecautionsAdd reagents accurately with pipettes, wash thoroughly between steps, and follow the correct sequence to ensure reliable results.

manual: Experiment Title: Blink Reflex Induced by AirflowSubject: Healthcare – Human PhysiologyI. Experiment ObjectiveTo observe and understand the human blink reflex triggered by a gentle airflow stimulus to the eye, and to relate the observed response to the protective reflex mechanisms of the nervous system.II. Experimental EquipmentHandheld air blower (manual bulb type), chair or stool, neutral indoor environment with adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits upright on a chair, keeps the head steady, and looks straight ahead with both eyes open.2. Positioning: The operator holds the handheld air blower at the side of one eye, approximately 5–10 cm away, ensuring it does not touch the eye or eyelashes.3. Core Operation: The operator briefly releases a gentle puff of air toward the exposed eye from the side.4. Observation: The subject’s eye response is observed immediately after the airflow.5. Completion: The airflow stops, and the subject relaxes and resumes a normal blinking pattern.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject’s eyes are open and stable, with no deliberate blinking.2. During Stimulation: When the gentle airflow reaches the eye, the eyelids rapidly and involuntarily close.3. After Stimulation: The eyelids reopen shortly after, returning to a normal resting state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe blink reflex is a protective, involuntary reflex controlled primarily by the trigeminal (sensory input from the eye surface) and facial (motor output to eyelid muscles) nerves. When airflow stimulates receptors on the cornea or conjunctiva, sensory signals are transmitted to the brainstem, which rapidly activates the orbicularis oculi muscles, causing the eyelids to close. This reflex helps protect the eye from potential injury or drying.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of the human blink reflex elicited by a non-contact airflow stimulus. Minimum assumptions: a healthy human subject, intact vision, and a gentle airflow sufficient to stimulate ocular surface receptors without causing discomfort.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – subject sits upright, looks forward, eye clearly visible; (2) Stimulation phase – handheld air blower approaches from the side and releases a brief airflow; (3) Response phase – immediate involuntary blink occurs; (4) Recovery phase – eye reopens and returns to rest. Key causal transition: airflow stimulus → sensory nerve activation → rapid eyelid closure. Visibility constraints: the eye, blower position, and eyelid movement must be clearly visible from a stable perspective to verify causality and sequence.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Intestinal Amylase Activity Detection (Starch–Iodine Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Intestinal Amylase Activity Detection Using the Starch–Iodine Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the activity of intestinal amylase on starch by comparing an enzyme-treated tube with a control tube, and to master standard operations such as tube labeling, liquid transfer, incubation, and indicator testing.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes (2), test tube rack, droppers or pipettes, starch solution, intestinal amylase solution, iodine solution, warm water bath or incubator (approximately 37°C).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean test tubes in a rack and label them clearly as Tube A (intestinal amylase) and Tube B (control).2. Addition of Substrate: Use a dropper to add an equal volume of starch solution into each test tube.3. Enzyme Treatment: Add a measured amount of intestinal amylase solution into Tube A only. Do not add enzyme to Tube B.4. Mixing: Gently shake or tap both tubes to ensure uniform mixing of the liquids.5. Incubation: Place both test tubes in a warm environment at approximately body temperature for a short period to allow enzymatic action.6. Indicator Addition: After incubation, add iodine solution dropwise to Tube A first, then to Tube B, observing the sequence of operations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes contain a uniform, colorless starch solution before iodine addition.2. After Incubation and Iodine Addition: The appearance of the solutions changes upon iodine addition, allowing comparison between the enzyme-treated tube and the control tube.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIntestinal amylase is a digestive enzyme that breaks down starch into smaller sugar molecules. Iodine reacts with intact starch to produce a characteristic color. By comparing an enzyme-treated tube with a control tube after iodine addition, the presence or absence of starch indicates whether enzymatic digestion has occurred, demonstrating intestinal amylase activity.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure accurate labeling to avoid confusing the enzyme tube and control tube.2. Use equal volumes of solutions to maintain experimental validity.3. Add iodine after incubation and in correct sequence.4. Handle iodine carefully to avoid staining skin or clothing.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of intestinal amylase activity using the starch–iodine method, emphasizing controlled comparison and correct experimental sequence. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: intestinal amylase digests starch at body temperature; iodine indicates remaining starch. Phased storyline: (1) clearly labeled test tubes with starch solution; (2) enzyme added to one tube only, gentle mixing; (3) brief incubation at body temperature shown via time-lapse; (4) iodine added sequentially to each tube for comparison. Visibility constraints: close-up framing on tubes, labels, droppers, and liquid changes; no verbal or textual result interpretation, only procedural display.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Grasping Reflex in Human NewbornsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Grasping Reflex in a Newborn Infant2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology (Neonatal Reflexes)3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the innate grasping reflex of a human newborn through gentle tactile stimulation of the palm.II. Experimental Equipment and Conditions1. Healthy newborn infant (resting, awake, calm).2. Adult experimenter with clean hands.3. Quiet, warm environment with soft lighting.4. Camera with close-up focus; time-lapse or slightly accelerated recording mode.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the infant is calm and lying comfortably. Wash hands and warm the adult’s index finger.2. Initial State Observation: Observe the infant’s hand in a relaxed, open position.3. Core Operation: Gently place the adult’s index finger horizontally into the infant’s open palm, lightly touching the center of the palm without applying force.4. Stimulation and Response: Maintain light contact and observe the infant’s hand response.5. Withdrawal: Slowly withdraw the finger while maintaining camera focus on the hand.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The infant’s palm is open or semi-open.2. Upon Stimulation: Immediately after the finger touches the center of the palm, the infant’s fingers flex and close around the finger.3. Maintenance Phase: The infant maintains the grasp briefly.4. Release Phase: As the finger is gradually withdrawn, the grasp weakens and the hand relaxes back to an open state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe grasping reflex is an innate neonatal reflex mediated by the spinal cord and brainstem. Light tactile stimulation of mechanoreceptors in the palm triggers an automatic flexion of the fingers. This reflex is present at birth, does not require conscious control, and gradually diminishes as higher cortical control develops.

Visibility constraints: close-up framing of hand and finger, stable lighting, clear view of contact point and finger flexion; time-lapse or accelerated pacing allowed while preserving event order.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Alcohol Disinfection Effect Detection (Bacterial Simulation Method)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Alcohol Disinfection Effect Detection (Bacterial Simulation Method)Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology & ImmunologyObjective: To visually demonstrate the disinfecting effect of 75% alcohol by comparing simulated bacterial growth on treated and untreated agar plates.II. MaterialsAgar plates (2, sterile), simulated bacteria solution or dye suspension, sterile cotton swabs, 75% alcohol, marker for labeling, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two agar plates on a clean bench and label them Control and Alcohol.2. Inoculation: Dip a sterile cotton swab into the simulated bacteria. Evenly swab the surface of both agar plates using the same pattern and pressure.3. Disinfection Treatment: Dip a new cotton swab into 75% alcohol. Gently swab the entire surface of the Alcohol plate only. Do not treat the Control plate.4. Closure: Close both plates promptly to avoid contamination.5. Observation Setup: Place plates side by side, keep camera focused on both plates, and use time-lapse or accelerated presentation to show comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both agar plates appear similar after inoculation.After Treatment: The Alcohol plate shows明显 reduction or absence of simulated bacterial growth, while the Control plate retains visible simulated growth.Comparison Result: A clear contrast is observed between treated and untreated plates.V. Experimental Principle Summary75% alcohol denatures proteins and disrupts cell membranes of microorganisms, leading to loss of structure and function. As a result, simulated bacteria on the treated agar plate are inactivated, while those on the untreated plate remain, demonstrating the disinfecting effect of alcohol.VI. PrecautionsUse separate swabs for inoculation and alcohol application; avoid touching agar surfaces with hands; ensure clear labeling and identical inoculation conditions.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the disinfecting effect of 75% alcohol on simulated bacteria using a controlled comparison of two agar plates. Minimum assumptions: alcohol inhibits microbial viability; identical inoculation ensures fair comparison.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase – two identical agar plates placed side by side and labeled; (2) Inoculation phase – both plates evenly swabbed with simulated bacteria; (3) Intervention phase – only one plate treated with 75% alcohol; (4) Outcome phase – plates closed and shown in comparison, with treated plate exhibiting reduced simulated growth. Visibility constraints: camera remains focused on plates, clear labeling, and side-by-side framing to verify causal contrast.

manual: Experiment Title: Demonstration of the Flexor ReflexSubject: Healthcare – Human PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the human flexor (withdrawal) reflex by applying a light cutaneous stimulus to a finger and observing the immediate involuntary withdrawal response and return to rest.Equipment and Materials: Table; chair; reflex hammer or blunt pin (non-sharp); camera capable of focused or time-lapse recording.Experimental Procedure: 1) Ask the subject to sit comfortably and relaxed on a chair with one forearm resting naturally on a table, palm down, fingers relaxed. 2) Ensure the subject is not actively tensing the hand and is looking away to reduce voluntary anticipation. 3) Using a reflex hammer or blunt pin, lightly and briefly stimulate the skin of one finger (no skin penetration). 4) Keep the camera focused on the hand to clearly capture the moment of stimulation, the immediate response, and the recovery. 5) After the response, allow the hand to relax and return to its resting position.Observation of Experimental Phenomena: Initial state: The hand and fingers are relaxed and motionless on the table. During stimulation: Immediately after the skin of the finger is stimulated, the finger and/or hand rapidly flexes and withdraws away from the stimulus. After response: The movement stops, and the hand gradually returns to a relaxed resting position on the table.Summary of Experimental Principle: The flexor reflex is a protective spinal reflex. Cutaneous receptors in the skin detect a potentially harmful stimulus and transmit sensory signals via afferent neurons to the spinal cord. Interneurons activate motor neurons supplying flexor muscles, causing rapid withdrawal of the stimulated body part. This response is involuntary, fast, and occurs without initial involvement of conscious brain processing, followed by muscle relaxation once the stimulus ends.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Human flexor (withdrawal) reflex. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a relaxed human subject, intact sensory receptors, a brief noxious or tactile cutaneous stimulus, and an involuntary spinal reflex arc producing flexion.Phased storyline: Phase 1 – Rest: subject seated, hand relaxed on table, no movement. Phase 2 – Stimulus: reflex hammer or blunt pin makes brief contact with finger skin (cause). Phase 3 – Immediate response: rapid finger/hand flexion and withdrawal away from stimulus (effect). Phase 4 – Recovery: movement ceases and hand returns to resting position. Visibility constraints: camera must stay focused on the hand and stimulus point, with clear temporal separation of phases; time-lapse or accelerated timing may be used but event order must remain intact.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Bacillus cereus Detection (Chromogenic Medium Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Bacillus cereus Using Chromogenic AgarSubject: Healthcare – Microbiology-ImmunologyObjective: To demonstrate aseptic inoculation of a prepared food sample onto Bacillus cereus chromogenic agar, incubation at 35–37°C, and observation of characteristic colony growth.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentBacillus cereus chromogenic agar plate (prepared), sterile inoculation loop, prepared food sample homogenate, alcohol lamp or equivalent sterilization source, incubator set at 35–37°C, biosafety workspace.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the chromogenic agar plate on a clean work surface. Maintain aseptic conditions throughout the procedure.2. Loop Sterilization: Heat the inoculation loop until sterile; allow it to cool without contacting non-sterile surfaces.3. Inoculation: Dip the cooled loop into the prepared food sample.4. Streaking: Gently streak the loop across the agar surface using a standard streaking method to disperse microorganisms.5. Plate Handling: Close the plate immediately after streaking to prevent contamination.6. Incubation: Invert the plate and place it in an incubator at 35–37°C.7. Observation: After incubation, remove the plate and observe colony growth on the agar surface.IV. Bacillus cereus colonies display characteristic colors specific to the chromogenic medium.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleChromogenic media contain substrates that react with specific enzymes produced by Bacillus cereus. Following aseptic inoculation and incubation under optimal temperature conditions, Bacillus cereus grows and metabolizes the chromogenic substrates, producing colonies with distinctive colors that allow visual detection and differentiation from other microorganisms.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Methylene Blue Staining (Yeast Observation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Methylene Blue Staining (Yeast Observation)2. Subject: Healthcare - Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To learn the basic method of staining yeast cells with methylene blue, correctly prepare a temporary slide, and observe yeast cell morphology under a light microscope from low to high magnification, including focusing and time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentLight microscope, clean glass slide, coverslip, dropper, yeast suspension (fresh yeast culture in water), methylene blue staining solution, absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Slide Preparation: Place a clean glass slide on the workbench. Using a dropper, add one small drop of yeast suspension to the center of the slide.2. Staining: Add exactly one drop of methylene blue stain into the yeast suspension on the slide and gently mix by touching the edge of the drop with the dropper tip.3. Coverslip Placement: Hold the coverslip at an angle and gently lower it onto the drop to avoid trapping air bubbles. Ensure the liquid spreads evenly under the coverslip.4. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the microscope stage. Observe first under low magnification to locate the stained area, then switch to high magnification to observe individual yeast cells.5. Focusing and Time-lapse Observation: Adjust coarse and fine focus knobs until yeast cells appear clear. Maintain focus and observe continuously for a short time, recording time-lapse changes if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Under low magnification, the stained area appears light blue, and clusters of small dots can be seen.2. Under high magnification, individual yeast cells are visible as round or oval structures, stained blue, with clear outlines against a lighter background.3. During time-lapse observation, yeast cells maintain stable shape and position, with no rapid movement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesMethylene blue is a basic dye that increases contrast between yeast cells and the surrounding medium. Yeast cells absorb the dye, making their morphology clearly visible under a light microscope. Proper slide preparation and focusing are essential to obtain clear microscopic images and accurately observe microbial structure.VI. PrecautionsUse only one drop of stain to avoid overstaining; avoid air bubbles when placing the coverslip; start observation with low magnification before switching to high magnification; handle the microscope gently.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment UV Sterilization Effect Detection (Microbial Culture Simulation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: UV Sterilization Effect Detection (Microbial Culture Simulation)2. Subject: Healthcare - Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the inhibitory effect of ultraviolet radiation on microbial growth by comparing a UV-exposed agar plate with a covered control plate, and to understand the basic principle of UV sterilization.II. Experimental EquipmentAgar culture plates (2 identical plates), microbial culture medium (pre-poured agar), sterile plate covers/lids, UV lamp, ruler or fixed spacer (to control distance), marker pen for labeling, incubation environment (simulated), camera for time-lapse photography, protective equipment (UV-protective goggles).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation Stage: Place two identical agar culture plates side by side on a clean bench. Label one plate Control and keep it covered with its lid. Label the other plate UV.UV Exposure: Remove the lid of the UV plate only. Position the UV lamp directly above the plate at a fixed distance (e.g., 30 cm). Turn on the UV lamp and expose the plate for a short, fixed time (e.g., 30 seconds). The control plate remains covered and unexposed.Closure and Labeling: After exposure, turn off the UV lamp, replace the lid on the UV plate, and ensure both plates are clearly labeled with group and date.Incubation: Place both plates in the same incubation environment. Set up time-lapse photography focusing on both plates to record changes during incubation.Conclusion: After the simulated incubation period, compare the microbial growth between the two plates.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both agar plates appear clear and similar, with no visible colonies.2. After Incubation: The control plate shows more microbial colonies or denser growth. The UV-exposed plate shows significantly fewer or no visible colonies.3. Comparative Result: A clear difference in microbial growth is observed between the two plates.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesUltraviolet light, especially UV-C, damages microbial DNA by causing thymine dimer formation, which interferes with DNA replication and transcription. As a result, exposed microorganisms lose viability or reproductive ability. Therefore, the agar plate exposed to UV shows reduced microbial growth compared to the covered control plate, demonstrating the sterilization effect of UV radiation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Avoid direct exposure of skin or eyes to UV light; always use protective equipment.2. Keep the UV exposure time and distance consistent to ensure fair comparison.3. Ensure the control plate remains fully covered throughout the experiment.4. Dispose of culture materials according to biosafety guidelines.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: UV sterilization reduces microbial viability by damaging DNA. Minimum assumptions: two identical agar plates, one serving as control, one receiving brief UV exposure at fixed distance.Phased storyline: (1) Static setup with two plates side by side; (2) Control plate remains covered while UV plate is exposed under lamp; (3) Plates are closed, labeled, and moved to incubation; (4) Accelerated time-lapse shows differential growth, with fewer colonies on UV plate. Visibility constraints: overhead or angled view showing plate surfaces clearly; UV lamp position and exposure implied visually; incubation time compressed while preserving chronological order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Mycobacterium tuberculosis Detection (Simplified Acid-Fast Staining)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by Simplified Acid-Fast StainingSubject: Healthcare – PathologyObjective: To demonstrate the preparation of a sputum smear and the simplified acid-fast staining procedure, observe acid-fast bacilli under a microscope, and understand the staining principle.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean glass slides, sputum sample, applicator stick or loop, alcohol lamp or slide warmer, carbol fuchsin solution, water, acid-alcohol decolorizer, methylene blue counterstain, staining rack, microscope (oil immersion), immersion oil, absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Smear Preparation: Place a small amount of sputum on the center of a clean glass slide and spread into a thin, even smear.2. Air-Drying and Heat-Fixing: Allow the smear to air-dry completely, then pass the slide gently through a flame 2–3 times to fix the specimen.3. Primary Staining: Place the slide on a staining rack and flood the smear with carbol fuchsin. Gently heat until steam rises (do not boil) and maintain for about 3–5 minutes, adding stain if needed to prevent drying.4. Rinsing: Rinse the slide gently with water to remove excess stain.5. Decolorization: Flood the slide with acid-alcohol for 1–2 minutes until no more red color runs off.6. Rinsing Again: Rinse thoroughly with water.7. Counterstaining: Flood the slide with methylene blue for about 1 minute.8. Final Washing and Drying: Rinse with water, blot dry with absorbent paper, and allow to air-dry.9. Microscopic Observation: Apply immersion oil and examine under oil immersion (100× objective), focusing the image. Time-lapse photography may be used to show the sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Smear appears colorless to pale.After Staining: Acid-fast bacilli appear bright red or pink against a blue background of non–acid-fast cells and debris.Microscopy: Slender, rod-shaped red bacilli are visible if Mycobacterium tuberculosis is present.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMycobacterium tuberculosis has a cell wall rich in mycolic acids, which retain carbol fuchsin dye even after decolorization with acid-alcohol. Non–acid-fast organisms lose the primary stain and take up the methylene blue counterstain. This differential staining allows identification of acid-fast bacilli under the microscope.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Simplified acid-fast staining for Mycobacterium tuberculosis detection. Minimum assumptions include a laboratory setting, correct reagents, and standard microscopy.Phased Storyline: (1) Preparation phase – sputum smear on slide, air-drying, heat-fixing; (2) Staining phase – carbol fuchsin application with gentle heating, followed by rinsing and decolorization; (3) Counterstaining phase – methylene blue application and washing; (4) Observation phase – dried slide examined under microscope showing red bacilli on blue background. Key causal transitions include heat-fixing enabling dye retention and acid-alcohol causing selective decolorization. Visibility requires close-up views of slide handling and microscopic field focusing.

manual: Instructions for Acid-Fast Staining (Mycobacterium Differentiation)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Acid-Fast Staining (Mycobacterium Differentiation)Subject: Healthcare – PathologyObjective: To master the Ziehl–Neelsen acid-fast staining method, observe acid-fast bacilli under oil-immersion microscopy, and understand the principle of acid-fastness.II. Materials and ReagentsClean glass slide, inoculating loop, bacterial culture smear (e.g., Mycobacterium), Bunsen burner or alcohol lamp, carbol fuchsin, acid-alcohol (decolorizer), methylene blue, distilled water, staining rack, bibulous paper, oil-immersion microscope.III. Experimental Procedure1. Smear Preparation: Prepare a thin bacterial smear on a clean slide, air-dry, and heat-fix by passing through flame.2. Primary Staining: Flood the slide with carbol fuchsin. Gently heat until steaming (do not boil) for about 3–5 minutes, keeping the stain moist.3. Rinsing: Rinse the slide gently with water to remove excess stain.4. Decolorization: Apply acid-alcohol until no more red color runs off. Immediately rinse with water.5. Counterstaining: Flood with methylene blue for 1 minute, then rinse with water.6. Drying: Blot dry with bibulous paper and air-dry completely.7. Observation: Add immersion oil and observe under an oil-immersion microscope; focus the image and record with time-lapse photography if required.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Smear appears uniformly stained red after carbol fuchsin.After Decolorization: Acid-fast organisms remain red; non–acid-fast cells become colorless.After Counterstain: Background cells appear blue, while acid-fast bacilli remain bright red against a blue background.V. Experimental Principle SummaryAcid-fast bacteria have cell walls rich in mycolic acids, which strongly bind carbol fuchsin when heated. Once stained, these cells resist decolorization by acid-alcohol, unlike non–acid-fast bacteria. Counterstaining with methylene blue provides contrast, enabling differentiation under microscopy.

Inoculation of Lactose Medium: Open the bacterial culture tube and lactose medium tube using proper test tube handling. Use the sterile loop to pick a small amount of bacteria and streak or inoculate the lactose medium. Flame tube mouths before and after inoculation.4. Incubation: Place the inoculated lactose medium into the incubator at 35–37°C. Use time-lapse representation to indicate incubation.5. Transfer to Citrate Medium: After incubation, sterilize the loop again. Transfer a small amount of growth from the lactose medium to the citrate medium using aseptic technique.6. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Identification of Gentamicin by Ninhydrin Color ReactionSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryObjective: To identify gentamicin by observing the characteristic color reaction with ninhydrin after heating, and to master the basic operations of weighing, dissolving, reagent addition, and water-bath heating.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsElectronic balance, weighing paper, gentamicin sulfate sample, test tube, test tube rack, dropper, distilled water, ninhydrin reagent, beaker (water bath), hot plate or heater, test tube holder.III. Experimental Procedure1. Weighing: Accurately weigh a small amount of gentamicin sample (about 5–10 mg) using an electronic balance and transfer it into a clean test tube.2. Dissolving: Add 1–2 mL of distilled water into the test tube and gently shake until the gentamicin dissolves to form a clear solution.3. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of ninhydrin reagent into the test tube and mix gently.4. Heating: Place the test tube into a hot water bath (about 90–100 °C) and heat for a short time. Use time-lapse observation to focus on the heating process.5. Inspection: Remove the test tube from the water bath and observe the color change of the solution.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial solution is colorless or pale. After adding ninhydrin and heating, the solution gradually develops a blue-violet to purple color, indicating a positive reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGentamicin contains multiple free amino groups. Ninhydrin reacts with amino groups upon heating to form a colored complex (Ruhemann’s purple). The appearance of a blue-violet or purple color after heating confirms the presence of gentamicin or other aminoglycoside structures.VI. PrecautionsAvoid overheating or drying the solution; handle hot test tubes with a holder; ninhydrin reagent should be added in small, controlled amounts.

Rinsing: Gently rinse the slide with distilled water to remove excess stain without washing off the smear.5. Counterstaining: Apply the counterstain evenly over the smear for the specified time.6. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Wright’s Staining (Bacteria vs. Cell Differentiation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Wright’s Staining for Cell Differentiation2. Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To master the standard Wright staining procedure and observe differential staining of cellular components, distinguishing cells based on nucleus and cytoplasm coloration under a microscope.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean glass slides with fixed smear (blood or cell smear), Wright stain solution, phosphate buffer or distilled water (pH ~6.4–6.8), dropper or pipette, staining rack, wash bottle, microscope, absorbent paper, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, fixed smear slide horizontally on a staining rack. Handle the slide by the edges to avoid contamination.2. Staining: Add enough Wright stain to completely cover the smear. Allow it to act for a short time (about 1–3 minutes) so the dye penetrates cells.3. Dilution: Add an equal volume of buffer directly onto the stain to dilute it. Gently mix by slight rocking of the slide and wait another 2–3 minutes.4. Rinsing: Gently rinse the slide with buffer or distilled water, directing the flow along the slide surface without washing off the smear.5. Drying: Stand the slide upright on absorbent paper and allow it to air-dry completely.6. Microscopic Observation: Place the dried slide on the microscope stage. Focus under low power first, then switch to high power to observe stained cells clearly.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The fixed smear is colorless or faint before staining.2. After Staining: Cells show differential coloration; nuclei appear blue to purple, while cytoplasm appears pink to light red.3. Microscopic View: Different cell types can be distinguished by size, shape, and staining characteristics.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleWright stain is a Romanowsky-type stain containing acidic and basic dyes. The basic dye binds to acidic cell components such as nucleic acids, staining nuclei blue-purple, while the acidic dye binds to basic components such as cytoplasmic proteins, staining them pink-red. Buffer dilution optimizes pH, ensuring clear differential staining for cell identification.VI. PrecautionsUse gentle rinsing to prevent smear loss; ensure correct staining time and buffer pH; allow complete air-drying before microscopy.

Key causal transitions: stain application plus buffer leads to differential binding and visible color changes. Visibility constraints: close-up views for staining steps, stable slide orientation, and a clear microscope field of view with focused image; time-lapse or accelerated transitions acceptable while preserving step order.

Experiment Title: Detection of Clostridium perfringens by Colorimetric Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic procedure and principle of detecting Clostridium perfringens using a selective culture medium and chromogenic reagent, and to observe characteristic colorimetric changes.II. Reagent Addition: After incubation, remove the tube and add the specified amount of chromogenic reagent directly into the culture tube.5. manual: I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Naturally Occurring Nitrite Detection by Griess Reagent MethodSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryExperiment Objective: To detect nitrite ions in an aqueous sample using the Griess reagent method through visual color development, and to understand the diazotization–coupling reaction principle.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, transparent), test tube rack, droppers or pipettes, nitrite-containing sample solution (or standard nitrite solution), sulfanilic acid reagent (acidic solution), N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine dihydrochloride reagent, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Add an appropriate volume (about 2–3 mL) of the sample solution into the test tube.2. Addition of Sulfanilic Acid: Using a dropper, add sulfanilic acid reagent to the test tube. Gently mix by lightly swirling the tube to ensure uniform reaction.3. Addition of Coupling Reagent: Add N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine reagent dropwise along the inner wall of the test tube. Swirl briefly and gently after addition.4. Observation: Keep the test tube still and closely observe the solution as the reaction proceeds. Focus the visual field on the test tube; time-lapse photography may be used to record gradual color changes.5. Completion: After color development stabilizes, record the final color and dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The solution is colorless or nearly colorless.During Reaction: After addition of the second reagent, a light pink color gradually appears.Final State: The solution develops a stable pink to red coloration, with intensity related to nitrite concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUnder acidic conditions, nitrite reacts with sulfanilic acid to form a diazonium salt. This intermediate then couples with N-(1-naphthyl)ethylenediamine to form a pink or red azo dye. The appearance and intensity of this color serve as a qualitative or semi-quantitative indicator of nitrite presence.VI. PrecautionsAdd reagents in the correct order; mix gently to avoid splashing; observe color change under good lighting; wear protective equipment throughout the experiment.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Staphylococcus epidermidis Detection Using Glycerol–Phenol Red MediumSubject: Healthcare – PathologyObjective: To demonstrate the correct aseptic transfer of a bacterial sample into glycerol–phenol red medium, proper tube handling, gentle mixing, and incubation, emphasizing standardized microbiological操作流程 without describing final color outcomes.II. Experimental EquipmentSterile inoculating loop, alcohol lamp or electric loop sterilizer, test tube containing glycerol–phenol red medium, test tube rack, bacterial culture of Staphylococcus epidermidis, incubator (35–37°C), gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves and lab coat. Place the glycerol–phenol red test tube upright in a rack. Light the alcohol lamp or activate the sterilizer.2. Sterilization of Loop: Hold the inoculating loop like a pen and sterilize it in the flame until red-hot. Allow it to cool briefly without touching any surface.3. Tube Handling: Hold the test tube at a slight angle. Remove the cap using the little finger of the loop hand, keeping the cap opening facing downward.4. Sample Transfer: Use the cooled sterile loop to gently pick a small amount of bacterial culture. Insert the loop into the glycerol–phenol red medium without touching the tube rim and release the sample into the liquid.5. Mixing: Withdraw the loop and recap the tube. Gently mix the tube by rolling it between the palms to evenly distribute the bacteria.6. Incubation: Place the inoculated tube back into the rack and transfer it to the incubator at 35–37°C for the required incubation period.7. Completion: Sterilize the inoculating loop again and dispose of waste according to biosafety procedures.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The glycerol–phenol red medium appears clear and uniformly prepared before inoculation.2. During Operation: The loop is visibly sterile, the tube is opened briefly and carefully, and the bacterial sample is introduced smoothly into the medium.3. After Mixing: The liquid remains uniform with no spillage or contamination, and the tube is properly sealed and positioned for incubation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis method is based on the ability of Staphylococcus epidermidis to metabolize glycerol under incubation conditions. The phenol red indicator serves as a pH-sensitive component to reflect metabolic activity. Proper aseptic transfer ensures that any subsequent changes in the medium are attributable solely to the inoculated organism, making correct technique essential for reliable detection.VI. Experimental PrecautionsMaintain strict aseptic technique throughout; avoid touching sterile tools to non-sterile surfaces; open tubes briefly and at an angle; mix gently to prevent aerosols; follow biosafety disposal rules.

manual: Urine Phosphorus Detection (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Urine Phosphorus Detection by Colorimetric MethodSubject: Healthcare – Renal PhysiologyObjective: To detect and estimate phosphorus content in urine by forming a colored complex and comparing its intensity with standards.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tubes and rack, dropper or pipette, water bath, thermometer (optional), color chart or colorimeter; fresh urine sample; acidic reagent (e.g., sulfuric acid-based); ammonium molybdate reagent; standard phosphorus solutions.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Collect a fresh urine sample and add about 2–3 mL into a clean test tube placed on a rack.2. Acidification: Add a measured amount of acidic reagent to the urine sample and mix gently to ensure uniform acidification.3. Color Development: Add ammonium molybdate reagent dropwise, gently shaking the test tube to mix.4. Heating: Place the test tube in a warm water bath for a short time (about 1–2 minutes) to accelerate color formation.5. Cooling: Remove the test tube and allow it to cool to room temperature.6. Comparison: Compare the developed color with standard tubes using a color chart or measure absorbance with a colorimeter.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial urine appears pale yellow and transparent. After adding reagents and heating, a yellow-colored complex gradually forms. The depth of yellow color increases with higher phosphorus concentration. After cooling, the color stabilizes for comparison.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn acidic conditions, inorganic phosphate in urine reacts with ammonium molybdate to form a yellow phosphomolybdate complex. The intensity of the yellow color is directly proportional to the phosphorus concentration. By comparing the color intensity with standards or measuring absorbance, the phosphorus level in urine can be estimated.VI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Colchicine Detection Using Test Strip MethodSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the rapid qualitative detection of colchicine in a prepared sample solution using a test strip, master correct strip operation steps, observe result phenomena, and understand the basic detection principle.II. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: DNA Extraction from Strawberries Using Detergent and Alcohol PrecipitationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: DNA Extraction from Strawberries2. Subject: Healthcare - Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate the extraction of DNA from plant cells by cell lysis with detergent and DNA precipitation with cold alcohol, and to observe DNA as a visible substance.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsGlass beaker or clear glass cup, fresh strawberries (2–3), detergent or dish soap, cold ethanol or isopropyl alcohol (pre-chilled), stirring rod or spoon, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove stems from strawberries and place them into the glass beaker. Mash thoroughly with a spoon until a uniform pulp forms.2. Cell Lysis: Add a small amount of detergent to the mashed strawberries. Gently mix to avoid excessive foaming, ensuring the pulp is evenly combined with detergent.3. Alcohol Layering: Slowly pour cold alcohol down the inner side of the beaker so that it forms a clear top layer above the strawberry-detergent mixture without mixing.4. Core Demonstration: Gently swirl the beaker once or twice to slightly increase contact at the interface while keeping layers mostly separate. Keep the camera focus fixed and record the process for time-lapse observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The lower layer is red and cloudy from strawberry pulp mixed with detergent; the upper alcohol layer is clear and colorless.2. After Alcohol Addition: At the interface between the two layers, a white, cloudy material begins to appear.3. Over Time: White, stringy or fibrous precipitates accumulate and become more visible, floating into the alcohol layer. This material can be seen clumping together.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleDetergent breaks down the cell membrane and nuclear membrane of strawberry cells, releasing DNA into solution. Cold alcohol reduces DNA solubility, causing DNA to precipitate out of the aqueous solution. Because DNA is insoluble in alcohol, it appears as visible white strands at the interface between the alcohol and strawberry mixture.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse cold alcohol for clear precipitation; pour alcohol slowly to maintain layering; avoid vigorous stirring; ensure stable camera positioning for clear time-lapse recording.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Demonstration of the Pile Reflex Induced by ColdSubject: Healthcare – Skin PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To observe and understand the pile reflex (piloerection) of human skin when exposed briefly to a cold stimulus.II. Experimental EquipmentHuman subject (forearm exposed), cold metal object or ice wrapped in a cloth, timer or time-lapse recording device, clean working environment.III. manual: Aspergillus Detection (Fluorescence Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Aspergillus Fluorescence Strip Detection2. Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the rapid detection of Aspergillus antigen using a fluorescence immunochromatographic strip and to understand its operational steps and detection principle.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentFluorescence test strip for Aspergillus (1 strip), liquid sample (prepared test solution), disposable dropper, handheld UV lamp (appropriate excitation wavelength), clean laboratory bench.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the fluorescence test strip flat on a clean bench with the sample pad facing upward.2. Sample Addition: Use the dropper to draw the liquid sample and add the specified number of drops (typically 2–3 drops) onto the sample pad of the strip.3. Reaction Waiting: Allow the sample to migrate along the strip for a short period (about 1–2 minutes; may be time-lapse accelerated).4. Detection: Turn off ambient bright light if necessary and illuminate the strip evenly with a handheld UV lamp from above.5. Observation: Observe the test and control regions under UV light and record the fluorescence result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The strip appears uncolored or faint under normal light, with no visible signal.2. After Sample Addition and Waiting: Under normal light, the strip shows no obvious color change.3. Under UV Illumination: Distinct fluorescent bands appear at the control line; if Aspergillus antigen is present, a fluorescent signal is also visible at the test line.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis method is based on fluorescence immunochromatography. The sample migrates along the strip by capillary action. If Aspergillus antigens are present, they bind to fluorescently labeled antibodies and are captured at the test line, emitting fluorescence under UV excitation. The control line confirms proper sample flow and reagent validity. The presence or absence of fluorescence at the test line determines the detection result.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine Ketone Body Detection (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urine Ketone Body Detection by Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Renal Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the correct operational steps for detecting ketone bodies in urine using a test strip, understand the observation of color change, and summarize the basic detection principle.II. Experimental MaterialsClean urine sample container with fresh urine, ketone test strips (commercial reagent strips), tissue or absorbent paper, gloves (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean urine sample container on a stable surface. Ensure hands are clean and dry; wear gloves if available.2. Strip Removal: Open the test strip container and remove one ketone test strip, holding it by the non-reactive end. Close the container promptly.3. Immersion: Briefly immerse only the reactive end of the strip into the urine sample for about 1–2 seconds.4. Removal and Draining: Remove the strip promptly. Gently tap or drag the edge against the container to drain excess urine. Do not wipe the reactive pad.5. Reaction Waiting: Hold the strip horizontally and wait for the specified short reaction time (about 30–60 seconds), using time-lapse visualization if needed.6. Reading: Observe the color of the reactive pad and compare it with the color chart on the strip container.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The reactive pad is a light, uniform base color.2. After Reaction: Within the waiting time, the reactive pad changes color. The depth of color corresponds to the ketone body concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleKetone test strips use the nitroprusside reaction. Acetoacetic acid in urine reacts with sodium nitroprusside under alkaline conditions to produce a color change. The intensity of the color is proportional to the ketone body concentration, allowing semi-quantitative assessment.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh urine and unexpired strips.2. Do not touch the reactive pad.3. Do not immerse the strip for too long or read results too late.4. Dispose of used strips properly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Skin Erythema Reaction Caused by FrictionI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Skin Erythema Reaction (Friction)2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe the erythema reaction of human skin caused by mechanical friction, understand skin microcirculation responses, and learn basic methods of controlled skin stimulation and visual observation.II. Experimental MaterialsClean human forearm (volunteer), smooth cotton pad, timer or stopwatch, clean environment with sufficient lighting, camera for close-up and time-lapse recording (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the forearm skin is clean, dry, and free of existing redness or lesions. Position the forearm comfortably with the skin fully exposed.2. Friction Stimulation: Using a smooth cotton pad, rub the same area of the forearm skin back and forth with moderate, even pressure for approximately 5–10 seconds.3. Stop and Exposure: Stop rubbing and remove the cotton pad. Keep the stimulated skin area fully exposed and still.4. Observation: Focus on the rubbed area and observe changes in skin color over time. If recording, use close-up framing and time-lapse photography to capture gradual changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The forearm skin appears normal in color, without visible redness.2. After Friction: Shortly after rubbing stops, the stimulated area gradually becomes red (erythema), localized to the rubbed region.3. Subsequent Change: The redness may intensify briefly, then slowly stabilize or begin to fade during continued observation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMechanical friction stimulates skin mechanoreceptors and causes mild local tissue stress, leading to vasodilation of superficial capillaries. This increases local blood flow, producing visible erythema. The reaction reflects normal skin microcirculation and inflammatory response mechanisms and is transient under moderate stimulation.VI. PrecautionsUse moderate pressure only; avoid damaged or sensitive skin. Stop immediately if discomfort occurs. This demonstration is for observation only and not for diagnosis.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Respiratory Alkalosis Simulation Using pH and CO2 Test StripsSubject: Healthcare – Respiratory PhysiologyObjective: To simulate respiratory alkalosis by controlled hyperventilation and to detect decreased CO2 and increased pH in exhaled air using indicator test strips.II. Equipment and MaterialsSealed transparent container with inlet; pH indicator test strip; CO2 indicator test strip; holder or clip for strips; timer; data recording sheet; gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves. Fix pH and CO2 test strips side by side on the holder. Record initial colors/values according to manufacturer scale.2. Apparatus Setup: Place the holder inside the sealed container without touching walls. Ensure container is closed and transparent.3. Controlled Hyperventilation: The subject breathes rapidly and shallowly for 20–30 seconds to induce hyperventilation.4. Exposure: Immediately exhale continuously into the container inlet for 10–15 seconds, keeping the container sealed.5. Observation and Recording: Wait 10–30 seconds. Observe color changes of both strips. Record pH shift and CO2 level change. Use time-lapse imaging to capture before–during–after states.6. Completion: Open container, remove strips, dispose according to instructions, and ventilate the area.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: pH strip shows baseline (near neutral); CO2 strip shows normal CO2.After Exposure: CO2 strip indicates decreased CO2; pH strip shifts toward alkaline.V. Experimental Principle SummaryHyperventilation increases alveolar ventilation, washing out CO2 from blood and exhaled air. Reduced CO2 lowers carbonic acid concentration, raising pH. The test strips visually reflect decreased CO2 and increased pH, simulating respiratory alkalosis.VI. PrecautionsAvoid prolonged hyperventilation; stop if dizziness occurs. Keep container sealed during exposure. Follow strip manufacturer timing and color charts.
