manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Chlorpromazine Hydrochloride Drug Identification (Nitric Acid Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Identification of Chlorpromazine Hydrochloride by Nitric Acid Color Reaction2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To identify chlorpromazine hydrochloride by observing its characteristic color reaction with concentrated nitric acid under mild heating, and to master standardized laboratory operations including reagent addition, controlled heating, and careful observation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, dry), test tube rack, glass dropper, water bath setup, heat source, chlorpromazine hydrochloride sample (small amount), concentrated nitric acid, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack and wear protective goggles and gloves. Add a small amount of chlorpromazine hydrochloride solid to the bottom of the test tube.2. Reagent Addition: Using a glass dropper, add concentrated nitric acid dropwise into the test tube. Gently shake or tap the test tube to mix, avoiding splashing.3. Heating: Place the test tube into a water bath and apply mild heating. Maintain controlled temperature and avoid direct flame contact.4. Observation: Observe the color change in the test tube during and after heating, maintaining a stable and careful observation posture.5. Completion: Remove the test tube from the water bath, allow it to cool, and dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Chlorpromazine hydrochloride appears as a light-colored solid.2. After Nitric Acid Addition: The sample begins to show a light yellow to orange coloration.3. After Mild Heating: The color deepens to a more intense orange or reddish tone, indicating a positive identification reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleChlorpromazine hydrochloride contains a phenothiazine structure that undergoes oxidation and nitration when treated with concentrated nitric acid. Mild heating accelerates the reaction, producing characteristic colored products. The appearance and deepening of color serve as the basis for qualitative identification of the drug.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle concentrated nitric acid with care to avoid burns.2. Add acid dropwise and mix gently to prevent splashing.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Gram Staining (Bacterial Differentiation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Gram Staining of Bacteria2. Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology & Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To master the standard Gram staining procedure, correctly differentiate Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria based on staining results, and understand the underlying structural principles of bacterial cell walls.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsGlass slide with fixed bacterial smear, staining rack, forceps, dropper bottles of crystal violet, Gram iodine solution, alcohol decolorizer (95% ethanol), safranin, distilled water, light microscope with oil immersion lens (100×), immersion oil, absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the glass slide with a heat-fixed bacterial smear on a staining rack. Hold the slide horizontally using forceps.2. Primary Staining: Flood the smear with crystal violet for about 1 minute. Gently rinse with distilled water.3. Mordant Treatment: Flood the smear with iodine solution for about 1 minute to form a crystal violet–iodine complex. Gently rinse with water.4. Decolorization: Apply alcohol decolorizer dropwise for 10–20 seconds until runoff is nearly colorless. Immediately rinse gently with water to stop decolorization.5. Counterstaining: Flood the smear with safranin for about 30–60 seconds. Rinse gently with water.6. Drying: Blot the slide gently with absorbent paper; do not wipe.7. Microscopic Observation: Place a drop of immersion oil on the stained smear. Observe under a light microscope using the oil immersion objective. Adjust focus carefully. Capture focused images and present staining progression using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After crystal violet and iodine: All bacteria appear purple.2. After alcohol decolorization: Gram-positive bacteria remain purple; Gram-negative bacteria become colorless.3. After safranin counterstaining: Gram-positive bacteria remain purple; Gram-negative bacteria appear red or pink.4. Under oil immersion: Clear morphological differences and color contrast between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria are observed.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGram staining is a differential staining method based on differences in bacterial cell wall structure. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains the crystal violet–iodine complex during alcohol decolorization, appearing purple. Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane; the complex is removed by alcohol, and cells are subsequently stained red by safranin. This method enables rapid bacterial differentiation and guides clinical diagnosis and treatment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sulfonamide Drug Identification (Diazo-Coupling Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sulfonamide Drug Identification by Diazo-Coupling Color Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To identify sulfonamide drugs by observing the characteristic color reaction produced through diazotization and azo-coupling, and to master correct reagent addition order, low-temperature control, and visual observation of color changes.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, ice bath (beaker with ice-water mixture), droppers or pipettes, glass stirring rod (optional), sulfonamide sample solution, sodium nitrite solution, dilute hydrochloric acid, alkaline coupling reagent solution, safety goggles and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube in a rack. Add an appropriate amount of sulfonamide sample solution into the test tube. Wear safety goggles.2. Cooling: Place the test tube into an ice bath to cool the solution, maintaining a low temperature throughout the diazotization step.3. Diazotization: While cooling, add sodium nitrite solution dropwise into the test tube and gently shake to mix.4. Acidification: Add dilute hydrochloric acid slowly to the mixture to form the diazonium salt, continuing gentle shaking while keeping the test tube in the ice bath.5. Coupling Reaction: Remove the test tube from the ice bath if necessary, then add the alkaline coupling reagent solution while gently shaking the test tube.6. Observation: Allow the reaction to proceed briefly and observe the color change in the solution.7. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack, record observations, then dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations and clean the glassware.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The sulfonamide sample solution is clear or lightly colored.2. After Diazotization: No obvious color change, solution remains clear at low temperature.3. After Coupling: Upon addition of the alkaline coupling reagent, a distinct and stable color (such as orange-red or reddish-brown) appears, indicating a positive sulfonamide reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSulfonamide drugs contain an aromatic primary amine group. Under low-temperature acidic conditions, sodium nitrite reacts with the amine to form a diazonium salt (diazotization). The diazonium compound then couples with an alkaline coupling reagent to form an azo compound with a characteristic color. The appearance of this color confirms the presence of sulfonamide drugs.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Maintain low temperature during diazotization to ensure stability of the diazonium salt.2. Add reagents in strict order to avoid false results.3. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Neisseria meningitidis Detection (Gram Staining + Oxidase Test)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Neisseria meningitidis by Gram Staining and Oxidase Test2. Subject: Healthcare - Pathology (Medical Microbiology)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the identification of Neisseria meningitidis by preparing a bacterial smear, performing Gram staining for microscopic observation, and conducting an oxidase test to verify oxidase positivity; to master basic smear preparation, staining techniques, and rapid biochemical testing.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean glass slides, inoculating loop, Bunsen burner or alcohol lamp, staining rack, microscope with oil immersion lens, Gram stain reagents (crystal violet, iodine solution, decolorizer, safranin), distilled water, absorbent paper, bacterial culture plate (suspected Neisseria meningitidis), oxidase reagent, filter paper, sterile toothpick or loop, personal protective equipment (lab coat, gloves).III. Experimental Procedure1. Smear Preparation: Place a drop of sterile water on a clean glass slide. Using a sterile loop, pick a small amount of bacterial colony and emulsify it in the water to form a thin, even smear. Air-dry completely.2. Heat Fixation: Pass the dried slide quickly through a flame 2-3 times with the smear side up to fix the bacteria.3. Gram Staining Sequence:   (1) Flood the smear with crystal violet for about 1 minute, then gently rinse with water.   (2) Add iodine solution for 1 minute to form a dye-mordant complex; rinse gently.   (3) Decolorize with alcohol or acetone briefly until runoff is clear; immediately rinse with water.   (4) Counterstain with safranin for 30-60 seconds; rinse and blot dry.4. Microscopic Examination: Observe the stained smear under oil immersion (100× objective), focusing on bacterial shape and color.5. Oxidase Test:   (1) Place a piece of clean filter paper on the bench and add 1-2 drops of oxidase reagent.   (2) Using a sterile loop or toothpick, pick a fresh colony and smear it onto the reagent-soaked area.   (3) Observe the color change within 10-30 seconds.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Gram Staining: Neisseria meningitidis appears as pink/red, kidney-shaped Gram-negative diplococci under the microscope.2. Oxidase Test: The smeared area on filter paper rapidly turns dark purple, indicating a positive oxidase reaction.V. Summary of Experimental Principles1. Gram Staining Principle: Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane, causing the crystal violet-iodine complex to be removed during decolorization; they are subsequently counterstained red by safranin.2. Oxidase Test Principle: Neisseria meningitidis produces cytochrome c oxidase, which oxidizes the reagent to form a purple-colored compound, indicating a positive result.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse fresh cultures for the oxidase test; avoid over-decolorization during Gram staining; observe oxidase results promptly, as delayed readings may cause false results; dispose of biological waste according to biosafety regulations.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Identification of Levofloxacin Hydrochloride by UV Fluorescence MethodSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryObjective: To identify levofloxacin hydrochloride by comparing the fluorescence response of a reference solution and a test solution under ultraviolet irradiation at a specified wavelength, mastering solution preparation, quartz cuvette operation, and fluorescence comparison.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsUV lamp (specified wavelength for levofloxacin hydrochloride fluorescence), quartz cuvettes (2, clean and dry), levofloxacin hydrochloride reference substance, test sample of levofloxacin hydrochloride, suitable solvent as specified in pharmacopeia (e.g., dilute acid or water), volumetric flasks, pipettes, gloves, dark observation environment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves and ensure the UV lamp is functional. Clean and dry two quartz cuvettes.2. Solution Preparation: Prepare the reference solution by accurately dissolving a specified amount of levofloxacin hydrochloride reference substance in solvent to the required concentration. Prepare the test solution using the same method and concentration.3. Cuvette Filling: Transfer equal volumes of the reference solution and test solution into separate quartz cuvettes. Avoid bubbles and wipe the outer walls clean.4. Placement: Place the two cuvettes side by side in the same orientation under the UV lamp to ensure identical irradiation conditions.5. UV Irradiation: Turn on the UV lamp at the specified wavelength. Irradiate both cuvettes simultaneously. Use focused framing and time-lapse photography to capture changes.6. Comparison: Observe and compare the fluorescence color and intensity of the reference and test solutions under UV light.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaBefore UV irradiation, both solutions appear clear and colorless. Under UV light, the reference solution emits characteristic fluorescence. The test solution should show fluorescence of the same color and similar intensity. Any significant difference indicates non-conformity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLevofloxacin hydrochloride contains a fluorophore that absorbs ultraviolet light at a specific wavelength and emits visible fluorescence. Under identical conditions, substances with the same chemical structure exhibit similar fluorescence characteristics. Therefore, comparing the fluorescence response of a test sample with a reference allows qualitative identification of levofloxacin hydrochloride.VI. PrecautionsUse quartz cuvettes only; ensure identical concentrations and volumes; avoid ambient light interference; do not look directly at UV light; clean equipment after use.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Prolactin Detection Using Test Strip MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Prolactin Detection (Test Strip Method)Subject: Healthcare – Reproductive PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the correct use of a prolactin rapid test strip by applying a liquid sample, maintaining proper strip orientation, observing result window changes, and understanding the immunochromatographic principle of prolactin detection.II. Experimental MaterialsProlactin test strip (lateral flow type), liquid sample (e.g., serum, plasma, or prepared demonstration sample), disposable dropper, clean flat surface, timer or clock, gloves (optional for hygiene).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove the prolactin test strip from its packaging and identify the sample pad and result window. Place the strip on a clean, flat surface.2. Sample Application: Use a dropper to draw the sample. Apply 2–3 drops directly onto the sample pad without touching the pad with the dropper tip.3. Placement: Keep the test strip horizontal and stationary to ensure even capillary flow of the sample.4. Waiting: Allow the sample to migrate along the strip. Wait briefly (about 1–5 minutes). For demonstration, this period may be shown using time-lapse photography.5. Result Reading: Observe the result window. Identify the control line and test line, and read the result according to the instructions provided with the test strip.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The strip is dry, with no visible lines in the result window.During Reaction: The liquid sample moves laterally along the strip by capillary action.Final Result: Colored lines appear in the result window. The control line confirms test validity; the presence or intensity of the test line indicates the prolactin level relative to the detection threshold.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on lateral flow immunochromatography. Prolactin in the sample binds to labeled antibodies and migrates along the strip. The antigen–antibody complex is captured at the test line, producing a visible colored band. A separate control line captures excess labeled antibodies to verify proper sample flow and reagent activity. The appearance and pattern of lines allow qualitative or semi-quantitative assessment of prolactin levels.VI. PrecautionsEnsure correct sample volume; excessive or insufficient drops may affect results. Keep the strip horizontal during the test. Read results within the specified time window to avoid misinterpretation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Giemsa Staining for Mycoplasma ObservationI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Giemsa Staining for Mycoplasma Observation2. Subject: Healthcare – Pathology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the use of Giemsa staining to visualize mycoplasma associated with fixed cell smears under a light microscope, and to understand the staining principle and basic operational workflow.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClean glass slides with fixed cell smears, diluted Giemsa stain, dropper or pipette, buffered water (pH 6.8), staining rack, absorbent paper, light microscope.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a glass slide with a properly fixed cell smear on a staining rack, smear side up.2. Staining: Use a dropper to gently apply enough diluted Giemsa stain to completely cover the smear. Avoid touching the smear surface with the dropper tip.3. Staining Time: Allow the stain to act for a short, defined period (approximately 10–15 minutes; in demonstration, shown as time-lapse).4. Rinsing: Gently rinse the slide with buffered water, allowing water to flow over the smear without direct force.5. Drying: Place the slide upright or flat on absorbent paper and allow it to air-dry naturally. Do not wipe the smear.6. Microscopic Examination: Once dry, place the slide on the stage of a light microscope. Focus under low power first, then switch to higher magnification for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. After staining and drying, the smear shows differential coloration.2. Host cell nuclei and cytoplasm appear in characteristic blue to purple shades.3. Mycoplasma appear as very small, dark blue to purple granular or dot-like structures around or on host cells.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleGiemsa stain is a Romanowsky-type stain composed of methylene blue, azure, and eosin. Basic dyes bind to acidic cellular components such as nucleic acids, while acidic dyes bind to basic components. Mycoplasma, containing DNA and lacking a rigid cell wall, take up the basic dye components and appear as small, dark-stained particles, allowing visualization under a light microscope.VI. Experimental NotesUse gentle rinsing to prevent smear detachment; ensure complete air-drying before microscopy; maintain correct buffer pH to ensure optimal staining results.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Metronidazole Drug Stability Detection (UV Fluorescence Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Metronidazole Drug Stability Detection by UV Fluorescence Method2. Subject: Healthcare - Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To evaluate the photostability of metronidazole by comparing the fluorescence intensity of a UV-exposed sample with a non-exposed control, and to master basic procedures of solution preparation, UV irradiation, and fluorescence measurement.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsMetronidazole reference standard; distilled water or suitable buffer; volumetric flask; pipette; quartz cuvettes (2); UV light source (e.g., 254 nm UV lamp); aluminum foil; UV spectrofluorometer; labels; protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Accurately weigh metronidazole and dissolve it in distilled water to prepare a clear, colorless solution of known concentration. Mix thoroughly. Divide the solution equally into two labeled quartz cuvettes: Control and UV-exposed.2. UV Exposure: Wrap the control cuvette completely with aluminum foil to avoid light exposure. Place the UV-exposed cuvette under the UV lamp at a fixed distance. Irradiate for a set time (e.g., accelerated exposure shown by time-lapse).3. Fluorescence Measurement: After exposure, place each cuvette into the UV spectrofluorometer. Set appropriate excitation and emission wavelengths for metronidazole. manual: Instructions for the Experiment Urine Phosphate Detection by Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Urine Phosphate Detection (Molybdenum Blue Colorimetric Method)Subject: Healthcare – Renal PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To qualitatively demonstrate the presence of inorganic phosphate in urine using the molybdenum blue colorimetric reaction, and to master correct reagent addition order, test tube handling, and basic laboratory heating operations.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or micropipette, beaker (water bath), hot plate or water bath heater, urine sample (clear), acidic ammonium molybdate reagent, reducing agent (such as stannous chloride or ascorbic acid solution), glass stirring rod (optional), protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Using a dropper, add approximately 2–3 mL of urine sample into the test tube.2. Addition of Molybdate Reagent: Add an appropriate amount (about 1 mL) of acidic ammonium molybdate reagent into the urine sample. Gently mix by lightly shaking the test tube to ensure uniform mixing.3. Addition of Reducing Agent: Add several drops of the reducing agent to the mixture. Mix gently again, avoiding splashing or vigorous shaking.4. Heating: Place the test tube into a warm water bath and heat briefly (about 1–2 minutes). Remove the test tube and allow the reaction to proceed.5. Observation: Hold the test tube against a light background and observe the color change.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The urine sample is pale yellow and transparent.After Molybdate Addition: The solution remains clear or slightly yellow, with no obvious color change.After Reducing Agent and Heating: A blue to deep blue color gradually appears in the solution. The intensity of the blue color correlates with the phosphate content in the urine.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIn acidic conditions, inorganic phosphate in urine reacts with ammonium molybdate to form phosphomolybdic acid. Upon addition of a reducing agent and heating, phosphomolybdic acid is reduced to molybdenum blue, a blue-colored complex. The appearance and intensity of the blue color indicate the presence and relative amount of phosphate, which is an important parameter in renal physiology assessment.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct order of reagent addition; do not add reducing agent before ammonium molybdate. Heat gently using a water bath to avoid boiling. Handle all biological samples and reagents using appropriate safety measures and dispose of waste properly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rapid Detection of Calcium Gluconate Drug Content (Calconcarboxylic Acid Indicator Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rapid Detection of Calcium Gluconate Drug Content by EDTA Titration (Calconcarboxylic Acid Indicator Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To determine the calcium ion content in calcium gluconate injection using complexometric titration with EDTA, master standardized titration operations, endpoint judgment, and understand the chelation principle.II. Experimental Reagents and Equipment1. Reagents: Calcium gluconate injection (sample), standardized EDTA solution, calconcarboxylic acid indicator, distilled water.2. Glassware and Tools: Conical flask (250 mL), burette (25 or 50 mL), pipette (measured volume), pipette filler, beaker, burette stand and clamp.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Rinse the burette with standardized EDTA solution and fill it, removing air bubbles; record the initial burette reading. Place a clean conical flask on the bench.2. Sampling and Dilution: Use a pipette to accurately measure a fixed volume of calcium gluconate injection and transfer it into the conical flask. Add an appropriate amount of distilled water to dilute the solution.3. Indicator Addition: Add 2–3 drops of calconcarboxylic acid indicator into the conical flask. Gently swirl to mix; the solution shows the initial indicator color.4. Titration: Place the conical flask under the burette. Slowly add EDTA solution while gently swirling the flask continuously.5. Endpoint Judgment: As titration approaches the endpoint, add EDTA dropwise until the solution color changes sharply and remains stable for about 30 seconds.6. Completion: Record the final burette reading, calculate EDTA consumption, and stop the titration.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The diluted calcium gluconate solution is clear; after adding indicator, it displays the characteristic initial color of the Ca2+-indicator complex.2. During Titration: With continuous EDTA addition and swirling, the color gradually weakens.3. Endpoint: At the endpoint, the solution undergoes a clear and stable color change, indicating complete chelation of Ca2+ by EDTA.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on complexometric titration. EDTA is a hexadentate chelating agent that forms a stable 1:1 complex with Ca2+. Before the endpoint, Ca2+ binds with calconcarboxylic acid indicator to form a colored complex. During titration, EDTA preferentially chelates free Ca2+. When all Ca2+ ions are complexed by EDTA, the indicator is released, producing a distinct color change that marks the endpoint. The amount of EDTA consumed is proportional to the calcium content in the sample.VI. Precautions1. Ensure accurate volume measurement and proper burette operation.2. Swirl gently to avoid splashing and ensure complete reaction.3. Add EDTA slowly near the endpoint to avoid overshooting.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Aflatoxin B1 Detection (Fluorescence Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Aflatoxin B1 Detection by Fluorescence Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the use of a fluorescence immunochromatographic test strip for detecting aflatoxin B1 by observing capillary flow and fluorescence signal under UV illumination.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsFluorescence test strip for aflatoxin B1, sample extract solution, dropper, flat clean surface (e.g., lab bench), UV lamp (365 nm), timer (optional), gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves and ensure the working surface is clean and dry. Remove the test strip from its package and place it horizontally on a flat surface with the sample pad facing upward.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper to draw the liquid sample extract. Add the specified number of drops (usually 2–3) vertically onto the sample pad without touching the strip.3. Capillary Migration: Allow the liquid to migrate along the strip by capillary action. Keep the strip stationary. Observe the gradual wetting and movement of the liquid front from the sample pad toward the reaction zone.4. Reaction Time: Wait for the recommended reaction time (typically 3–5 minutes; may be accelerated or shown by time-lapse for demonstration).5. Result Reading: Illuminate the strip with a UV lamp in a darkened environment. Focus the camera on the strip and observe fluorescence signals at the control line and test line regions.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The strip is dry, with no visible fluorescence under ambient light.2. During Migration: The liquid sample visibly migrates along the strip, forming a uniform flow path.3. Under UV Illumination: Fluorescent lines appear at specific positions. The control line shows stable fluorescence, while the test line fluorescence intensity varies inversely with aflatoxin B1 concentration.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on a competitive fluorescence immunochromatographic assay. Aflatoxin B1 in the sample competes with immobilized antigen on the test line for binding to fluorescently labeled antibodies. During capillary flow, immune complexes form and are captured at defined regions. Under UV light, fluorescent labels emit visible signals. The presence and intensity of fluorescence at the test and control lines indicate the detection result.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure correct drop volume, avoid touching the strip with the dropper, keep the strip flat during migration, and avoid direct eye exposure to UV light.

Visibility constraints: close-up focus on strip surface, stable perspective, clear transition from ambient to UV lighting for verification.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Bordetella pertussis by ImmunofluorescenceSubject: Healthcare – PathologyObjective: To demonstrate the use of fluorescent-labeled antibodies to specifically detect Bordetella pertussis in respiratory smears and to observe characteristic fluorescence under a fluorescence microscope.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentGlass microscope slides with fixed respiratory smear, fluorescent-labeled anti–Bordetella pertussis antibody reagent, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) or rinse buffer, dropper or micropipette, humid incubation chamber, absorbent paper, fluorescence microscope, timer, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the glass slide with a fixed respiratory smear on a clean, flat surface. Ensure the smear is completely fixed and dry.2. Reagent Addition: Add an appropriate volume of fluorescent-labeled antibody reagent dropwise to fully cover the smear area.3. Incubation: Place the slide in a humid chamber and incubate at room temperature for a short period (about 15–30 minutes) to allow antigen–antibody binding.4. Rinsing: Remove the slide and gently rinse with PBS to wash away unbound antibody, avoiding direct strong streams on the smear.5. Drying: Allow the slide to air-dry naturally or gently blot the edges with absorbent paper.6. Microscopy: Place the dried slide on the fluorescence microscope stage. Select the appropriate excitation filter, focus the image, and observe the smear. Perform brief time-lapse observation if required.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before staining: The smear appears non-fluorescent under fluorescence microscopy.2. After staining and rinsing: Under fluorescence microscopy, Bordetella pertussis organisms appear as small, bright apple‑green or yellow‑green fluorescent coccobacilli against a dark background.3. Time-lapse observation: Fluorescent signals remain stable and localized to bacterial structures without spreading.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the immunofluorescence principle. Fluorescent-labeled antibodies specifically bind to Bordetella pertussis antigens present in the respiratory smear. When excited by light of a specific wavelength in a fluorescence microscope, the fluorophore emits visible fluorescence, allowing specific visualization and identification of the pathogen. The specificity of antigen–antibody binding ensures accurate detection.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Respiratory Acidosis Simulation Detection (pH + CO2 Test Strip)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Respiratory Acidosis Simulation Detection Using pH and CO2 Test Strips2. Subject: Healthcare – Respiratory Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate carbon dioxide retention during hypoventilation and its effect on acidity by observing color changes in pH and CO2 test strips using a sealed exhalation chamber.II. Experimental EquipmentMouthpiece with one-way valve, sealed transparent test chamber, combined pH and CO2 indicator test strip, chamber holder or stand, timer, disposable gloves, disinfectant wipes.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a fresh pH and CO2 test strip inside the sealed transparent chamber, ensuring it is clearly visible. Attach the mouthpiece securely. Wear gloves.2. Baseline Measurement: The subject breathes normally and exhales once or twice through the mouthpiece into the sealed chamber. Wait briefly and observe the initial color of the pH and CO2 indicators as the baseline.3. Simulated Hypoventilation: Instruct the subject to simulate hypoventilation by taking slower, shallower breaths, then exhale steadily into the chamber for several cycles.4. Recheck Measurement: Keep the chamber sealed and observe the test strip again. Use time-lapse photography or accelerated observation to highlight color changes.5. Completion: Record the final colors, open the chamber, dispose of the strip safely, and disinfect the mouthpiece.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Test strip shows baseline CO2 level and near-neutral pH color.2. After Hypoventilation: CO2 indicator shows a darker or more intense color corresponding to higher CO2 concentration; pH indicator shifts toward acidic range.3. Comparison: The difference between baseline and post-hypoventilation states is visually apparent.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHypoventilation reduces alveolar ventilation, causing carbon dioxide retention in exhaled air. Increased CO2 forms carbonic acid when dissolved in moisture, lowering pH. The pH and CO2 test strips respond with characteristic color changes, visually demonstrating the mechanism of respiratory acidosis.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the chamber is sealed to prevent gas leakage; use a new test strip for each trial; avoid prolonged breath-holding that may cause discomfort; follow hygiene and disposal protocols.

Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of borax in a food sample by observing the characteristic color change of curcumin after heating, and to master the basic operations of reagent addition, mixing, and gentle heating using simple laboratory glassware.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube or small evaporating dish, test tube rack, dropper, glass rod, alcohol lamp or hot plate (low setting), curcumin reagent (ethanol solution), sample extract suspected of containing borax, tweezers or holder, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube or evaporating dish on the rack. Add a small amount (about 1–2 mL) of the prepared sample extract into the vessel.2. Mixing: Gently stir the mixture with a glass rod until the reagent and sample are evenly mixed.4. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect cyanogenic glycosides in plant materials by observing the color change of a picric acid test strip after enzymatic hydrolysis and release of hydrogen cyanide gas.II. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Blue-Green Color Vision Screening Using Test ChartSubject Area: Healthcare – Sensory PhysiologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the screening method for blue-green color vision deficiency by observing a subject’s perception of a standardized color vision test chart and understanding the physiological basis of color vision impairment.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsBlue-green color vision test chart (containing the number 6 composed of color dots), chair for subject seating, fixed-distance marker (approximately 75–100 cm), camera or video recording device with focus and time-lapse capability, neutral lighting environment.III. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation: Arrange a quiet, evenly lit room. Place the blue-green color vision test chart at eye level on a vertical surface. Mark a fixed viewing distance in front of the chart.2. Subject Positioning: Ask the blue-green colorblind subject to sit upright on the chair at the marked distance, facing the chart directly.3. Observation Phase: Instruct the subject to look steadily at the test chart without moving closer or farther away. Begin focused video recording with time-lapse enabled.4. Response Recording: Ask the subject to report the number they perceive on the chart. Capture the subject’s verbal or written response within the video frame.5. Completion: Stop recording after the response is clearly documented. Ensure the chart and subject remain in the frame until the end.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The test chart clearly displays a number 6 formed by blue-green color dots against a contrasting background.During Observation: The blue-green colorblind subject may show hesitation or report difficulty in recognizing the number or may perceive an incorrect or unclear number.Final Outcome: The subject’s reported perception differs from that of a person with normal color vision, demonstrating blue-green color vision deficiency.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleHuman color vision depends on cone photoreceptors sensitive to different wavelengths of light. Blue-green color blindness results from abnormal or absent function of cones sensitive to short- or medium-wavelength light. Therefore, the subject’s inability or altered ability to correctly identify the number reflects the underlying sensory physiological mechanism of color vision impairment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Skin Sebum Component Detection (Sudan III Staining Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Skin Sebum Component Detection (Sudan III Staining Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To detect and observe lipid (sebum) components on the skin surface using Sudan III staining, understand the distribution characteristics of skin sebum, and master a simplified microscopic staining and observation method.II. Experimental EquipmentClean glass slide, sterile cotton swab, Sudan III staining solution, dropper, distilled water (for rinsing), absorbent paper or filter paper, microscope (with low to medium magnification), disposable gloves (optional for hygiene).III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Collection: Use a sterile cotton swab to gently rub the skin surface (such as the forehead or nose) to collect a small amount of sebum.2. Smearing: Evenly smear the collected sample onto the center of a clean glass slide, forming a thin film.3. Air Drying: Place the slide on a clean surface and allow it to air dry naturally.4. Staining: Use a dropper to add 1–2 drops of Sudan III staining solution onto the dried smear, ensuring it fully covers the sample.5. Waiting: Let the stain act for a short time (about 30–60 seconds).6. Rinsing: Gently rinse the slide with a small amount of distilled water to remove excess stain without washing off the sample.7. Blot Drying: Use absorbent paper to carefully blot the edges of the slide until dry.8. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide under a microscope and observe under low to medium magnification. Adjust focus to obtain a clear image. The process can be recorded with focused, time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before Staining: The smear appears nearly colorless or slightly translucent.2. After Staining: Under the microscope, lipid components (sebum droplets) appear orange-red or red, while non-lipid components remain lightly stained or colorless.3. Distribution: Stained lipid droplets are unevenly distributed, often appearing as small round or irregular spots.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSudan III is a fat-soluble dye that selectively dissolves in and stains lipid substances. When applied to a skin smear, Sudan III preferentially colors sebum (rich in lipids) orange-red. Non-lipid components do not retain the dye after rinsing. Therefore, the presence and distribution of sebum can be identified by microscopic observation of stained lipid droplets.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Smearing should be thin to ensure clear staining and observation.2. Rinsing must be gentle to avoid removing the sample.3. Avoid contact of stain with skin or eyes; handle dyes carefully.4. Dispose of used swabs and clean slides properly after the experiment.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Aspirin Purity Detection (Ferric Chloride Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Aspirin Purity Detection by Ferric Chloride Color Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To determine the purity of an aspirin sample by observing its reaction with ferric chloride solution, and to understand the principle of phenolic impurity detection.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1), test tube rack, dropper, aspirin sample (small amount), ethanol (analytical grade), ferric chloride solution (FeCl3, dilute aqueous solution).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the test tube rack. Add a small amount of aspirin sample into the test tube.2. Dissolution: Use a dropper to add an appropriate amount of ethanol into the test tube. Gently swirl or shake the test tube until the aspirin sample is completely dissolved, forming a clear solution.3. Reaction: Using a clean dropper, add several drops of ferric chloride solution into the test tube while gently shaking to ensure uniform mixing.4. Observation: Hold the test tube steady and observe the color change of the solution.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Aspirin solid is visible at the bottom of the test tube before ethanol addition.2. After Dissolution: The aspirin dissolves in ethanol, producing a clear and colorless solution.3. After Adding Ferric Chloride: If the aspirin is pure, the solution shows no purple coloration or only a very faint yellow-brown color from ferric chloride itself; if phenolic impurities (such as salicylic acid) are present, a purple or violet color appears.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe ferric chloride color method is based on the reaction between ferric ions (Fe3+) and phenolic hydroxyl groups. Pure aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) lacks a free phenolic hydroxyl group and therefore does not produce a purple complex with ferric chloride. If aspirin contains salicylic acid or other phenolic impurities, ferric ions react with these groups to form a purple-colored complex. The presence or absence of this color indicates the purity of the aspirin sample.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstration of aspirin purity detection using the ferric chloride color method, focusing strictly on the operational sequence of reagent handling and observable color change.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Aspirin dissolves in ethanol; ferric chloride reacts only with phenolic impurities; color change (or lack thereof) is visually detectable in a test tube.Phased Storyline:Phase 1 – Setup: Static, focused view of a test tube containing an aspirin sample.Phase 2 – Dissolution: Ethanol is added; solid aspirin disappears, forming a clear solution.Phase 3 – Reaction: Ferric chloride is added dropwise with gentle shaking.Phase 4 – Outcome: Solution remains colorless/light yellow (pure aspirin) or turns purple (impurity present).Visibility and Perspective Constraints: Camera remains centered on the test tube; dropper and reagent addition are clearly visible; time-lapse accelerates dissolution and mixing while preserving correct chronological order.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Formaldehyde Detection by Acetylacetone Color MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Formaldehyde Detection by Acetylacetone Color Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of formaldehyde in food samples by observing color changes after reaction with acetylacetone under heating conditions, and to understand the basic detection principle.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (1), test tube rack, droppers, warm water bath (about 60°C), food sample extract, acetylacetone reagent, ammonium acetate solution, thermometer (optional), protective gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube containing an appropriate volume of food sample extract upright on the test tube rack.2. Reagent Addition: Using droppers, add a fixed number of drops of acetylacetone reagent to the test tube, followed by the same volume of ammonium acetate solution.3. Mixing: Gently shake or tap the test tube to mix the solutions evenly, avoiding splashing.4. Heating: Place the test tube into a warm water bath maintained at approximately 60°C. Heat for several minutes to allow the reaction to proceed.5. Cooling and Observation: Remove the test tube from the water bath and allow it to cool to room temperature. Observe and record the color change.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The food sample extract is usually colorless or lightly colored and transparent.2. During Heating: No immediate dramatic change may be seen, but gradual color development begins.3. After Cooling: If formaldehyde is present, the solution appears light yellow to yellow; if absent, the solution remains nearly colorless.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe acetylacetone color method is based on the reaction of formaldehyde with acetylacetone and ammonium ions under mild heating to form a yellow-colored compound (3,5-diacetyl-1,4-dihydrolutidine). The intensity of the yellow color is proportional to the amount of formaldehyde present, allowing qualitative detection through visual observation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Control the water bath temperature near 60°C to ensure reliable color development.2. Add reagents in the correct order and mix gently.3. Observe color changes after cooling for consistent comparison.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Alum Detection (Barium Chloride Color Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Alum Detection in Food by Barium Chloride Color MethodSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneExperiment Objective: To detect the presence of alum (sulfate ions) in food extracts through visual observation of precipitate formation, and to master the correct reagent addition sequence in a qualitative test.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean, transparent), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, food extract (aqueous extract of suspected food), dilute hydrochloric acid, barium chloride solution, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Add a small amount (about 2–3 mL) of the prepared food extract into the test tube.2. Acidification: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube to acidify the solution. Gently shake the test tube to mix evenly.3. Detection Step: Add barium chloride solution dropwise into the test tube while gently shaking.4. Observation: Observe the change in clarity of the solution during and after the addition of barium chloride.5. Completion: Stop adding reagent once a stable phenomenon is observed. Place the test tube back on the rack.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The food extract is usually light-colored or colorless and transparent or slightly turbid.After Acidification: No obvious precipitate appears; the solution remains clear.After Adding Barium Chloride: If alum is present, a white, fine precipitate or turbidity appears and persists, indicating a positive result.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAlum contains sulfate ions (SO4^2−). After acidification with dilute hydrochloric acid to eliminate interference, the addition of barium chloride introduces Ba^2+ ions, which react with sulfate ions to form barium sulfate (BaSO4), a white insoluble precipitate. The formation of this precipitate serves as the visual basis for alum detection.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Tetracycline Hydrochloride Drug Identification (Ferric Chloride Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Tetracycline Hydrochloride Drug Identification (Ferric Chloride Color Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To identify tetracycline hydrochloride by observing the characteristic color reaction formed between tetracycline and ferric ions, and to master the standard operational steps of dissolution and controlled reagent addition.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (clean and dry), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, glass stirring rod (optional), tetracycline hydrochloride powder (small amount), purified water, ferric chloride solution, protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the test tube rack. Ensure all glassware is transparent and free of contaminants.2. Sample Dissolution: Use a spatula to transfer a small amount of tetracycline hydrochloride powder into the test tube. Add an appropriate amount of purified water to the test tube.3. Dissolving: Gently shake or swirl the test tube until the powder is completely dissolved, forming a clear or slightly yellow solution.4. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, add ferric chloride solution dropwise into the test tube while gently swirling to ensure uniform mixing.5. Observation: Observe the color change of the solution after each drop until a stable and distinct color appears.6. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack for final observation. Dispose of the solution according to laboratory waste regulations and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Tetracycline hydrochloride dissolves in purified water to form a clear or pale yellow solution.2. During Ferric Chloride Addition: Upon dropwise addition of ferric chloride, the solution gradually develops a characteristic yellow-brown to dark coloration.3. Final State: After sufficient ferric chloride is added, the color stabilizes, indicating a positive identification reaction.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleTetracycline hydrochloride contains phenolic and enolic functional groups that can chelate with ferric ions (Fe3+). When ferric chloride is added, a colored coordination complex is formed. The appearance of a characteristic color change serves as qualitative evidence for the presence of tetracycline hydrochloride, forming the basis of this drug identification method.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use only a small amount of sample to avoid overly dark coloration that may obscure observation.2. Add ferric chloride solution strictly dropwise to clearly observe the gradual color change.3. Ensure uniform mixing during reagent addition to avoid localized color concentration.4. Wear protective equipment and handle reagents according to laboratory safety guidelines.

Experimental EquipmentElectronic balance, agar powder, beaker (250 mL), distilled water, glass rod or magnetic stirrer, heating plate, mold or small container, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the beaker on the electronic balance, weigh a fixed mass of agar powder (e.g., 1–2 g), and record the mass. Add a measured volume of water (e.g., 100 mL) into the beaker.2. Dissolution: Place the beaker on a heating plate. Heat the mixture while continuously stirring with a glass rod. Maintain heating until the agar powder is completely dissolved and the solution becomes clear.3. Pouring: Carefully remove the beaker from the heat source. While the solution is still hot and fluid, slowly pour it into a clean mold.4. Cooling and Setting: Leave the mold undisturbed at room temperature. Use time-lapse observation to record the cooling process until the solution sets into a semi-solid gel.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Agar powder appears as a light-colored solid dispersed in water.2. During Heating: With heating and stirring, the solid particles gradually disappear and the solution becomes transparent.3. After Pouring and Cooling: The liquid solution gradually loses fluidity and finally forms a uniform, elastic gel.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAgar is a natural polysaccharide that does not dissolve well in cold water but dissolves upon heating. When heated, agar molecules disperse uniformly in water. Upon cooling, these molecules reassociate to form a three-dimensional network that traps water, resulting in gel formation. This reversible physical process is widely used in food and healthcare products.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Stir continuously during heating to prevent burning or clumping.2. Handle hot solutions carefully to avoid burns.3. Do not disturb the mold during cooling to ensure uniform gel formation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Industrial Salt (Nitrite) Detection Using the Griess Reagent MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Industrial Salt (Nitrite) Detection Using the Griess Reagent Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To detect the presence of nitrite in food by observing the color reaction produced by the Griess reagent, and to master the basic operational steps of adding reagents, mixing, and observing reaction phenomena.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tube (clean and dry), test tube rack, dropper, clear food extract (filtered and transparent), Griess reagent, protective gloves (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube vertically on the test tube rack. Ensure the food extract is clear and free of suspended solids.2. Sample Addition: Pour an appropriate amount (about one third of the test tube volume) of the clear food extract into the test tube.3. Reagent Addition: Use a dropper to add several drops of Griess reagent into the test tube containing the food extract.4. Mixing: Gently shake or tap the test tube to ensure thorough mixing of the reagent and the extract.5. Reaction and Waiting: Allow the test tube to stand for a short time. Keep the camera focused on the test tube, using time-lapse photography to record changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The food extract is colorless or lightly colored and transparent before reagent addition.2. After Reagent Addition and Mixing: If nitrite is present, the solution gradually develops a pink to red coloration.3. Final State: The color stabilizes after a brief waiting period; deeper color indicates higher nitrite content.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe Griess reagent method is based on a diazotization reaction. Nitrite in the food extract reacts under acidic conditions to form nitrous acid, which then reacts with aromatic amines in the Griess reagent to produce a diazonium compound. This compound further couples to form a pink or red azo dye. The appearance and intensity of the color indicate the presence and relative amount of nitrite in the sample.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of Pickling on Food Acidity (Kimchi Pickling)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Pickling on Food Acidity (Kimchi Pickling)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how pickling and fermentation change food acidity by observing the decrease in pH of cabbage during salt-based fermentation; to master the basic operational steps of pickling, safe sampling, and acidity testing using pH paper or a pH meter.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsFresh cabbage (clean, raw leaves), clean transparent glass jar with lid, edible salt, clean hands or food-safe gloves, spoon or tamper (for pressing cabbage), pH paper or digital pH meter, clean small container or dropper (for sampling liquid), label/marker (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wash and dry the glass jar. Rinse cabbage if needed and drain excess water. Prepare salt and testing tools.2. Loading Cabbage: Place fresh cabbage pieces into the clean glass jar until about 3/4 full.3. Salting and Mixing: Sprinkle salt evenly over the cabbage. Use clean hands or a spoon to mix thoroughly so salt contacts all cabbage surfaces.4. Pressing: Firmly press the cabbage downward using a spoon or tamper until liquid is released and partially covers the cabbage.5. Sealing and Fermentation: Seal the jar with the lid. Place the jar at room temperature to ferment.6. Acidity Testing (Intervals): At selected time points (e.g., start and later stage), open the jar briefly. Collect a small amount of liquid and test acidity using pH paper (compare color to scale) or a pH meter (record numerical value). Reseal the jar after testing.7. Documentation: Record pH results at each interval. For demonstration, use time-lapse photography to show changes over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Fresh cabbage appears crisp and pale green/white; little or no liquid is visible; pH is near neutral (higher pH).2. During Fermentation: After salting and pressing, liquid accumulates in the jar; cabbage softens slightly.3. Acidity Change: Over time, pH readings decrease; pH paper shows color change toward acidic range or pH meter shows lower values.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesPickling relies on salt-induced fermentation. Salt draws water from cabbage cells, creating a liquid environment. Naturally present lactic acid bacteria ferment sugars in the cabbage, producing lactic acid. The accumulation of lactic acid lowers the pH, increasing acidity. This acidic environment contributes to flavor development and food preservation.VI. Precautions1. Use a clean jar and tools to avoid contamination.2. Ensure cabbage remains mostly submerged in liquid after pressing.3. Open the jar briefly during testing to minimize disturbance.4. Handle pH testing tools according to instructions and keep them clean.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Heat Denaturation of Protein Using Egg WhiteI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Heat Denaturation of Protein (Egg White)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that protein denatures and coagulates when heated, using egg white as an example, and to understand the effect of heat on protein structure.II. Experimental EquipmentTest tube (1), test tube rack, beaker (500 mL), thermometer (0–100°C), hot water bath or heating plate, liquid egg white (fresh, filtered), glass rod or gentle shaking by hand, water.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Separate fresh egg white and filter to remove impurities. Pour approximately 2–3 mL of liquid egg white into a clean test tube.2. Water Bath Setup: Fill the beaker with water and place it on a heating plate to form a hot water bath. Insert a thermometer into the water to monitor temperature.3. Heating Operation: Place the test tube containing egg white into the hot water bath. Heat gradually while gently shaking the test tube to ensure even heating.4. Controlled Heating: Slowly raise the water temperature (about 60–80°C), maintaining gentle agitation and avoiding direct flame contact with the test tube.5. Completion: Continue heating until obvious changes in the egg white are observed, then remove the test tube and place it on the rack to cool.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The egg white is colorless or slightly transparent and viscous.2. During Heating: As temperature increases, the egg white gradually becomes cloudy.3. Final State: The egg white turns opaque white and coagulates into a solid or semi-solid mass.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesEgg white is rich in protein (mainly albumin). When heated, the protein molecules unfold and lose their natural structure (denaturation). The unfolded proteins aggregate and form a network, causing the liquid egg white to coagulate and turn opaque. This process is irreversible and illustrates heat denaturation of protein, a key concept in nutrition and food hygiene.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a water bath instead of direct heating to avoid sudden overheating.2. Heat gradually and observe temperature changes carefully.3. Handle hot glassware with care to prevent burns.4. Dispose of biological waste properly after the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Heat denaturation of protein, assuming that egg white protein unfolds and coagulates when heated above a critical temperature in a water bath.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Heating increases molecular motion; protein structure is sensitive to temperature; denaturation leads to visible coagulation.Phased Storyline: (1) Clear liquid egg white in test tube at room temperature; (2) Test tube placed in hot water bath with thermometer visible; (3) Gradual heating with gentle shaking shown via time-lapse; (4) Egg white becomes cloudy; (5) Egg white fully opaque and coagulated. Visibility Constraints: Close-up focus on test tube contents, stable view of beaker and thermometer, no extraneous objects or actions.

manual: Organophosphorus Pesticide Residue Detection (Cholinesterase Inhibition Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Organophosphorus Pesticide Residues in Vegetables by Cholinesterase Inhibition Test Strip Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To understand and master the rapid detection method for organophosphorus pesticide residues in vegetables using the cholinesterase inhibition principle; to observe color changes on test strips and judge inhibition strength by comparison with a reference card.II. Experimental Materials and ReagentsTest tubes and rack, dropper or pipette, vegetable extract (prepared by soaking or homogenizing vegetables in water), cholinesterase enzyme reagent, organophosphorus pesticide detection test strips, reference color card, timer or stopwatch, disposable gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Wear gloves to ensure hygiene and safety.2. Sample Addition: Use a dropper to add a fixed volume of vegetable extract into the test tube.3. Enzyme Reaction: Add the specified amount of cholinesterase enzyme reagent into the test tube, gently shake or tap to mix evenly.4. Incubation: Allow the mixture to stand for a short incubation period (brief waiting), which can be shown using time-lapse photography.5. Test Strip Insertion: Insert the detection test strip vertically into the test tube, ensuring the reaction zone is fully immersed but not exceeding the marked line.6. Reaction Timing: After the required reaction time, remove the strip and place it horizontally for color development.7. Result Judgment: Compare the color of the test strip with the reference card to judge the degree of enzyme inhibition and infer the level of organophosphorus pesticide residue.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Vegetable extract and enzyme reagent mixture appears clear or lightly colored, with no obvious change.2. After Reaction: The test strip gradually develops color.3. Result Comparison: Stronger inhibition corresponds to lighter color development on the test strip; weaker inhibition corresponds to darker color, as compared with the reference card.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOrganophosphorus pesticides inhibit cholinesterase activity. In this method, normal enzyme activity causes the substrate on the test strip to react and produce color. If organophosphorus pesticides are present in the vegetable extract, they inhibit cholinesterase, reducing or preventing color development. The degree of color change on the test strip, compared with a standard reference card, reflects the inhibition strength and thus the level of pesticide residue.VI. Precautions1. Ensure correct volumes of sample and reagent for reliable results.2. Insert the test strip vertically and do not exceed the marked immersion line.3. Observe reaction time strictly; premature or delayed reading may affect accuracy.4. Dispose of used strips and reagents according to laboratory hygiene requirements.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Methanol Detection (Fuchsin–Sulfurous Acid Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Methanol Detection by Fuchsin–Sulfurous Acid Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To detect methanol in a clear liquid sample by oxidizing methanol to formaldehyde and observing the characteristic purple coloration with fuchsin–sulfurous acid; to master sequential reagent addition, gentle heating, and observation of color changes.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or pipette, alcohol lamp or electric heater, test tube holder, potassium permanganate solution (dilute, purple), oxalic acid solution (colorless), fuchsin–sulfurous acid reagent (colorless), clear liquid sample (suspected methanol-containing), safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Addition: Place the test tube on the rack and add 2–3 mL of the clear liquid sample.2. Oxidation: Add 2–3 drops of potassium permanganate solution; gently shake to mix.3. Heating: Hold the test tube with a holder and gently heat for a short time until the purple color weakens, then remove heat.4. Cooling: Allow the test tube to cool naturally to room temperature.5. Decolorization: Add oxalic acid solution dropwise until the purple color of permanganate is completely decolorized.6. Color Development: Add 1–2 mL of fuchsin–sulfurous acid reagent, mix gently, and observe.7. Finish: Place the test tube back on the rack for final observation and record results.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Sample is colorless and transparent.2. After KMnO4 Addition and Heating: Solution appears purple and gradually lightens.3. After Oxalic Acid Addition: Purple color disappears, solution becomes colorless.4. After Fuchsin–Sulfurous Acid Addition: If methanol is present, the solution gradually develops a purple to magenta color.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleMethanol is oxidized by potassium permanganate under heating to form formaldehyde. Excess permanganate is removed by oxalic acid to prevent interference. Formaldehyde reacts with fuchsin–sulfurous acid to produce a characteristic purple coloration. The appearance of this color indicates the presence of methanol.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse gentle heating to avoid boiling; ensure complete decolorization before adding fuchsin reagent; observe color changes promptly; wear safety goggles and handle reagents carefully.

Minimum assumptions: standard lab glassware, clear reagent colors, accelerated time-lapse allowed. Phased storyline: (1) Clear sample in test tube; (2) Purple KMnO4 added and gentle heating causes oxidation; (3) Cooling followed by oxalic acid removes purple color; (4) Addition of fuchsin–sulfurous acid leads to visible purple coloration. Key causal transitions must be visually linked to reagent addition; camera remains focused on test tube with clear perspective for color verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sodium Formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite) Detection by Colorimetric MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Colorimetric Detection of Sodium Formaldehydesulfoxylate (Rongalite)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To qualitatively detect the presence of sodium formaldehydesulfoxylate in a sample through an acidified fuchsin-sulfurous acid colorimetric reaction, and to master simple reagent addition and visual color observation techniques.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Equipment: Clean transparent glass test tube (1), test tube rack, droppers (2), stopwatch or timer (optional).2. Reagents: Test solution (suspected to contain Rongalite), dilute hydrochloric acid, fuchsin-sulfurous acid reagent.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clean test tube on the rack. Add 2–3 mL of the test solution into the tube, ensuring it is clear and free of bubbles.2. Acidification: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of dilute hydrochloric acid into the test tube.3. Mixing: Gently shake the test tube to mix the solution evenly.4. Colorimetric Reaction: Using another dropper, add 2–3 drops of fuchsin-sulfurous acid reagent.5. Reaction Standing: Gently shake once more, then keep the test tube still on the rack to allow the reaction to proceed. Observe the solution under good lighting; time-lapse observation may be used to highlight gradual color changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The test solution is colorless or lightly colored and transparent.2. After Adding Hydrochloric Acid: No obvious color change, solution remains clear.3. After Adding Fuchsin-Sulfurous Acid and Standing: If Rongalite is present, the solution gradually develops a characteristic color change (such as fading of fuchsin color or a distinct coloration), becoming clearly distinguishable from the initial state.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleSodium formaldehydesulfoxylate is a strong reducing agent. Under acidic conditions, it reacts with the fuchsin-sulfurous acid reagent, affecting the chromophore structure of fuchsin and causing a visible color change. The appearance or disappearance of color after standing indicates the presence of Rongalite. This qualitative colorimetric method relies on redox reactions and visual comparison, making it suitable for rapid screening in food hygiene inspection.VI. Precautions1. Use clean glassware to avoid contamination affecting color observation.2. Add reagents in the specified order; reversing the order may affect results.3. Observe color changes under consistent lighting conditions.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory safety regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Sudan Red (I–IV) Detection in Chili Powder (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Sudan Red (I–IV) Detection in Chili Powder (Test Strip Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To master the rapid detection method for illegal Sudan Red dyes (I–IV) in chili powder using test strips; to understand standardized sample extraction, correct test strip operation, observation of results, and interpretation based on food hygiene principles.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClean test tube (10–15 mL), test tube rack, ground chili powder sample, Sudan Red (I–IV) extraction solvent, disposable dropper or pipette, Sudan Red (I–IV) test strip, timer or stopwatch, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Sample Preparation: Place a small amount of ground chili powder (about 0.2–0.5 g) into a clean, dry test tube.2. Extraction: Add an appropriate volume of extraction solvent (about 2–3 mL) into the test tube containing the chili powder.3. Mixing: Cap or hold the test tube and shake gently for several seconds to ensure sufficient contact between solvent and sample.4. Standing: Place the test tube upright in a rack and allow it to stand for a short time until solid particles settle and the supernatant becomes relatively clear.5. Test Strip Detection: Take a Sudan Red test strip and insert it vertically into the supernatant liquid, ensuring the arrow end points downward and the liquid level does not exceed the maximum mark on the strip.6. Timing and Removal: After the specified reaction time (usually 3–5 minutes, according to kit instructions), remove the test strip and place it flat on a clean surface.7. Result Reading: Observe the color development of the control line (C) and test line (T) on the strip and record the result.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Chili powder is solid; extraction solvent is clear or lightly colored.2. After Extraction: The solvent becomes colored due to pigment extraction, while solid particles settle at the bottom.3. Test Strip Reaction: After insertion and standing, colored lines appear on the strip.- Negative Result: Two visible lines (C and T) appear, indicating no Sudan Red detected.- Positive Result: Only the control line (C) appears, indicating the presence of Sudan Red dyes.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesSudan Red (I–IV) detection by test strip is based on immunochromatographic competitive binding. Sudan Red dyes, if present in the extracted sample, compete with labeled antigens on the test strip for antibody binding sites. When the dye concentration exceeds the detection limit, the test line does not develop color, indicating a positive result. The control line confirms the validity of the test and proper strip function. This method provides a rapid qualitative screening tool for illegal dyes in food samples.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use clean containers to avoid cross-contamination.2. Insert the test strip vertically and do not exceed the marked immersion line.3. Strictly follow the specified reaction time when reading results.4. Dispose of used strips and samples according to laboratory waste regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Emulsification Stability Test (Oil-Water Emulsion)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Emulsification Stability Test (Oil-Water Emulsion)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To observe the role of an emulsifier in forming and stabilizing an oil-water emulsion, understand basic emulsification principles in food systems, and master standard experimental操作 and observation methods.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTransparent test tube (1), test tube rack, stopper or sealing film, measuring cylinder or dropper, water, edible oil (e.g., vegetable oil), emulsifier (e.g., lecithin solution or food-grade emulsifier), label marker (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry transparent test tube upright on a test tube rack. Ensure all materials are ready and clearly visible.2. Adding Liquids: Measure equal volumes of water and edible oil (e.g., 5 mL each). Pour water into the test tube first, followed by the edible oil, forming two clear layers.3. Adding Emulsifier: Add a small amount of emulsifier (2–3 drops or a pinch) into the test tube.4. Sealing: Seal the test tube tightly with a stopper or sealing film to prevent leakage.5. Shaking: Hold the sealed test tube firmly and shake vigorously for 5–10 seconds to fully mix the contents.6. Standing and Observation: Place the test tube upright on the rack. Observe immediately and then over time. Use time-lapse observation to record changes in layer separation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Before shaking, water and oil form two distinct layers, with oil floating above water.2. Summary of Experimental PrincipleOil and water are immiscible due to differences in polarity. This principle is fundamental in food and nutrition systems such as milk, sauces, and dressings.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use equal volumes of water and oil for clear comparison.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Protease (Gelatinase) Liquefies Gelatin but Not Starch GelI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Protease Liquefies Gelatin but Not Starch Gel2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate substrate specificity of protease (gelatinase) by observing its effect on gelatin gel versus starch gel, and to understand how digestive enzymes act selectively on proteins.II. Experimental Materials and Equipment1. Two clear plastic or glass cups (same size)2. Gelatin gel (prepared and fully set)3. Starch gel (prepared and fully set)4. Protease (gelatinase) solution (same concentration for both cups)5. Dropper or pipette6. Flat surface at room temperature7. Camera or phone with fixed focus for time-lapse recordingIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clear cups side by side on a flat surface. Ensure one cup contains fully set gelatin gel and the other contains fully set starch gel. Both gels should be similar in volume and firmness.2. Initial Observation: Observe and record that both gels are solid and maintain their shape when the cups are gently tilted.3. Addition of Enzyme: Using a dropper, add an equal volume of protease (gelatinase) solution onto the surface of each gel at the same time.4. Incubation: Leave both cups at room temperature. Fix the camera focus and start time-lapse recording. Gently tilt the cups occasionally to test whether the gels maintain their shape.5. Observation and Recording: Continue observing for visible changes in the state of the gels.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both gelatin gel and starch gel are solid and do not flow when tilted.2. After Enzyme Addition: Over time, the gelatin gel gradually softens and then liquefies, showing fluid movement when the cup is tilted.3. Control Comparison: The starch gel shows no obvious change and remains solid, maintaining its shape throughout the observation period.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleProtease (gelatinase) is an enzyme that specifically hydrolyzes proteins. Gelatin is a protein derived from collagen, so it can be broken down by protease into smaller peptides and amino acids, causing the gel structure to collapse and liquefy. Starch gel is composed of polysaccharides rather than proteins, so protease cannot act on it. Therefore, starch gel remains solid. This experiment demonstrates enzyme specificity and reflects how digestive enzymes selectively act on different nutrients.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure both gels are fully set before starting the experiment.2. Use the same volume and concentration of protease solution for both samples.3. Keep environmental conditions consistent to ensure fair comparison.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Protease specificity in nutrition and digestion, showing that gelatinase hydrolyzes protein (gelatin) but not carbohydrate (starch). Minimum assumptions: gelatin and starch gels are correctly prepared and visually distinguishable; protease solution is active; camera perspective remains fixed. Expected phased storyline: Phase 1 – two clear cups with solid gels side by side; Phase 2 – identical protease solution added to both gels; Phase 3 – time-lapse progression at room temperature with occasional tilting; Phase 4 – gelatin gel visibly liquefies and flows upon tilting, while starch gel remains solid and unchanged. Visibility constraints: cups must remain in frame simultaneously, gel states must be clearly observable, and transitions should emphasize causal sequence rather than real-time duration.
