manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodine Solution Reacting with Starch in Bread and PotatoI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Starch in Bread and Potato Using Iodine Solution2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition & Dietetics3. Experiment Objective: To identify the presence of starch in common foods (bread and raw potato) through the color reaction with iodine solution, and to visually compare starch content using time-lapse observation.II. Experimental MaterialsWhite ceramic plate (1); bread slices (2 small pieces); raw potato slices (2 thin pieces); iodine solution (dilute iodine–potassium iodide solution); dropper; camera or smartphone with fixed stand for time-lapse recording; disposable gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the white plate on a flat, well-lit surface. Set up the camera directly above the plate and fix the focus to ensure a clear, stable field of view for time-lapse photography.2. Sample Placement: Place one slice of bread and one slice of raw potato side by side on the plate, leaving a small gap between them for clear comparison.3. Core Operation: Using a dropper, add 1–2 drops of iodine solution onto the surface of the bread slice. Then add 1–2 drops of iodine solution onto the surface of the raw potato slice.4. Observation and Recording: Start time-lapse recording. Observe the color changes on both food surfaces for several seconds as the iodine reacts.5. Completion: Stop recording after the color change stabilizes. Dispose of food samples properly and clean the plate and dropper.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Bread and potato surfaces are light-colored; iodine solution is yellow-brown.2. After Adding Iodine: The areas of bread and raw potato in contact with iodine gradually turn blue-black or dark purple.3. Comparison: Both samples show a clear color change, indicating the presence of starch; intensity may vary slightly between bread and potato.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIodine solution reacts with starch to form a blue-black complex. Starch molecules (amylose) have a helical structure that binds iodine, producing a characteristic dark color. Bread and raw potato are rich in starch, so when iodine contacts their surfaces, a visible blue-black color appears. This reaction is commonly used in nutrition and food science to qualitatively detect starch.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use a white plate to enhance color contrast.2. Avoid excessive iodine drops to prevent spreading that obscures observation.3. Fix camera focus before adding iodine to ensure clear time-lapse recording.4. Iodine can stain; handle carefully and clean promptly after the experiment.

Minimum assumptions: bread and raw potato contain starch; iodine solution produces a blue-black color upon contact with starch; objects remain stationary on a white plate under fixed camera focus.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – white plate with bread and potato placed side by side, camera fixed overhead. (2) Action phase – iodine drops applied sequentially to bread and then potato. (3) Reaction phase – visible transition from yellow-brown iodine to blue-black coloration on contact areas. (4) Stabilization phase – color remains stable for comparison. Visibility constraints: overhead or slightly angled top-down view, clear lighting, stable framing to verify object placement, order of actions, and causal color change.

Basic InformationExperiment Title: Task-Specific Reaching and Grasping with Household Objects After StrokeSubject: Healthcare – PhysiotherapyObjective: To demonstrate and observe task-specific upper-limb rehabilitation in a stroke patient by practicing reaching and grasping common household objects with the affected hand, while ensuring correct movement patterns under therapist supervision and fixed-camera time-lapse recording.II. Experimental Operation Procedure1. Preparation Stage:Position the patient in a seated posture with feet flat on the floor and trunk upright. Place the table at elbow height. The therapist stands beside the affected side, observing joint alignment of shoulder, elbow, wrist, and fingers.3. Core Task Execution:The patient is instructed to reach forward with the affected hand toward the mug, open the fingers, grasp the mug handle, and lift it slightly. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Finger Pulse Oximeter Showing Rhythmic LED Pulsing with HeartbeatI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Heartbeat-Induced LED Pulsing in a Fingertip Pulse Oximeter2. Subject: Healthcare – Physiotherapy3. Experiment Objective: To observe the rhythmic pulsing of LEDs in a fingertip pulse oximeter synchronized with the heartbeat, and to understand the basic working principle of pulse oximetry.II. Experimental EquipmentFingertip pulse oximeter (with red and infrared LEDs), human subject (index finger), stable light source (ambient), camera or smartphone with fixed focus and time-lapse capability, tripod or fixed mount.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ensure the subject is seated comfortably and relaxed. Clean and dry the index finger. Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust framing to clearly include the fingertip and oximeter, and lock focus.2. Device Placement: Open the pulse oximeter and clip it onto the index finger, ensuring the finger is fully inserted and the nail faces upward as indicated by the device.3. Core Operation: Turn on the pulse oximeter. Keep the hand still on a flat surface to minimize motion artifacts.4. Recording: Start time-lapse or continuous recording with fixed focus. Maintain the setup for several seconds to capture multiple heartbeat cycles.5. Completion: Stop recording, turn off the oximeter, and remove it from the finger.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: After activation, the oximeter LEDs illuminate steadily for a brief moment.2. During Measurement: Red and/or infrared LEDs pulse rhythmically. The pulsing frequency corresponds to the subject’s heartbeat.3. Stable State: With the finger still, the LED pulsing remains regular and repeatable over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA fingertip pulse oximeter operates based on photoplethysmography. Red and infrared light emitted by LEDs passes through the fingertip. With each heartbeat, arterial blood volume in the finger increases and decreases, changing light absorption. A photodetector measures these periodic changes, producing a rhythmic signal synchronized with the heartbeat. This signal is used to calculate pulse rate and estimate blood oxygen saturation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep the hand still to avoid motion artifacts.2. Ensure proper finger placement to maintain signal quality.3. Avoid strong external light directly shining into the sensor.4. Fix camera focus and position to ensure clear time-lapse observation.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Adding a Corrective Convex Eyeglass Lens to Restore Near VisionI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Demonstration of Near-Vision Correction Using a Convex Eyeglass LensSubject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision ScienceObjective: To demonstrate how placing a thin convex eyeglass lens in front of the cornea allows a transparent eye model to clearly focus light from a nearby object onto the retina, visualizing the optical correction of reduced near vision.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent eye model with cornea, lens, and retina clearly visible; thin convex eyeglass lens (positive diopter); small nearby object (e.g., printed symbol or arrow card); visible light source or laser beam for ray tracing; adjustable lens holder or hand-held frame; camera fixed on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent eye model on a stable surface. Fix the camera position and manually set the focus so it does not change during recording.2. Initial Observation: Position the nearby object in front of the eye model at a short distance. Shine the visible light beam from the object direction into the eye model and observe the light focusing behind the retina, indicating blurred near vision.3. Core Operation: Slowly place the thin convex eyeglass lens directly in front of the cornea of the eye model, keeping the object, eye, and camera positions unchanged.4. Observation During Adjustment: Observe the change in the light path as it passes through the convex lens and then the eye model.5. Completion: Keep the convex lens steady and record the stabilized light focus on the retina for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Without the eyeglass lens, light rays from the nearby object diverge and focus behind the retina, producing an unfocused image.During Lens Placement: As the convex lens is introduced, the light rays become more convergent before entering the eye.Final State: With the convex lens correctly positioned, the light rays focus precisely on the retinal plane, indicating restored near focus.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA convex eyeglass lens provides additional converging power to the optical system of the eye. For near objects, this compensates for insufficient accommodation by pre-converging incoming light so that the eye’s own lens can bring the image to focus on the retina. This experiment visually demonstrates the optical principle of near-vision correction using positive lenses.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the eye model is transparent and clean for clear light tracing; keep camera focus fixed; avoid moving the object or eye model during the demonstration; use low-power visible light to ensure safety and clarity.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lactic Acid Bacteria Detection (Chromogenic Medium Method)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Detection of Lactic Acid Bacteria Using Chromogenic AgarSubject: Healthcare – Microbiology-ImmunologyObjective: To demonstrate sterile sampling, streaking on chromogenic agar, incubation, and result reading to identify lactic acid bacteria based on colony color.II. Materials and EquipmentChromogenic agar plate for lactic acid bacteria; sterile inoculating loop; alcohol lamp or electric loop sterilizer; sample source (e.g., fermented food suspension); parafilm or plate seal; incubator (30–37°C); marker; gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves. Label the bottom of the agar plate with sample name and date. Keep the plate closed.2. Sterile Sampling: Sterilize the inoculating loop until red-hot; allow it to cool without touching any surface.3. Inoculation: Open the agar plate slightly. Dip the cooled loop into the sample and streak gently across the agar surface using a quadrant streak method. Close the lid promptly.4. Sealing: Seal the plate edge with parafilm to prevent contamination.5. Incubation: Place the inverted plate into the incubator at 30–37°C.6. Removal and Reading: After incubation (24–48 h; shown by time-lapse), remove the plate and observe colony color and distribution without opening the lid.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial: Agar surface is uniform in color with no colonies.After Incubation: Discrete colonies appear along streak lines. Lactic acid bacteria form characteristic colored colonies specified by the chromogenic medium, while non-target bacteria are inhibited or show different colors.V. Experimental PrincipleChromogenic media contain selective agents and chromogenic substrates. Lactic acid bacteria grow under selective conditions and metabolize specific substrates, releasing chromogens that produce characteristic colony colors. This allows visual differentiation and presumptive identification based on color after incubation.VI. PrecautionsMaintain sterile technique throughout. Do not open plates after incubation. Dispose of cultures according to biosafety rules.

Experiment Objective: To demonstrate correct operation of urine nitrite detection using a test strip, observe color change on the nitrite pad, and understand the biochemical principle of nitrite-based screening for urinary tract infection.II. Experimental MaterialsUrine nitrite test strips, fresh urine sample, clean flat surface, disposable dropper, standard color comparison chart, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves. Place one urine test strip flat on a clean, dry surface with the reagent pads facing upward.2. Sample Application: Use a dropper to draw a small amount of urine. Reaction Waiting: Keep the strip stationary and wait briefly (about 30–60 seconds) without shaking or moving the strip.4. Completion: Record the result, then dispose of the strip according to biohazard procedures.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. PrecautionsEnsure the strip is not touched on the reagent area, avoid excess urine, observe timing accurately, and read results promptly to prevent false interpretation.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Parallel Laser Beams Passing Through a Concave LensI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Divergence of Parallel Laser Beams by a Concave Lens2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand how a concave lens causes parallel light rays to diverge, demonstrating the optical principle of negative focal length lenses used in vision correction.II. Experimental EquipmentRay box with parallel laser beams, transparent concave lens, lens stand, optical bench or flat surface, light fog or smoke generator for beam visualization, camera on tripod (fixed focus, time-lapse mode).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the ray box on a stable surface and adjust it to emit several parallel laser beams horizontally. Turn on the light fog so the beam paths are visible in air. Fix the camera on a tripod, set focus manually, and ensure the entire beam path is in frame.Lens Placement: Mount the transparent concave lens vertically on the stand. Initially keep the lens out of the beam path.Core Operation: Slowly slide the concave lens into the path of the parallel laser beams while keeping the camera recording or in time-lapse mode.Observation Step: Allow the beams to pass fully through the lens and continue into the fog-filled space beyond.Completion: Stop recording after the beam paths are clearly visible before and after the lens.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Before the lens is introduced, the laser beams travel parallel to each other in straight lines.2. As the beams pass through the concave lens, each beam bends outward.3. After exiting the lens, the beams spread apart, appearing to diverge from a virtual focal point on the incident side of the lens.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesA concave lens is a diverging lens with a negative focal length. When parallel light rays pass through it, refraction at the lens surfaces causes the rays to bend away from the principal axis. The rays appear to originate from a virtual focus on the same side as the incoming light. This principle explains how concave lenses are used in optometry to correct myopia by diverging incoming light before it reaches the eye.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the lens is clean and properly aligned; avoid direct eye exposure to laser beams; keep camera focus fixed to maintain consistent visualization.

Experimental EquipmentIdentical human hair strands (2 strands, same length and thickness), clamps or clip holders (2), rigid support frame or stand, identical small weights (2), water container, absorbent paper, ruler or scale marker, camera with fixed tripod for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select two identical hair strands. Keep one strand completely dry. Soak the other strand in water for sufficient time, then gently blot excess surface water without drying it.2. Setup: Fix the support frame. Loading: Attach identical weights to the lower end of each hair strand simultaneously, ensuring equal gravitational force acts on both.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position so both strands remain fully visible. Start time-lapse or accelerated recording without changing focus or angle.5. Observation Period: Allow stretching to occur under constant load for a short, fixed duration suitable for time-lapse capture.6. Completion: Stop recording, remove the weights, and safely dismantle the setup.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both hair strands have the same original length before loading.2. Final State: After stabilization, the wet hair shows greater extension, while the dry hair shows less deformation or may break earlier in extended tests.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesHuman hair is composed mainly of keratin. When hair absorbs water, hydrogen bonds within keratin temporarily weaken, increasing flexibility and extensibility. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Cephalosporin Drug Identification (Hydroxamic Acid Iron Color Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Cephalosporin Drug Identification by Hydroxamic Acid Iron Color Method2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To identify cephalosporin drugs by forming a colored ferric–hydroxamate complex through visual observation, and to master the standard stepwise addition and mixing technique in qualitative drug identification.II. Experimental Equipment and Reagents1. Equipment: Test tube (1), test tube rack, droppers (3–4), glass stirring rod (optional).2. Reagents (aqueous): Cephalosporin sample solution, hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution, sodium hydroxide solution, ferric chloride solution.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube on the rack. Using a dropper, add about 1–2 mL of cephalosporin sample solution into the test tube.2. Hydroxylamine Reaction: Add several drops of hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution into the test tube. Gently shake or swirl to mix evenly.3. Alkalization: Add an appropriate amount of sodium hydroxide solution dropwise. Gently mix again and allow the reaction to proceed briefly, forming hydroxamic acid derivatives.4. Color Development: Add ferric chloride solution dropwise along the inner wall of the test tube. Observe the color change carefully.5. Completion: Stop adding ferric chloride once a stable color appears. Place the test tube back on the rack for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The cephalosporin sample solution is colorless or lightly colored and transparent.2. After Hydroxylamine and Sodium Hydroxide Addition: The solution remains clear or shows no obvious color change.3. After Ferric Chloride Addition: A distinct red-purple or reddish-brown color appears, indicating a positive reaction for cephalosporins.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCephalosporins contain a β-lactam structure that reacts with hydroxylamine under alkaline conditions to form hydroxamic acids. These hydroxamic acids subsequently react with ferric ions (Fe3+) to form a stable colored ferric–hydroxamate complex. The appearance of a red-purple or reddish-brown color serves as qualitative evidence for the presence of cephalosporin drugs.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Add reagents in strict order; incorrect sequence may affect results.2. Add ferric chloride dropwise to avoid excessive coloration.3. Use clean droppers to prevent cross-contamination.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory regulations.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Qualitative identification of cephalosporin drugs using the hydroxamic acid iron color method. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: cephalosporin reacts with hydroxylamine under alkaline conditions to form hydroxamic acids, which then complex with Fe3+ to produce a characteristic color. Phased storyline: (1) static clear sample solution in test tube; (2) hydroxylamine addition and gentle mixing without visible change; (3) sodium hydroxide addition enabling reaction, still minimal visual change; (4) ferric chloride added dropwise leading to rapid appearance of red-purple/reddish-brown color. Visibility constraints: close-up focus on test tube, clear view of droppers, sequential actions emphasized via time-lapse while preserving correct order and causality.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Triceps Brachii ReflexI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Triceps Brachii Tendon Reflex DemonstrationSubject: Healthcare - Human Physiology (Neurophysiology)Objective: To observe the triceps brachii reflex by tapping the triceps tendon and to understand the reflex arc involved in spinal reflexes.II. Experimental EquipmentReflex hammer; chair or stool; cooperative human subject; optional camera for focused or time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Seat the subject comfortably on a chair. Ask the subject to relax the upper limb.2. Positioning: Flex the subject’s elbow to approximately 90 degrees, allowing the forearm to hang loosely. Ensure the triceps muscle is relaxed.3. Examiner Hand Placement: The examiner stands to the side or behind, supporting the subject’s arm if necessary to maintain relaxation.4. Core Operation: Identify the triceps tendon just above the olecranon of the ulna. Position the reflex hammer above this point and tap the tendon once with a quick, controlled motion.5. Recording/Observation: Focus the camera on the elbow and forearm region. Time-lapse or slow-motion capture may be used to emphasize the tapping action and resulting movement.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The subject’s arm is relaxed, elbow flexed, with no voluntary movement.2. Upon Tapping: Immediately after the tendon is tapped, the triceps muscle contracts involuntarily.3. Result: The forearm extends briefly at the elbow, demonstrating the triceps reflex.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe triceps brachii reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex. Tapping the triceps tendon stretches the muscle, activating muscle spindle receptors. Sensory impulses travel via afferent neurons to the spinal cord (primarily C7–C8 segments), where they synapse directly with motor neurons. Motor impulses then return to the triceps muscle, causing contraction and resulting in elbow extension. This reflex tests the integrity of the peripheral nerve, spinal segment, and neuromuscular junction.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the subject is relaxed; excessive force or repeated tapping should be avoided; tap only once to elicit a clear reflex; stop if the subject feels discomfort.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Bile Fat Emulsification Detection (Simulation Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bile Fat Emulsification Detection (Simulation Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To simulate and observe the role of bile in fat emulsification, understand how bile promotes fat digestion by dispersing large fat droplets into smaller ones, and master basic experimental observation methods using transparent containers.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent test tube with cap (1), test tube rack, droppers (2–3), transparent beaker (optional support), clean water, edible oil (as simulated fat), simulated bile solution (e.g., dilute detergent or bile salt solution), paper towels.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the transparent test tube upright on the rack. Ensure it is clean and dry.2. Adding Materials: Use a dropper to add clean water to about half the volume of the test tube. Then add a small amount of edible oil so that a clear oil layer floats above the water.3. Initial Mixing: Cap the test tube and gently shake it for a few seconds. Place it back on the rack for brief observation.4. Adding Simulated Bile: Use a dropper to add several drops of simulated bile solution into the test tube.5. Core Operation: Cap the test tube again and shake gently but evenly for several seconds to allow full interaction between bile, oil, and water.6. Completion: Place the test tube back on the rack. Record observations. Dispose of liquids properly and clean all equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Oil and water form two distinct layers, with oil floating above water.2. After Initial Shaking (Without Bile): Oil temporarily disperses but quickly separates again into a clear upper layer.3. After Adding Simulated Bile and Shaking: The oil layer breaks into much smaller droplets dispersed throughout the water, remaining suspended for a longer time, indicating emulsification.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleBile contains bile salts that act as natural emulsifiers. They reduce surface tension between fat and water, breaking large fat globules into many smaller droplets. This increases the surface area of fats, making them easier for digestive enzymes to act upon. In this simulation, the bile solution performs a similar role, demonstrating how bile promotes fat emulsification rather than chemically digesting fats.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use transparent containers to clearly observe material changes.2. Shake gently to avoid leakage or splashing.3. Do not ingest any experimental materials.4. Clean all equipment after the experiment to maintain hygiene.

The camera remains focused on the test tube with time-lapse acceleration, avoiding explicit final outcome emphasis while clearly showing causal transitions.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Moro Reflex Demonstration (Human Infant)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Moro Reflex Demonstration in a Human Infant2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology – Neonatal Reflexes3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe the Moro reflex by applying a brief and gentle change in head support, understanding its physiological basis and typical behavioral pattern.II. Experimental Conditions and SafetyCaregiver trained in infant handling; calm environment; infant awake and not crying; infant placed on a firm, padded surface. Head and neck must be supported at all times except for a brief controlled lowering. Stop immediately if infant shows distress.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Lay the infant in a supine position on a padded surface. The caregiver positions both hands to support the infant’s head and upper back, fingers spread for stability.2. Initial State Observation: Confirm the infant is calm, with arms resting near the body and normal breathing.3. Core Operation: While maintaining full control, the caregiver briefly and gently lowers the support of the infant’s head by a few centimeters, creating a short sensation of falling.4. Immediate Restoration: Instantly restore full head and upper body support to the original position.5. Recording Method: Use focused framing on the infant’s head, shoulders, and arms. Apply time-lapse or slight acceleration to fit within a short demonstration while preserving sequence.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Immediately after the brief change in support, the infant exhibits a startle response.2. Phase One: Sudden abduction and extension of both arms, opening of hands; shoulders may move outward.3. Phase Two: Arms then move back toward the midline (adduction), often followed by flexion.4. Accompanying signs may include a brief cry or facial expression of surprise.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Moro reflex is a primitive neonatal reflex mediated by the brainstem and vestibular system. PrecautionsLowering must be minimal and gentle; never allow uncontrolled head drop. Ensure infant comfort and terminate the demonstration if distress persists.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Iodine Diffusing into a Starch Agar Gel BlockI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Diffusing into a Starch Agar Gel Block2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (basic biomedical diffusion model)3. Experiment Objective: To observe diffusion of a small molecule through a gel matrix and the color reaction between iodine and starch, and to understand diffusion as a model for substance transport in biological tissues.II. Experimental EquipmentStarch agar gel cube (clear, ~2–3 cm per side), iodine solution (brown), shallow transparent dish or Petri dish, dropper or pipette, camera or smartphone with tripod (for time-lapse), gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the clear starch agar gel cube at the center of a clean, transparent dish. Ensure the gel is intact and colorless.2. Core Operation: Using a dropper, gently pour iodine solution into the dish so that it surrounds all sides of the gel cube without disturbing its position.3. Time-Lapse Setup: Once the gel is fully surrounded, stop pouring and leave the system undisturbed. Fix the camera focus and position above or at the side of the dish for time-lapse recording.4. Observation Period: Allow the system to stand while recording. Do not shake or move the dish.5. Completion: After sufficient time, stop recording and dispose of iodine solution properly; clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The starch agar gel cube is clear and colorless; iodine solution around it is brown.2. During Diffusion: The outer surface of the gel gradually turns blue-black, forming a dark layer.3. Progression: The dark region slowly moves inward from the surface toward the center, showing a clear diffusion front.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesIodine molecules diffuse from a region of higher concentration (the surrounding solution) into a region of lower concentration (the gel). When iodine encounters starch in the agar, it forms a blue-black complex. The visible inward movement of color represents diffusion, a fundamental process relevant to medicine, such as drug penetration into tissues.VI. Experimental PrecautionsPour iodine gently to avoid moving the gel; keep the setup undisturbed; iodine stains skin and surfaces, so handle with care.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine pH Measurement (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Urine pH Measurement Using Test Strips2. Subject: Healthcare – Renal Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To determine the pH of urine using a pH test strip, understand the clinical significance of urine pH, and master the correct operational steps for test strip measurement.II. Experimental EquipmentClean urine sample container with fresh urine sample, urine pH test strips, standard pH color chart (provided with strips), disposable gloves, tissue or absorbent paper.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear disposable gloves and ensure the urine sample container is clean and properly labeled. Place the container on a stable surface.2. Strip Removal: Open the test strip container and remove one pH test strip without touching the reactive end.3. Dipping: Briefly dip the reactive end of the strip into the urine sample (about 1 second), ensuring only the reactive area contacts the urine.4. Removal: Remove the strip promptly from the urine to avoid over-soaking.5. Holding: Hold the strip horizontally to prevent reagent mixing or runoff.6. Comparison: After the specified reaction time (as per manufacturer, usually a few seconds), compare the color of the reactive area with the standard pH color chart.7. Reading: Determine and record the urine pH value that most closely matches the observed color.8. Disposal: Discard the used strip in appropriate waste and close the urine container.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The unused pH test strip has a uniform baseline color on the reactive pad.2. After Dipping: The reactive end changes color within seconds after contact with urine.3. Comparison Result: The final stabilized color corresponds to a specific pH value on the color chart.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleUrine pH test strips contain chemical indicators that change color in response to hydrogen ion concentration. When the strip contacts urine, the indicators undergo acid–base reactions, producing a color change proportional to the urine pH. Comparing this color with a calibrated chart allows estimation of urine acidity or alkalinity, which reflects renal regulation of acid–base balance.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh urine samples to ensure accuracy.2. Do not immerse the strip for too long to avoid inaccurate readings.3. Hold the strip horizontally during color development.4. Compare colors under adequate lighting and within the recommended time window.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Pupillary Accommodation Reflex (Far Object)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Pupillary Accommodation Reflex (Far Object)2. Subject: Healthcare – Human Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the pupillary accommodation reflex when shifting gaze from a near object to a distant object, focusing on changes in pupil size and eye gaze direction.II. Experimental EquipmentHuman subject (healthy adult), near fixation target (finger or small object held ~20–30 cm from eyes), distant fixation target (object placed >3 m away), camera with eye-level close-up capability, stable lighting, chair or stool.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: The subject sits upright on a chair, head facing forward, eyes open, under stable and moderate lighting. The camera is positioned to focus clearly on both eyes.2. Near Fixation: The subject holds a finger or small object in front of the eyes at near distance and fixates on it steadily for 2–3 seconds.3. Gaze Shift Operation: Upon instruction, the subject shifts gaze from the near finger to a distant target straight ahead, without moving the head.4. Recording: The camera continuously records the eyes during the entire process, using time-lapse or accelerated recording to clearly show pupil size changes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: During near fixation, the pupils are relatively constricted.2. During Gaze Shift: As the gaze moves from the near object to the distant target, the eyes reorient while the head remains still.3. Final State: After fixation on the distant object, the pupils gradually dilate compared with the near-fixation state.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe pupillary accommodation reflex is a physiological response controlled by the autonomic nervous system. When viewing near objects, parasympathetic activity causes pupil constriction to improve visual acuity. When shifting gaze to a far object, parasympathetic tone decreases and sympathetic influence allows the pupils to dilate, admitting more light. This coordinated change in pupil size accompanies lens accommodation and eye alignment adjustments, enabling clear vision at different distances.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure lighting remains constant, as light intensity also affects pupil size.2. The subject should avoid head movement and blinking as much as possible during recording.3. Camera focus must remain on the eyes to accurately capture pupil changes.

Verification requires a close-up eye perspective, stable framing, and sufficient temporal continuity to observe gradual pupil size change.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Colorimetric LAMP Reaction Showing Solution Color Change When Target DNA Is PresentI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Colorimetric LAMP Detection of Target DNA2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine – Molecular Diagnostics3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate that loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) can detect target DNA through a visible color change using a colorimetric indicator, and to compare a positive sample with a negative control under identical incubation conditions.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentClear reaction tubes (2 identical tubes), colorimetric LAMP reaction mix (containing primers, polymerase, buffer, and pH-sensitive indicator), target DNA sample, nuclease-free water (negative control), pipettes and tips, heated block or water bath set to 60–65°C, tube rack, lab bench, camera fixed on tripod for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two identical clear tubes on the lab bench. Add equal volumes of colorimetric LAMP mix to each tube.2. Sample Addition: Add target DNA solution to one tube (sample tube). Add an equal volume of nuclease-free water to the other tube (control tube).3. Mixing: Gently tap or briefly centrifuge both tubes to ensure uniform mixing, avoiding bubbles.4. Incubation Setup: Place both tubes together into a preheated heated block at 60–65°C.5. Recording: Fix the camera focus and angle on the tubes and begin time-lapse recording.6. Incubation: Incubate for 20–30 minutes (or accelerated for demonstration), without moving the tubes.7. Completion: Stop incubation and recording after a clear color difference is observed.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes show the same initial color (typically pink or red, depending on the indicator).2. During Incubation: The sample tube gradually changes color (for example, from pink to yellow), while the control tube remains unchanged.3. Final State: A clear color contrast is visible between the sample and control tubes.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLAMP is an isothermal nucleic acid amplification method. When target DNA is present, rapid amplification occurs, producing protons as byproducts. These protons lower the pH of the reaction mixture, causing the pH-sensitive colorimetric indicator to change color. In the absence of target DNA, no amplification occurs, the pH remains stable, and the solution color does not change.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Colorimetric LAMP detection relies on isothermal DNA amplification producing a visible pH-dependent color change only when target DNA is present. Minimum assumptions include identical tubes, equal reaction volumes, correct incubation temperature, and a fixed camera perspective.Phased Storyline: (1) Setup phase: two identical clear tubes with the same initial color are prepared on a lab bench. (2) Intervention phase: one tube receives target DNA, the other receives clear control. (3) Incubation phase: both tubes are placed together in a heated block, camera fixed for time-lapse. (4) Outcome phase: over time, only the sample tube changes color while the control remains unchanged. Visibility constraints: the tubes must stay in frame with stable lighting and focus so gradual color change and causal sequence can be verified.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Helicobacter pylori Detection (Urease Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Helicobacter pylori Detection by Urease Test Strip MethodSubject: Healthcare – Microbiology-ImmunologyExperiment Objective: To demonstrate the rapid detection of Helicobacter pylori based on urease activity by placing a gastric biopsy sample onto a urease test strip, adding reagent, and observing the indicator color change.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentUrease test strip (with pH indicator), small test card with closable cover, gastric biopsy sample (clinical specimen or simulated sample), reagent dropper bottle (urea-containing reagent), disposable forceps, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Wear gloves. Place the urease test strip flat inside the test card, ensuring the indicator area is clearly visible.2. Sample Placement: Using disposable forceps, gently place a small gastric biopsy sample directly onto the reactive area of the urease test strip.3. Reagent Addition: Hold the reagent dropper vertically and add one drop of reagent onto the test strip at the sample location.4. Card Closure: Close the test card carefully to ensure contact between sample, reagent, and strip.5. Waiting Period: Allow the card to stand briefly (seconds to minutes). In demonstration, this step may be shown using time-lapse photography.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The test strip indicator shows its original color (typically yellow or light orange).After Reaction: If Helicobacter pylori is present, the indicator area gradually changes to red or pink, indicating a rise in pH. Avoid cross-contamination between samples. Dispose of biological materials according to safety regulations.

manual: Experiment Instruction ManualI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Small vs Large Light Source on Shadow Sharpness (Penumbra Demonstration)2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences3. Knowledge Point: Small vs large light source casting shadows to model focal spot size and penumbra4. Experiment Objective: To visually demonstrate how light source size affects shadow sharpness and penumbra width, modeling the effect of small versus large focal spots in radiographic imaging.II. Experimental Equipment1. Light stand with interchangeable bulbs2. Small bare bulb (point-like light source)3. Large diffused bulb or bulb with diffuser (extended light source)4. Thin metal cutout (e.g., metal plate with holes or sharp edges)5. Flat wall or projection screen6. Measuring tape or fixed spacers (to maintain constant distances)7. Camera mounted on tripod (focus fixed, time-lapse or continuous capture enabled)8. Darkened room to reduce ambient lightIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:- Darken the room and clear the area between the light stand and the wall.- Mount the camera on a tripod facing the wall; fix focus, exposure, and zoom so they remain unchanged throughout the experiment.2. Setup:- Place the light stand at a fixed distance from the wall (e.g., 2 meters).- Position the thin metal cutout midway between the light source and the wall, perpendicular to the light beam.- Measure and confirm that distances between light source, cutout, and wall remain constant for all trials.3. Small Light Source Observation:- Install the small bare bulb on the light stand.- Turn on the bulb and allow the shadow of the metal cutout to fall on the wall.- Record images or video using the fixed camera.- Observe and note the sharpness of shadow edges.4. Large Light Source Observation:- Without moving the camera, wall, or cutout, replace the small bare bulb with the larger diffused bulb.- Turn on the diffused bulb and allow the shadow to form on the wall.- Record images or video under identical camera settings.5. Completion:- Turn off the light source.- Review recorded images or footage for comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. With the small bare bulb:- The shadow of the metal cutout appears dark with sharp, well-defined edges.- The penumbra region is minimal or nearly absent.2. With the large diffused bulb:- The shadow appears lighter with blurred, widened edges.- A clear penumbra region is visible between the full shadow (umbra) and illuminated area.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment models the radiographic principle of focal spot size and penumbra formation. A small light source behaves like a small focal spot, producing rays that diverge minimally, resulting in sharp shadows with narrow penumbra. A larger light source emits rays from multiple points, increasing geometric unsharpness and producing a wider penumbra with blurred shadow edges. In radiography, smaller focal spots improve spatial resolution, while larger focal spots increase penumbra and reduce image sharpness.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Keep all distances fixed when changing bulbs to ensure fair comparison.2. Do not adjust camera focus or position between trials.3. Avoid ambient light interference to maintain clear shadow contrast.4. Handle bulbs carefully to prevent burns or breakage.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate how light source size affects shadow sharpness and penumbra, modeling focal spot size in radiography. Minimum assumptions: a fixed wall, a stationary thin metal cutout, constant distances, and two light sources differing only in effective emitting area.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial setup shows wall, cutout, and small bare bulb aligned; (2) small source turned on, producing a sharp-edged shadow; (3) light source changes to larger diffused bulb without moving other elements; (4) shadow edges visibly broaden, forming a penumbra; (5) side-by-side or sequential comparison reinforces causal link between source size and geometric unsharpness. Camera perspective must remain fixed to verify differences clearly.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Effect of Vitamin E on Lipid Oxidation Inhibition (Simulation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Effect of Vitamin E on Lipid Oxidation Inhibition (Simulation)2. Subject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food Hygiene3. Experiment Objective: To simulate and demonstrate the inhibitory effect of vitamin E on lipid oxidation by comparing oxidation levels in edible oil samples with and without vitamin E under mild heating conditions, and to master basic操作流程 of antioxidant comparison experiments.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsBeakers (2, identical size), edible oil (same type and volume for both samples), vitamin E solution, dropper, electric heater or hot plate, glass stirring rods (2), thermometer (optional), peroxide value test strips, timer, heat-resistant gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean beakers side by side on a stable lab bench. Add equal volumes of edible oil into each beaker to ensure comparability.2. Group Setting: Label one beaker as the control group and the other as the vitamin E group.3. Addition of Vitamin E: Use a dropper to add a measured amount of vitamin E solution into the vitamin E group beaker. Do not add anything to the control beaker.4. Heating and Stirring: Place both beakers on the heater. Heat mildly while continuously stirring each sample with separate glass rods to ensure uniform heating and exposure to oxygen.5. Heating Termination: After a fixed heating time, turn off the heater and remove the beakers using heat-resistant gloves.6. Oxidation Testing: Dip peroxide value test strips into each oil sample according to the instructions, ensuring identical sampling time and method for both groups.7. Completion: Place used test strips aside for comparison and clean all equipment after the experiment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both oil samples are clear liquids before heating.2. During Heating: Oils remain in liquid state while being stirred and heated uniformly.3. After Testing: Test strips indicate different oxidation levels between the two samples (phenomenon recorded without describing color details).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLipid oxidation is accelerated by heat and oxygen, leading to the formation of peroxides. Vitamin E is a fat-soluble antioxidant that can interrupt free radical chain reactions during lipid oxidation. In this simulated experiment, mild heating accelerates oxidation, while the presence of vitamin E inhibits peroxide formation. Comparing peroxide value test results between the control and vitamin E groups demonstrates the antioxidant role of vitamin E in lipid systems.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure equal oil volumes and identical heating conditions for both beakers.2. Avoid overheating to prevent safety hazards.3. Use separate stirring rods to avoid cross-contamination.4. Follow test strip instructions strictly for reliable comparison.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Separation and Re-forming of a Topical Oil-in-Water Emulsion After AgitationSubject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Pharmaceutics)Objective: To demonstrate the physical instability and reversible dispersion behavior of a topical oil-in-water emulsion through visual observation after mechanical agitation.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTransparent glass or plastic jar with lid (1)White topical oil-in-water emulsion (commercial cream or lotion, filling ~1/2 jar)Flat table surfaceCamera with fixed focus and tripod (for time-lapse recording)III. Observation Stage: Place the jar back on the table in the same position and continue recording without disturbing it.5. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Orexin Detection by Immunological Test StripSubject: Healthcare – Digestive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the use of an immunological lateral flow test strip for detecting orexin in a biological sample, observe liquid migration and line formation, and understand the underlying immunological detection principle.II. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove the test strip from its packaging and place it on a clean, dry, flat surface. Ensure the strip is intact and clearly labeled.2. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: IgM Detection (Simplified ELISA)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Detection of Serum IgM by Simplified ELISA2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic procedure and principle of IgM detection using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and to understand antigen–antibody specificity and enzyme–substrate color development.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsPre-coated ELISA microplate (antigen-coated wells), adjustable micropipette with tips, diluted serum samples, wash buffer, enzyme-labeled anti-human IgM antibody, chromogenic substrate (e.g., TMB), stop solution, waste container.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the antigen-coated microplate on a flat surface. Prepare diluted serum samples and set the micropipette to the required volume.2. Serum Addition: Use the pipette to add diluted serum into designated wells. Avoid touching the well walls. Gently tap the plate to ensure even coverage.3. Incubation: Allow the plate to incubate briefly so that IgM in the serum can bind to the immobilized antigen.4. Washing: Discard liquid from the wells and wash with wash buffer 2–3 times to remove unbound components.5. Antibody Addition: Add enzyme-labeled anti-IgM antibody to each well using the pipette.6. Second Incubation: Incubate briefly to allow the labeled antibody to bind to captured IgM.7. Second Washing: Wash the wells again to remove unbound labeled antibody.8. Substrate Addition: Add chromogenic substrate to each well. Observe gradual color development.9. Reaction Stopping: Add stop solution to terminate the reaction, fixing the final color.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Wells are colorless after washing.2. After Substrate Addition: Wells containing IgM gradually develop a visible color, while negative wells remain colorless or faint.3. After Stopping: The color becomes stable and clearly distinguishable between positive and negative wells.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the ELISA principle. Antigen pre-coated on the microplate specifically binds IgM antibodies in the serum. An enzyme-labeled anti-IgM antibody then binds to the captured IgM. After washing away unbound substances, the added substrate reacts with the enzyme to produce a colored product. The presence and intensity of color indicate the presence of IgM in the sample.VI. PrecautionsPipette accurately, avoid cross-contamination, ensure proper washing, and follow the correct order of steps.

manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Classroom MRI Analogy Using Spinning TopsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Alignment and Precession of Spinning Tops Near a Magnet (MRI Analogy)2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences3. Experiment Objective: To use a mechanical analogy to illustrate how nuclear spins align and precess in an external magnetic field, helping students intuitively understand basic MRI concepts such as alignment, perturbation, and precession.II. Experimental EquipmentSmooth tabletop; shallow smooth tray (non-magnetic); identical spinning tops (3–6, same size and color); strong bar magnet (clearly marked poles); camera or smartphone with tripod; adequate lighting.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the smooth tray on the tabletop. Position the bar magnet beside one long edge of the tray, parallel to it. Fix the camera on a tripod above or at a slight angle to the tray; lock focus and exposure for time-lapse.2. Initial State Setup: Place identical spinning tops upright on the tray at similar distances from the magnet. Ensure no contact with the magnet.3. Core Operation: Spin all tops simultaneously so they rotate freely. Once stable spinning is achieved, briefly nudge the tray laterally and immediately release it, leaving the system undisturbed.4. Recording: Start time-lapse recording immediately after the nudge. Do not touch the tray, magnet, or tops during recording.5. Completion: Stop recording after observable changes in top orientation and motion are captured.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: All tops spin upright with random orientation relative to the magnet.2. After Nudge: The brief perturbation causes a change in motion; spinning axes wobble.3. During Undisturbed Spinning: Tops closer to the magnet tend to show a preferred orientation and exhibit steady precessional motion (wobbling around a mean direction) while continuing to spin.4. Time-Lapse View: Gradual, smooth changes in orientation become clear when viewed in accelerated time.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis demonstration is a mechanical analogy to MRI physics. In MRI, nuclear spins placed in a strong external magnetic field tend to align with the field and precess around its direction. The spinning tops represent nuclear spins; the bar magnet represents the external magnetic field (B0). The brief nudge simulates an excitation or perturbation, after which the tops continue spinning and precessing, analogous to how nuclear spins precess after excitation. While not a literal magnetic interaction, the analogy helps visualize alignment, perturbation, and precession in MRI.VI. Experimental PrecautionsEnsure the tray is smooth and level; keep magnet strength sufficient but not in contact; avoid touching the setup during recording; maintain fixed camera focus for clear time-lapse comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Dendritic Cell Detection (Fluorescent Antibody Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Fluorescent Antibody Detection of Dendritic Cells2. Subject: Healthcare – Basic Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To identify dendritic cells by specific binding of fluorescent-labeled antibodies and to master the basic workflow of immunofluorescence staining, including cell smear preparation, fixation, blocking, antibody incubation, washing, mounting, and fluorescence microscopy observation.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsGlass slides with prepared dendritic cell smears, fluorescence-labeled anti-dendritic cell antibody (e.g., anti-CD11c-FITC), fixative (4% paraformaldehyde or cold acetone), blocking solution (5% BSA or normal serum), PBS buffer, micropipettes and tips, humidified incubation box, wash bottle, mounting medium (with or without DAPI), coverslips, fluorescence microscope, gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the prepared dendritic cell smear on a clean glass slide and allow it to air-dry. Wear gloves and ensure the slide is properly labeled.2. Fixation: Add fixative to fully cover the cell smear and incubate for 10 minutes at room temperature to preserve cell morphology and antigens. Remove fixative and rinse gently with PBS.3. Blocking: Add blocking solution to cover the smear and incubate for 10 minutes to reduce non-specific antibody binding. Drain excess blocking solution without washing.4. Antibody Staining: Add fluorescent-labeled anti-dendritic cell antibody evenly onto the smear. Place the slide in a humidified box and incubate for 20 minutes in the dark.5. Washing: Gently rinse the slide with PBS 2–3 times to remove unbound antibody, avoiding direct strong flow on the smear.6. Mounting: Add one drop of mounting medium to the smear and carefully place a coverslip to avoid air bubbles.7. Observation: Place the slide on the fluorescence microscope stage. Select the appropriate excitation wavelength and observe dendritic cells showing specific fluorescence. Use time-lapse compression to show progression from staining to observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Under bright-field, cells appear colorless and transparent with visible morphology.2. After Staining: Under fluorescence microscopy, dendritic cells exhibit specific fluorescent signals on the cell surface or cytoplasm, while background remains dark.3. Final Observation: Fluorescently labeled dendritic cells are clearly distinguishable from non-labeled cells.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on the specific antigen–antibody reaction. Fluorescent-labeled antibodies bind selectively to surface markers expressed by dendritic cells. When excited by specific wavelengths of light in a fluorescence microscope, the fluorophore emits visible fluorescence, enabling visualization and identification of dendritic cells.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Perform antibody incubation in the dark to prevent photobleaching.2. Avoid drying of the cell smear during staining steps.3. Handle slides gently during washing to prevent cell loss.4. Dispose of biological waste according to laboratory safety regulations.

manual: Experiment Title: Parallel-Hole Plate Converting a Wide Light Source into Straight RaysI. Basic Experiment InformationSubject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging SciencesObjective: To demonstrate how a parallel-hole plate (collimator) converts divergent light from a wide-angle source into approximately straight, parallel rays, illustrating the basic principle of beam collimation used in radiographic imaging.II. Experimental Equipment1. Bright wide-angle lamp (continuous light source)2. Metal plate with straight, evenly spaced parallel holes (parallel-hole plate)3. Flat white wall or projection screen4. Camera mounted on tripod (focus fixed, time-lapse or continuous recording mode)5. Darkened room to enhance contrastIII. Experimental Procedure1. Setup: Place the lamp on a stable surface facing the wall at a distance of about 1–2 meters. Ensure the lamp emits a wide-angle beam illuminating a broad area of the wall.2. Camera Preparation: Mount the camera on a tripod facing the wall. Adjust framing to include the illuminated wall area. Fix focus and exposure; do not change settings during recording.3. Initial Observation: Turn on the lamp and record the initial state. Observe that the wall is illuminated broadly and diffusely by the wide-angle light.4. Core Operation: Slowly slide the metal plate with straight parallel holes into the path of the light beam between the lamp and the wall, keeping the plate perpendicular to the beam direction.5. Recording: Continue recording as the plate moves fully into the beam path, ensuring smooth motion for clear time-lapse or continuous visualization.6. Completion: Stop recording once the plate is fully inserted and the light pattern on the wall stabilizes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Without the plate, the wall shows a wide, diffuse روشن area with no distinct straight boundaries.2. During Plate Insertion: As the parallel-hole plate enters the beam, the illuminated area on the wall narrows. Diffuse light decreases, and distinct linear or band-like bright regions begin to appear.3. Final State: With the plate fully in place, the wall displays straighter, more collimated light patterns corresponding to rays that have passed through the parallel holes; oblique rays are largely blocked.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe parallel-hole plate acts as a collimator. Each straight hole allows only light traveling approximately parallel to the hole axis to pass through, while absorbing or blocking obliquely incident rays. As a result, a divergent wide-angle light source is transformed into a set of near-parallel rays. This principle is fundamental in radiography and nuclear medicine imaging, where collimators are used to improve image directionality and spatial resolution by controlling photon paths.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the lamp does not overheat during operation.2. Keep the plate steady and perpendicular to the beam to avoid misleading patterns.3. Maintain fixed camera focus and exposure throughout to ensure valid visual comparison.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Observation of Amoeba Movement and Pseudopodia Formation Under a Light MicroscopeI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Amoeba Movement and Shape Change via Pseudopodia2. Subject: Healthcare - Veterinary Medicine (Basic Cell Biology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the movement, deformation, and pseudopodia formation of a living amoeba in pond water under a light microscope; to understand amoeboid movement as a basic form of cell motility; to master the basic operation of live biological specimen observation and fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental EquipmentLight microscope (with 10× ocular and 10×–40× objective lenses), glass slides, cover slips, dropper or pipette, fresh pond water containing living amoebae, absorbent paper or tissue, microscope-mounted camera or external camera adaptor, stable light source.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Specimen: Use a dropper to place one small drop of pond water containing amoebae onto the center of a clean glass slide. Avoid introducing air bubbles.2. Mounting the Slide: Gently lower a cover slip over the water drop at an angle to minimize bubble formation. Use absorbent paper to remove excess water at the edge if necessary, ensuring the amoeba can still move freely.3. Initial Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the microscope stage. Start with a low-power objective (10×) and adjust the coarse focus until the field becomes clear. Locate a moving amoeba.4. Fine Focusing and Magnification: Switch to a higher magnification (20×–40×). Use the fine focus knob to obtain a sharp image of the amoeba’s outline and internal structures.5. Fixing Focus for Time-lapse Recording: Once a clearly visible amoeba is centered in the field of view, fix the microscope focus and camera position. Do not adjust focus during recording.6. Time-lapse Observation: Record continuously for a short period (or observe directly) while the amoeba moves across the field, noting changes in shape and the extension and retraction of pseudopodia.7. Ending the Experiment: Stop recording, remove the slide, clean the slide and cover slip, and turn off the microscope light source.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The amoeba appears as a transparent or slightly gray, irregularly shaped unicellular organism in pond water.2. During Observation: The amoeba slowly changes shape, extending one or more pseudopodia in a specific direction. The cytoplasm flows into the pseudopodia, and the cell body gradually moves forward.3. Continuous Movement: As pseudopodia retract and new ones form, the amoeba continuously alters its outline while migrating across the microscope field of view.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAmoeboid movement is a fundamental form of cell motility. The amoeba moves by forming pseudopodia through cytoplasmic streaming and cytoskeletal reorganization. Localized extension of the cell membrane and actin filament dynamics allow part of the cytoplasm to flow forward, anchoring to the substrate and pulling the rest of the cell along. Observing a living amoeba under a light microscope directly demonstrates the relationship between cell structure and function, as well as the basic physiological activity of single-celled organisms.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use fresh pond water to ensure amoebae remain alive and active.2. Avoid pressing the cover slip too tightly, which may restrict movement or damage the amoeba.3. Camera mounted on tripod with fixed focus for time-lapse photography.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Put on safety goggles. Place a clean beaker on the hot plate. Add a measured amount of impure copper sulfate crystals (about 5–10 g) into the beaker. Add a small volume of distilled water (just enough to cover the crystals).2. Dissolution by Heating: Turn on the hot plate and gently heat the mixture while stirring with a glass rod. As the temperature increases, the blue copper sulfate crystals gradually dissolve, forming a clear or slightly colored blue solution. Continue heating until most solid dissolves; avoid boiling dry.3. Hot Filtration: While the solution is still hot, set up a funnel with filter paper over a clean beaker. Carefully pour the hot solution through the filter paper. Insoluble impurities remain on the filter paper, and a clear blue filtrate is collected in the clean beaker.4. Cooling and Crystallization: Place the beaker with the filtrate on the lab bench, undisturbed. Do not move or stir. Fix the camera focus and start time-lapse recording. As the solution cools naturally to room temperature, blue copper sulfate crystals gradually form and grow.5. Completion: After crystallization is complete, stop recording. Allow the crystals to settle. Turn off equipment and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Impure copper sulfate appears as blue crystals with possible dull surfaces or attached impurities.2. During Heating: Crystals gradually dissolve in hot water; the solution becomes uniformly blue and clearer as temperature rises.3. During Filtration: Solid impurities remain on the filter paper; the filtrate is a transparent blue solution.4. During Cooling: As the solution cools, blue crystals slowly appear at the bottom or sides of the beaker and increase in size and number over time.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRecrystallization is a purification method based on the temperature-dependent solubility of solids. Copper sulfate has higher solubility in hot water than in cold water. When impure copper sulfate is dissolved in hot water, both the desired compound and soluble impurities enter solution, while insoluble impurities are removed by hot filtration. Upon cooling, the solubility of copper sulfate decreases, causing it to crystallize out of the solution, while most soluble impurities remain dissolved. Thus, purer copper sulfate crystals are obtained.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use minimal water to ensure effective crystallization during cooling.2. Perform filtration while the solution is hot to prevent premature crystallization in the funnel.3. Avoid shaking or stirring the solution during cooling to allow well-formed crystals.4. Handle hot glassware carefully to prevent burns.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Effect of an Inhibitor on Catalase Decomposition of Hydrogen PeroxideI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Catalase Decomposition of Hydrogen Peroxide with Inhibitor Comparison2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Biochemistry/Enzymology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe catalase-catalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide and demonstrate how an inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by comparing oxygen production in two test tubes.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTransparent test tubes (2, identical size), test tube rack, catalase solution (e.g., yeast or liver extract), hydrogen peroxide solution (3%), inhibitor solution (e.g., copper sulfate or ethanol, low concentration), dropper or pipette, tinted label or sleeve for inhibitor tube, camera with fixed tripod (time-lapse capable), protective gloves and goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean transparent test tubes side by side in a rack. Label one as Control (clear tube) and the other as Inhibitor (tinted tube).2. Camera Setup: Fix the camera position and focus on both test tubes; ensure the entire reaction area is visible and stable for time-lapse recording.5. Core Operation: Using two droppers or a split pipette, add equal volumes of hydrogen peroxide to both test tubes simultaneously.6. Materials and EquipmentClean glass slide, coverslip, light microscope, dropper or pipette, cerebrospinal fluid sample, India ink or Congo red stain, tissue paper, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Skin Capillary Refill TestI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Skin Capillary Refill Test (Nail Bed)2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and understand peripheral capillary blood refill by observing color changes in the nail bed after brief pressure and release.II. Experimental EquipmentHuman hand (examiner or subject), clean environment, adequate lighting; no instruments required.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Ask the subject to relax their hand on a flat surface at heart level. Ensure the fingertip and nail bed are clean and well lit.2. Initial State Observation: Observe and note the normal pink color of the nail bed at rest.3. Core Operation (Pressing): Using a finger or thumb, press firmly on the center of the nail bed for approximately 3–5 seconds until the nail bed turns pale or white.4. Release: Quickly remove the pressure while keeping the camera focused on the fingertip.5. Observation: Observe the immediate color change of the nail bed after release.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. At rest: The nail bed appears pink due to normal capillary blood flow.2. During pressing: The nail bed blanches (turns pale/white) as blood is temporarily displaced from the capillaries.3. After release: The pink color returns within about 1–2 seconds as blood refills the capillaries.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe skin capillary refill test is based on peripheral circulation physiology. Applying pressure to the nail bed temporarily expels blood from superficial capillaries, causing blanching. Upon release, arterial blood refills the capillaries. The speed of color return reflects capillary perfusion and peripheral blood flow status.VI. Precautions1. Do not press excessively hard or for too long to avoid discomfort.2. Ensure the finger is warm; cold conditions may slow refill and affect observation.3. Observe from a consistent angle with adequate lighting to accurately judge color changes.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Urine Cystine Detection (Colorimetric Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Urine Cystine Detection by Sodium Nitroprusside Colorimetric MethodSubject: Healthcare – Renal PhysiologyObjective: To detect the presence of cystine in urine using a colorimetric reaction under alkaline conditions, and to master the standard sequential operation of adding reagents and observing color change.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or micropipette, glass stirring rod (or gentle tapping for mixing), fresh urine sample, alkaline reagent (e.g., ammonium hydroxide or sodium carbonate solution), sodium nitroprusside reagent, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack. Wear gloves and goggles. Ensure reagents are clear and uncontaminated.2. Sample Addition: Using a dropper, add about 2–3 mL of urine sample into the test tube.3. Alkalinization: Add 0.5–1 mL of alkaline reagent to the urine. Gently mix by tapping the tube or lightly swirling to ensure uniform alkalinity.4. Colorimetric Reaction: Add 2–3 drops of sodium nitroprusside reagent into the test tube.5. Mixing and Observation: Gently mix again, then hold the test tube steady and observe the solution for color change under good lighting.6. Completion: After observation, place the tube back on the rack and dispose of waste according to laboratory regulations.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Urine appears pale yellow and transparent.After Alkaline Addition: No obvious color change; solution remains clear.After Sodium Nitroprusside Addition: If cystine is present, a purple or violet coloration develops within a short time; if absent, no significant color change occurs.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleCystine contains sulfhydryl-related groups that, under alkaline conditions, react with sodium nitroprusside to form a colored complex. The appearance of a purple or violet color indicates the presence of elevated cystine in urine, which is clinically relevant in conditions such as cystinuria. The color intensity is proportional to the amount of reactive cystine present.VI. PrecautionsEnsure alkaline conditions before adding sodium nitroprusside; mix gently to avoid splashing; observe promptly as color may fade over time; handle urine as a biohazard.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Coin at the Bottom of a Cup Becomes Visible as Water Is Poured InI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Coin Visibility Change Due to Refraction2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate how refraction of light at the water–air interface changes the light path entering the eye (or camera), causing an object previously hidden from view to become visible.II. Experimental EquipmentOpaque cup (non-transparent), coin (metallic, flat), table, clear water, water container for pouring, fixed camera placed at table height, stable support or tripod.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the opaque cup on the table. Put the coin flat at the bottom center of the cup. Adjust the camera to table height so that the coin is not visible from the camera’s viewpoint. Fix the camera position and focus.2. Initial Observation: Confirm that, with the empty cup, the coin cannot be seen in the camera frame due to the straight-line propagation of light.3. Core Operation: Slowly pour clear water into the cup while keeping the camera completely stationary. Continue pouring until the water level rises above the coin.4. Recording: Use time-lapse or continuous recording to capture the gradual change in visibility.5. Completion: Stop pouring once the coin becomes clearly visible. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The coin at the bottom of the empty opaque cup is invisible from the fixed camera viewpoint.2. During Pouring: As water is added, the water surface rises and the coin gradually begins to appear.3. Final State: When sufficient water is present, the coin becomes clearly visible without any movement of the camera or coin.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleLight normally travels in straight lines in air. When water is added, light rays reflected from the coin are refracted at the water–air interface. Refraction changes the direction of the light rays so that they can enter the camera (or eye), making the coin visible. This demonstrates the basic optical principle of refraction, which is fundamental to human vision and optometry.VI. Experimental Precautions1. The cup must be opaque to prevent side visibility.2. The camera position and focus must remain fixed throughout the experiment.3. Pour water slowly to clearly observe the gradual change in visibility.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate optical refraction and its effect on visibility, assuming straight-line light propagation in air and bending at the water–air interface.Minimum Assumptions: Opaque container blocks direct line of sight; camera represents a fixed eye position; water is clear and homogeneous.Phased Storyline: (1) Initial phase – empty cup, coin invisible due to blocked light path; (2) Transition phase – water level rises, refraction begins altering light paths; (3) Final phase – refracted light reaches camera, coin becomes visible. Visibility must change without camera or object movement, from a fixed perspective.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Mercury Detection (Thioacetamide Test Strip Method)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Mercury Detection Using Thioacetamide Test StripSubject: Healthcare – Nutrition and Food HygieneObjective: To demonstrate rapid qualitative detection of mercury ions in food extracts using a thioacetamide-based test strip, and to observe color change by comparison with an unused strip.II. Materials and EquipmentBeaker (50–100 mL); prepared food sample (solid food chopped); distilled water; glass rod; filter paper or simple decantation setup; thioacetamide-based mercury test strips; tweezers; gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Food Extract Preparation: Place a small amount of chopped food into a beaker, add distilled water to cover, stir for 1–2 minutes to obtain an aqueous extract. Allow solids to settle or filter to obtain a clear extract.2. Initial Comparison: Place one unused mercury test strip on a clean surface as the reference strip.3. Test Reaction: Using tweezers, immerse a second test strip vertically into the food extract so the reactive zone is fully in contact with the solution.4. Reaction Time: Keep the strip in the solution briefly (a few seconds). For video, use time-lapse to accelerate the reaction while maintaining chronological order.5. Removal and Comparison: Remove the strip, allow excess liquid to drain, and place it beside the original strip for direct visual comparison.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The original strip is light-colored (pale yellow/white) with no dark spots.After Reaction: The immersed strip shows a brown to black coloration on the reactive zone if mercury ions are present; the reference strip remains unchanged. The contrast is clearly visible when placed side by side.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThioacetamide on the test strip reacts with mercury ions (Hg2+) in the food extract to form mercury sulfide (HgS), an insoluble dark-colored compound. The formation of HgS causes the test strip to darken. The presence and intensity of the dark color indicate the presence of mercury qualitatively.VI. PrecautionsUse gloves and tweezers to avoid contamination; ensure clear extract for visibility; do not touch the reactive zone; dispose of used strips according to safety guidelines.
