manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Ibuprofen–Copper(II) Ion Complexation Reaction (Copper Ion Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Ibuprofen–Copper(II) Ion Complexation Reaction2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical Chemistry3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the coordination reaction between ibuprofen and copper(II) ions by dissolving ibuprofen in ethanol and adding aqueous copper(II) sulfate dropwise, observing the complexation process through visible solution changes.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsBeaker (100 mL), dropper, glass rod, ibuprofen (solid), ethanol (analytical grade), aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution (dilute, blue), camera for time-lapse recording.III. Experimental Procedure1. Solution Preparation: Place a clean beaker on the bench. Add a small amount of ibuprofen solid into the beaker, then pour an appropriate volume of ethanol. Stir gently with a glass rod until ibuprofen dissolves, forming a clear or slightly opalescent solution.2. Reagent Addition: Using a dropper, draw aqueous copper(II) sulfate solution. While continuously stirring the ibuprofen–ethanol solution, add the copper(II) sulfate solution dropwise.3. Mixing and Observation: Continue gentle stirring during and after addition. Record the process with time-lapse photography, focusing on the color and clarity changes of the solution.4. Completion: Stop addition when a stable color change is observed. Set the beaker aside for final observation.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Ibuprofen dissolves in ethanol to form a colorless or nearly colorless solution.2. During Addition: Upon dropwise addition of copper(II) sulfate, the solution gradually develops a blue-green coloration or intensified blue tone, indicating interaction between Cu2+ and ibuprofen.3. Final State: A uniform colored solution is obtained, showing successful complex formation without obvious precipitation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleIbuprofen contains functional groups capable of coordinating with metal ions. When Cu2+ ions are introduced, they form coordination bonds with ibuprofen molecules, generating a metal–drug complex. This coordination alters the electronic environment of Cu2+, producing a visible color change that serves as evidence of complexation.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use dilute copper(II) sulfate to ensure controlled dropwise observation.2. Stir gently to avoid splashing and to ensure uniform mixing.3. Ethanol is flammable; keep away from open flames.4. Dispose of waste solutions according to laboratory regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Acetaminophen Purity Detection (Sodium Nitroprusside Color Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Acetaminophen Purity Detection by Sodium Nitroprusside Color MethodSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryExperiment Objective: To identify acetaminophen and preliminarily assess its purity by observing the characteristic color reaction under alkaline conditions using sodium nitroprusside; to master correct reagent addition order and controlled mixing in a test tube.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsTest tube (15×150 mm), test tube rack, dropper or Pasteur pipette, glass stirring rod (optional), acetaminophen sample (small amount of powder or solution), alkaline solution (e.g., sodium hydroxide solution), sodium nitroprusside reagent, safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, dry test tube vertically on the test tube rack. Wear safety goggles. Add a small amount of acetaminophen sample into the test tube.2. Alkalization: Using a dropper, add an appropriate amount of alkaline solution into the test tube so that the sample is fully wetted or dissolved. Gently shake the test tube to mix evenly.3. Color Reaction: Using another clean dropper, add sodium nitroprusside reagent dropwise into the alkaline mixture. After each drop, gently shake the test tube to ensure uniform mixing.4. Observation: Keep the test tube stationary and observe the color change of the solution. Use focused framing to clearly capture the sequence of reagent addition and the gradual color development.5. Completion: After observation, place the test tube back on the rack. Dispose of the reaction mixture according to laboratory waste regulations and clean all glassware.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAcetaminophen contains a phenolic functional group. Under alkaline conditions, it can react with sodium nitroprusside to form a colored complex. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Bile pH Detection (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Bile pH Detection Using pH Test Strips2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To determine the pH of bile using a pH indicator strip, understand the alkaline nature of bile, and master the correct operation of pH strip testing and result interpretation.II. Experimental EquipmentClean test tube, test tube rack, fresh bile sample, pH test strips (wide-range), forceps, standard pH color chart, gloves (optional).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean test tube on the rack and add an appropriate amount of bile sample to the tube (about 1/3 volume). Ensure the bile is free of visible contaminants.2. Strip Handling: Use forceps to take one pH test strip, avoiding contact with fingers to prevent contamination.3. Immersion: Briefly immerse the reactive end of the pH strip into the bile sample for 1–2 seconds, ensuring full contact with the liquid.4. Removal and Stabilization: Remove the strip and hold it flat in the air. Wait a few seconds for the color on the strip to stabilize.5. Comparison: Compare the stabilized color of the strip with the standard pH color chart to determine the pH value of the bile.6. Completion: Record the pH result, dispose of the used strip properly, and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The bile appears yellow-green or brownish, and the pH strip shows its original indicator color.2. After Immersion: The reactive area of the strip changes color immediately upon contact with bile.3. Stabilization: After a few seconds, the color becomes stable and uniform.4. Result: The color corresponds to an alkaline pH range when matched with the standard color chart.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesBile contains bicarbonate and bile salts, making it weakly alkaline. pH test strips are impregnated with indicators that change color depending on hydrogen ion concentration. When the strip contacts bile, the indicator reacts with the solution, producing a color change that corresponds to the bile’s pH. Comparing this color with a standard chart allows rapid estimation of bile pH.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Use clean equipment to avoid contamination.2. Do not immerse the strip for too long, as prolonged soaking may affect accuracy.3. Read the result only after color stabilization.4. Dispose of biological samples according to safety guidelines.

Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Progesterone Receptor Detection in Uterine Tissue by Colorimetric ImmunohistochemistrySubject: Healthcare – Reproductive PhysiologyObjective: To demonstrate the detection of progesterone receptor in fixed uterine tissue sections using a colorimetric immunohistochemical method and to observe receptor localization under a light microscope.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentFixed uterine tissue sections on glass slides, blocking solution (e.g., serum or BSA), primary antibody against progesterone receptor, PBS or buffer for rinsing, enzyme-labeled secondary antibody (e.g., HRP-conjugated), chromogenic substrate (e.g., DAB), stop solution or water, mounting medium, coverslips, humidified incubation chamber, pipettes, light microscope.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the fixed uterine tissue section slide on a clean bench and ensure the section is dry and firmly attached.2. Blocking: Add sufficient blocking solution to cover the tissue section. Incubate for a short time to block non-specific binding.3. Primary Antibody Incubation: Remove blocking solution and add primary antibody against progesterone receptor. Incubate in a humid chamber.4. Rinsing: Rinse the slide gently with buffer to remove unbound primary antibody.5. Secondary Antibody Incubation: Add enzyme-labeled secondary antibody and incubate.6. Rinsing: Rinse again with buffer to remove excess secondary antibody.7. Color Development: Add chromogenic substrate. Observe gradual color development on the tissue section.8. Reaction Termination: When appropriate color intensity appears, stop the reaction with water or stop solution.9. Mounting: Add mounting medium, place coverslip, and prepare the slide for microscopy.10. Microscopy: Observe under a light microscope, adjust focus, and record images using time-lapse or sequential photography.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on immunohistochemistry. The primary antibody specifically binds to progesterone receptors in uterine cell nuclei. The enzyme-labeled secondary antibody binds to the primary antibody. Upon addition of the chromogenic substrate, the enzyme catalyzes a reaction that produces an insoluble colored precipitate at the site of the antigen, allowing visualization of progesterone receptor distribution under a light microscope.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Time-lapse Light Microscopy of Cultured Animal Cells Dividing in a Petri DishI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Time-lapse Observation of Cultured Animal Cell Division2. Subject: Healthcare – Microbiology-Immunology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the dynamic process of animal cell mitosis by using time-lapse light microscopy, and to identify characteristic morphological changes during cell division.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsInverted light microscope with time-lapse imaging function, sterile petri dish with adherent cultured animal cells (e.g., HeLa or fibroblast cells), complete culture medium, CO2 incubator or microscope incubation chamber (37°C, 5% CO2), camera and computer with time-lapse software, sterile forceps and gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove the cultured cell petri dish from the incubator, check that cells are healthy, adherent, and evenly distributed in the medium.2. Microscope Setup: Place the petri dish on the stage of an inverted light microscope; adjust temperature and CO2 control if available.3. Focusing: Select a field of view with several isolated cells; adjust focus and light intensity to obtain clear cell boundaries.4. Time-lapse Recording: Set the time-lapse interval (e.g., one frame every 2–5 minutes); start continuous imaging for an accelerated observation period.5. Completion: Stop recording after observing cell division; save image sequence or video for analysis.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Cells appear flattened and spread during interphase.2. Mitosis Onset: Dividing cells gradually round up and become brighter under phase contrast.3. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesAnimal cells proliferate through mitosis, a process including interphase, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, and cytokinesis. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Vitamin C Drug Stability Detection (Oxidation Color Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Vitamin C Drug Stability Detection by Oxidation Color MethodSubject: Healthcare – Pharmaceutical ChemistryExperiment Objective: To detect the oxidative stability of vitamin C through a color change reaction, and to understand the principle of vitamin C oxidation and indicator response.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsBeaker (clear glass, 100–250 mL), glass rod or gentle hand shaking for mixing, dropper, vitamin C solution (freshly prepared, colorless), oxidation indicator reagent (e.g., starch-iodine or suitable redox indicator), oxidizing agent solution (e.g., iodine solution or dilute hydrogen peroxide), labels for reagents.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean, clear beaker on a stable surface. Add an appropriate volume of freshly prepared vitamin C solution to the beaker. Ensure the solution is colorless and transparent.2. Indicator Addition: Using a dropper, add 2–3 drops of the indicator reagent into the vitamin C solution. Gently shake the beaker to mix evenly. Observe that no obvious color change occurs at this stage.3. Oxidation Process: Use a dropper to add the oxidizing agent into the beaker drop by drop while gently shaking the solution. Maintain steady hand movements and add the oxidant gradually.4. Completion: Stop adding the oxidizing agent once a stable and clear color change is observed. Place the beaker still for observation.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The vitamin C solution is colorless or very light in color.After Indicator Addition: The solution remains unchanged, indicating vitamin C has not yet been oxidized.During Oxidizing Agent Addition: As the oxidizing agent is added dropwise, the solution gradually shows a color change (e.g., light blue or brown, depending on the indicator), which deepens with further addition.Final State: A stable color indicates that vitamin C has been oxidized and the indicator is responding to excess oxidant.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleVitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a strong reducing agent. In this experiment, it is gradually oxidized by an oxidizing agent. Initially, vitamin C consumes the oxidant, preventing the indicator from changing color. Once vitamin C is sufficiently oxidized, excess oxidizing agent reacts with the indicator, producing a visible color change. The appearance of color therefore reflects the oxidative stability and remaining reducing capacity of vitamin C in solution.VI. manual: Instructions for the Demonstration Experiment: Exaggerated Squinting and Eye Closure During Gradual Increase of Room LightingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Exaggerated Squinting and Eye Closure During Gradual Increase of Room Lighting2. Subject: Healthcare – Optometry / Vision Science3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the visual discomfort response (squinting and eye closure) of an adult when ambient light intensity gradually increases, and to relate this behavior to glare sensitivity and light adaptation mechanisms of the human visual system.II. Experimental Equipment1. A dimly lit room with controllable ambient lighting2. Floor lamp with adjustable brightness (placed near but not blocking the face)3. Camera or smartphone on a tripod (fixed focus and fixed position)4. Adult participant with no headwear or eye obstructionIII. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Set the room to a dim lighting condition. Position the camera directly in front of the participant, ensuring the face and both eyes are clearly visible. Fix the camera focus and framing for time-lapse recording.2. Initial State Recording: Ask the participant to face the camera naturally with eyes open. Begin recording while the floor lamp is at its lowest brightness.3. Core Operation: Gradually and continuously increase the brightness of the nearby floor lamp over several seconds without changing camera position or focus.4. Observation Phase: Maintain recording as the light intensity increases, allowing the participant to react naturally without instructions to exaggerate or suppress responses.5. Completion: Stop increasing brightness once clear squinting or brief eye closure is observed. End recording.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: In dim light, the participant’s eyes remain open comfortably with minimal blinking.2. During Brightening: As the lamp brightness increases, blinking frequency rises, eyelids narrow, and facial muscles around the eyes contract.3. High Brightness Stage: With further brightening, exaggerated squinting and brief involuntary eye closure occur, indicating visual discomfort or glare sensitivity.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis demonstration is based on the principles of light adaptation and glare response in vision science. As ambient luminance increases, excessive light stimulates retinal photoreceptors and triggers protective reflexes, including squinting and eye closure, to reduce retinal illumination. These behaviors help limit discomfort and potential visual stress when the visual system is exposed to increasing brightness.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Skin Allergic Reaction (Pollen)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Skin Allergic Reaction Test Using Pollen Allergen2. Subject: Healthcare – Skin Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To observe and understand the local allergic reaction of human skin to pollen allergen using a skin prick test method, and to recognize the visual characteristics and physiological basis of allergic responses.II. Experimental EquipmentSterile pollen allergen solution, dropper, sterile disposable lancet, alcohol swab, cotton ball or gauze, timer or clock, camera or imaging device capable of time-lapse photography, disposable gloves.III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Select the inner forearm of the subject. Clean the skin area with an alcohol swab and allow it to dry. Ensure the arm is supported and kept still.Allergen Application: Use a dropper to place one small drop of pollen allergen solution onto the marked skin area.Skin Prick: Using a sterile lancet, gently puncture the skin through the allergen drop without causing bleeding.Waiting and Imaging: Ask the subject to keep the arm still. Focus the camera on the skin area and begin time-lapse photography. Wait for a short period to observe changes.Completion: After observation, gently wipe off the allergen with cotton or gauze and dispose of used materials safely.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Skin appears normal with no redness or swelling.After Allergen Exposure: Within a short time, localized redness and slight swelling appear at the puncture site.Progression: The reaction may develop into a small raised wheal surrounded by redness, clearly visible in the time-lapse sequence.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThis experiment is based on the skin prick test principle in allergy diagnosis. When pollen allergen enters the superficial skin layer, it interacts with IgE antibodies on mast cells in sensitized individuals. This triggers the release of histamine and other mediators, causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, redness, and swelling (wheal-and-flare reaction). The visible skin changes reflect the underlying immune and physiological response of the skin.VI. Experimental PrecautionsUse sterile, disposable lancets to avoid infection. Do not perform on damaged or inflamed skin. Observe the subject for excessive reactions and stop if discomfort occurs.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Atherosclerotic Plaque in an Artery Revealed by Longitudinal SlicingI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Longitudinal Slicing of an Excised Artery to Reveal Atherosclerotic Plaque2. Subject: Healthcare – Veterinary Medicine (Pathology)3. Experiment Objective: To observe the macroscopic appearance of atherosclerotic plaque by longitudinally opening an excised artery and exposing the inner (luminal) surface.II. Experimental EquipmentExcised animal artery specimen (fixed or fresh), disposable gloves, scalpel or dissecting knife, cutting board, forceps (optional), absorbent paper, camera with fixed focus (for time-lapse photography).III. Experimental ProcedurePreparation: Place the cutting board on a stable surface. Put on disposable gloves. Position the excised artery straight on the cutting board with the longitudinal axis visible. Set the camera above the board, fix focus and framing, and start time-lapse recording.Core Operation: Using the scalpel, make a careful longitudinal incision along the length of the artery. Maintain steady pressure to avoid transverse cuts. Continue slicing until the arterial wall is fully opened.Exposure: Use fingers or forceps to gently spread the artery open, laying it flat with the inner surface facing upward.Completion: Keep the specimen stationary for clear recording. Stop recording after the inner surface is fully visible. Dispose of biological material according to biosafety rules and clean tools.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Orexin Detection (Immunological Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Orexin Detection by Immunological Test Strip2. Subject: Healthcare – Digestive Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the detection of orexin in a biological sample using an immunochromatographic test strip; to master correct sample application, observe capillary migration and result formation, and understand the underlying immunological principle.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentOrexin immunological test strip (with sample pad, test line, control line), prepared biological sample, disposable dropper or micropipette, clean flat surface, timer or clock, gloves (recommended).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the test strip on a clean, dry, and flat surface. Ensure the strip is intact and the result window is visible.2. Sample Application: Using a dropper, draw the prepared biological sample. Gently dispense 2–3 drops onto the sample pad at the designated end of the strip.3. Incubation and Migration: Lay the strip flat and undisturbed. Start timing. Allow the liquid to migrate along the strip by capillary action toward the test and control regions.4. Observation and Reading: After a brief wait (approximately 1–5 minutes), hold or show the strip horizontally. Focus the image on the result window and observe the appearance of colored lines. Time-lapse photography may be used to show line development.5. Completion: Record the result. Dispose of the used strip according to biological waste guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The strip is dry with no visible lines.2. During Migration: The sample liquid moves steadily from the sample pad toward the test and control regions.3. Result Formation: The control line appears to indicate valid flow. If orexin is present above the detection threshold, a test line appears; if absent or below threshold, the test line does not appear.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on immunochromatography. The sample migrates along the strip by capillary action, carrying labeled antibodies. Orexin in the sample binds specifically to anti-orexin antibodies and is captured at the test line, forming a visible colored band. The control line captures excess labeled antibodies to confirm proper flow and reagent activity. The presence or absence of the test line reflects the qualitative detection of orexin.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Apply the correct volume of sample to avoid overflow or insufficient migration.2. Keep the strip flat and do not move it during migration.3. Read results within the recommended time window to avoid misinterpretation.

Phased storyline: (1) Setup—strip placed flat, sample prepared; (2) Action—2–3 drops applied to sample pad; (3) Transition—liquid migrates along strip in time-lapse; (4) Outcome—control line appears, test line appears or not depending on orexin presence. Visibility constraints: close-up framing of strip, horizontal orientation, clear focus on sample pad and test/control regions for verification.

Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the milk sample, test strip, dropper, timer, and color card on a clean, well-lit surface. If required by the kit, ensure the milk sample has been pretreated according to instructions and is at room temperature.2. Sampling: Use the dropper to draw an appropriate amount of the prepared milk sample solution.3. Core Operation: Hold the test strip horizontally and add the specified number of drops of the milk sample solution onto the reaction area (sample pad) of the test strip, avoiding overflow.4. Timing: Start the timer immediately after adding the sample. Allow the strip to react for the specified short time (typically 3–5 minutes; in demonstration, this can be shown by time-lapse photography).5. Result Interpretation: After the reaction time, compare the color or line pattern on the test strip with the standard color card. Determine whether sulfonamide residues are present or absent based on the comparison.6. Completion: Record the result. Dispose of the used test strip according to laboratory waste guidelines and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The test strip is dry, with no visible color development in the test or control areas.2. During Reaction: After the milk sample is added, liquid migrates along the strip, and colored lines or color intensity gradually appear.3. Final Result: A visible control line confirms the strip is valid. The presence or absence, or intensity, of the test line compared with the standard color card indicates whether sulfonamide residues are present.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on immunochromatographic assay principles. Sulfonamide antibiotics in the milk sample compete with immobilized antigens on the test strip for binding to labeled antibodies. During capillary migration, this competitive reaction produces different color intensities or line patterns. By comparing the developed strip with a standard color card, the presence or absence of sulfonamide antibiotic residues in milk can be qualitatively determined.VI. PrecautionsEnsure correct sample volume is added; do not interpret results before or after the specified reaction time; always use the provided color card for judgment; discard expired or damaged test strips.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment Cytoplasmic Streaming in Elodea Leaf CellsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Cytoplasmic Streaming in Elodea Leaf Cells2. Subject: Healthcare - Microbiology-Immunology (Cell Biology Foundation)3. Experiment Objective: To observe cytoplasmic streaming in living plant cells by viewing a fresh Elodea leaf under a light microscope, understand intracellular transport phenomena, and practice continuous microscopic observation and time-lapse recording.II. Experimental EquipmentLight microscope, glass slides, cover slips, fresh Elodea leaf, dropper, distilled water, forceps, lens paper, camera or microscope imaging system.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Select a fresh, green Elodea leaf and place it flat on a clean glass slide using forceps.2. Mounting: Add one drop of distilled water onto the leaf to prevent dehydration; gently place a cover slip over the leaf, avoiding air bubbles.3. Microscopy Setup: Place the slide on the microscope stage; start with low magnification to locate the leaf, then switch to medium or high magnification.4. Focus Adjustment: Carefully adjust coarse and fine focus until individual rectangular cells and chloroplasts are clearly visible.5. Fixed-Field Observation: Select one clear field of view and fix the microscope focus and camera position.6. Time-Lapse Recording: Continuously observe and record the same field for several minutes, or accelerate recording for demonstration purposes.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Elodea cells appear rectangular with green chloroplasts distributed mainly along the cell periphery.2. During Observation: Chloroplasts move slowly and directionally along the inner surface of the cell wall, forming continuous circulating paths.3. Sustained Observation: The direction of movement within a single cell remains consistent over time, demonstrating cytoplasmic streaming.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesCytoplasmic streaming is the directed flow of cytoplasm within living cells, driven by interactions between the cytoskeleton (actin filaments) and motor proteins. In Elodea leaf cells, this process transports chloroplasts and other organelles, enhancing material distribution and metabolic efficiency. The movement is visible under a light microscope because chloroplasts are pigmented and move along defined intracellular pathways.

manual: Complement C4 Detection (Test Strip Method)I. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Complement C4 Detection by Test StripSubject: Healthcare – Basic ImmunologyObjective: To demonstrate the correct use of a Complement C4 immunochromatographic test strip by placing it on a flat surface, applying a measured drop of serum, waiting briefly, and reading control and test lines to determine the presence of Complement C4.II. Experimental MaterialsComplement C4 test strip (sealed, room temperature), serum sample, disposable dropper, flat clean surface, timer (optional), biohazard waste container.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Remove the C4 test strip from its packaging and place it horizontally on a clean, flat surface with the sample pad facing upward.2. Sample Application: Use a dropper to draw serum. Apply one measured drop vertically onto the sample pad without touching the strip surface.3. Reaction Waiting: Allow the serum to migrate along the strip by capillary action. Wait approximately 3–5 minutes (can be visually accelerated for demonstration).4. Result Reading: Observe the result window. Confirm the presence of the control line, then check for the appearance or absence of the test line.5. Disposal: Dispose of the used strip and dropper in a biohazard container.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The test strip shows no visible lines in the result window.During Reaction: Serum migrates laterally along the strip.Final Result: A colored control line appears, indicating a valid test. If Complement C4 is present at or above the detection threshold, a colored test line appears; if absent, no test line is visible.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThe Complement C4 test strip is based on immunochromatographic assay principles. Serum flows along the membrane via capillary action. Complement C4 in the sample binds to specific anti-C4 antibodies conjugated with colored particles. The immune complexes are captured at the test line, forming a visible band. The control line captures excess conjugate to confirm proper flow and reagent activity. The presence of the control line validates the test, while the test line indicates Complement C4 presence.

manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Vibrio cholerae Detection by Alkaline Peptone Water Color MethodI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Enrichment of Vibrio cholerae Using Alkaline Peptone WaterSubject: Healthcare – Pathology – Medical MicrobiologyObjective: To demonstrate the correct enrichment procedure for suspected Vibrio cholerae using alkaline peptone water, and to understand the selective enrichment principle.II. Experimental Materials and EquipmentTest tube containing alkaline peptone water (pH 8.5–9.0), sterile inoculating loop, alcohol lamp or Bunsen burner, suspected Vibrio cholerae sample, test tube rack, incubator set at 37°C, marker pen, personal protective equipment.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the test tube with alkaline peptone water on a rack and label it. Ensure aseptic conditions.2. Loop Sterilization: Hold the inoculating loop and sterilize it in a flame until red-hot; allow it to cool briefly.3. Inoculation: Use the cooled sterile loop to collect a small amount of the suspected sample and gently insert it into the alkaline peptone water.4. Mixing: Lightly rotate or tap the test tube to mix without causing splashing or contamination.5. Incubation: Place the inoculated tube upright into a 37°C incubator for enrichment.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: The alkaline peptone water is clear and colorless.After Incubation: The medium may show slight turbidity or surface growth, indicating enrichment of Vibrio species (no immediate color change required in the short demonstration).V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleAlkaline peptone water is a selective enrichment medium with high pH and peptone content. Vibrio cholerae tolerates alkaline conditions better than most intestinal bacteria and multiplies rapidly at 37°C. Enrichment increases the number of Vibrio organisms, facilitating subsequent detection and identification.VI. PrecautionsMaintain strict aseptic technique; sterilize the loop before and after use; avoid overheating the medium; dispose of cultures according to biosafety regulations.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Iodine Solution Reacting with Starch in Food Pieces (Potato vs Sugar Cube)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Iodine Test for Starch in Food Pieces2. Subject: Healthcare – Medicine (Basic Biochemistry / Nutrition Testing)3. Experiment Objective: To identify the presence of starch in common food items by observing the color reaction between iodine solution and starch, and to compare the reaction results of a starch-rich food (raw potato) and a starch-free food (white sugar cube). The experiment also demonstrates standardized observation and recording using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment1. Raw potato slice (freshly cut, flat surface)2. White sugar cube (dry, intact)3. Iodine solution (dilute iodine–potassium iodide solution)4. Dropper (1)5. White ceramic plate or glass slide (to place samples)6. Disposable gloves (recommended)7. Camera or smartphone with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation Stage:   a. Clean the lab bench and place a white plate at the center.   b. Put on disposable gloves.   c. Place a raw potato slice on the left side of the plate and a white sugar cube on the right side, ensuring both are clearly visible in the same frame.   d. Set up the camera on a tripod, adjust framing so both samples are centered, and fix focus and exposure. Start time-lapse or continuous recording.2. Core Operation:   a. Use a dropper to draw a small amount of iodine solution.   b. Add 2–3 drops of iodine solution onto the surface of the potato slice.   c. Using the same or a clean dropper, add 2–3 drops of iodine solution onto the surface of the sugar cube.   d. Do not move the samples after adding iodine; keep the camera fixed to record changes over time.3. Observation Stage:   a. Observe the color changes on both food samples over several seconds.   b. Record the final appearance once the color change stabilizes.4. Conclusion and Cleanup:   a. Stop recording once the phenomenon is clear.   b. Dispose of food samples according to lab rules.   c. Clean the plate and dropper, and return equipment to storage.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Alumina-Packed Column Chromatography for Separation of Plant PigmentsI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Separation of Plant Pigments from Leaf Extract Using an Alumina-Packed Column2. Subject: Healthcare – Pharmacy (Pharmaceutical Analysis / Chromatography)3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the basic principle of column chromatography using alumina as the stationary phase, visually observe the separation of plant pigments from a leaf extract, and record the separation process using fixed-focus time-lapse photography.II. Experimental Equipment and Materials1. Clear glass chromatography column (straight, transparent)2. Neutral or slightly basic white alumina (stationary phase)3. Leaf extract (dark green, prepared by extracting fresh leaves with organic solvent)4. Eluent/solvent (clear, e.g., petroleum ether–acetone mixture or ethanol-based solvent)5. Funnel or pipette for sample addition6. Beaker or flask to collect eluate7. Stand and clamp to hold the column vertically8. Camera with tripod (focus fixed for time-lapse recording)III. Experimental Procedure1. Column Preparation: Secure the clear glass column vertically on a stand. Add a small amount of solvent to the column, then slowly pack white alumina to form a uniform, compact column without air bubbles. Keep the alumina surface level and covered with a thin layer of solvent.2. Sample Loading: Using a pipette, carefully add a small volume of dark green leaf extract onto the top surface of the alumina. Allow the extract to adsorb onto the alumina without disturbing the packed layer.3. Elution Operation: Gently add clear solvent to the top of the column, maintaining a constant liquid level. Open the column outlet to allow the solvent to flow downward at a steady rate.4. Recording: Fix the camera focus and position facing the column. Start time-lapse photography to continuously record the pigment separation process.5. Completion: Continue elution until distinct colored bands are clearly separated and move down the column. Stop solvent flow, then properly dispose of solvents and clean the equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The alumina column appears uniformly white, with dark green leaf extract concentrated as a narrow band at the top.2. During Elution: As the clear solvent flows downward, the green band separates into multiple colored bands (e.g., yellow, light green, dark green), which gradually move down the column at different speeds.3. Final State: Distinct pigment bands are clearly visible and spatially separated along the length of the alumina column, demonstrating effective separation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThis experiment is based on column chromatography. Alumina acts as the stationary phase, while the solvent is the mobile phase. Different plant pigments have varying polarities and adsorption affinities for alumina. As the solvent flows downward, pigments with weaker adsorption move faster, while strongly adsorbed pigments move slower, resulting in spatial separation into colored bands. This demonstrates differential adsorption and desorption, a core principle widely used in pharmaceutical analysis and separation science.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Ensure the alumina is evenly packed to avoid channeling.2. Add solvent gently to prevent disturbing the sample layer.3. Maintain a steady flow rate for clear separation.4. Fix camera focus and position before starting elution to ensure consistent time-lapse recording.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Esterase-Catalyzed Hydrolysis of Fluorescein DiacetateI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Esterase-Catalyzed Hydrolysis of Fluorescein Diacetate Producing Visible FluorescenceSubject: Healthcare - PharmacyObjective: To demonstrate that esterase hydrolyzes non-fluorescent fluorescein diacetate into fluorescent fluorescein, observable under UV light using an enzyme-treated sample and a buffer control.II. Experimental MaterialsClear glass or plastic vials (2), vial rack, fluorescein diacetate solution in buffer, esterase solution, micropipette or dropper, handheld UV lamp (365 nm), lab bench, camera on tripod for fixed-focus time-lapse, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place two clean, clear vials side-by-side on a lab bench and label them Left (Esterase) and Right (Control). Add equal volumes of fluorescein diacetate buffer solution to both vials. Ensure both solutions are clear and colorless.2. Enzyme Addition: Using a pipette, add a measured amount of esterase solution to the left vial only. Do not add enzyme to the right vial; it remains buffer-only.3. Illumination Setup: Position the handheld UV lamp so it can illuminate both vials simultaneously. Set the camera with fixed focus and stable framing for time-lapse recording.4. Observation: Turn on the UV lamp and begin time-lapse recording. Maintain illumination and avoid moving the vials or camera during observation.5. Completion: After clear fluorescence differences are observed, turn off the UV lamp, stop recording, and dispose of solutions according to laboratory safety guidelines.IV. Summary of Experimental PrincipleFluorescein diacetate is a non-fluorescent ester that can diffuse in aqueous buffer. Esterase catalyzes its hydrolysis, removing acetate groups to produce fluorescein, which exhibits strong green fluorescence under UV light. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual: Tabletop Diffusion Cloud ChamberI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Observation of Background Radiation Using a Diffusion Cloud Chamber2. Subject: Healthcare – Radiography / Imaging Sciences3. Experiment Objective: To visually observe particle tracks produced by background radiation, understand ionizing radiation behavior, and learn the basic principle of cloud chamber imaging.II. Experimental EquipmentTransparent sealed container (cloud chamber body), black felt strip, high-purity isopropyl alcohol (90% or above), metal base plate, dry ice, insulating tray, dark background surface, side LED light source, camera with tripod, gloves and safety goggles.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the metal base plate on an insulating tray. Add dry ice beneath or in contact with the plate to cool it. Put on gloves and goggles.2. Alcohol Setup: Soak the black felt strip evenly with isopropyl alcohol. Attach the felt around the inner upper wall of the container.3. Chamber Assembly: Place the container upside down on the cooled metal plate, ensuring a good seal so outside air does not enter.4. Lighting and Background: Set a dark background behind the chamber. Position the LED light at a low angle from the side to illuminate the chamber interior.5. Camera Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod facing the chamber. Adjust focus manually and lock it. Start continuous observation or time-lapse recording.6. Observation Stage: Wait 1–3 minutes for the base to cool and vapor to become supersaturated. Observe the region just above the cold base.7. Completion: After observation, stop recording, remove the chamber, allow dry ice to sublimate safely, and clean equipment.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The chamber interior appears clear with faint mist near the cold base.2. Core Phenomenon: Thin white streaks or short lines suddenly appear and disappear near the base. Some tracks are straight and fast, others are thicker or curved.3. Continuous Observation: Tracks appear intermittently over time without any active radiation source, indicating background radiation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleThe diffusion cloud chamber works by creating a supersaturated layer of alcohol vapor above a very cold surface. When ionizing particles from background radiation pass through this layer, they ionize air molecules along their paths. Alcohol vapor condenses on these ions, forming tiny droplets that outline the particle trajectories as visible tracks. Different track shapes correspond to different types of particles and energies.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Handle dry ice with insulated gloves to avoid frostbite.2. Ensure good ventilation when using alcohol.3. Do not seal the chamber airtight under pressure.4. Avoid touching the cold metal plate directly.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Rhizopus Detection by Malt Extract–Phenol Red Color MethodI. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Rhizopus Detection (Malt Extract–Phenol Red Color Method)2. Subject: Healthcare – Pathology – Medical Mycology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate the metabolic activity of Rhizopus in malt extract medium containing phenol red by observing color and growth changes over time. Students will learn how to prepare phenol red malt extract medium in test tubes, perform sterile inoculation with Rhizopus using a loop, incubate at a warm temperature, and compare results with an uninoculated control through time-lapse observation.II. Experimental Equipment and MaterialsTest tubes with caps (2 tubes, one experimental and one control), test tube rack, malt extract agar/broth with phenol red indicator (prepared and sterilized), sterile inoculating loop, Rhizopus culture (plate or slant), alcohol lamp or Bunsen burner, incubator or warm environment (30–37 °C), marker pen for labeling, gloves and lab coat.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation of Medium: Place two clean test tubes containing equal volumes (about 5–10 mL) of phenol red malt extract medium on a test tube rack. Label one tube as Rhizopus and the other as Control. Observe and record the initial color of the medium (uniform red/orange).2. Sterile Inoculation: Light the alcohol lamp. Flame-sterilize the inoculating loop until red-hot and allow it to cool briefly. Using aseptic technique, gently touch the Rhizopus colony with the loop. Open the Rhizopus-labeled test tube near the flame, insert the loop into the medium without touching the tube wall, and lightly agitate to introduce spores/mycelial fragments. Flame the tube mouth and recap. Do not inoculate the control tube.3. Incubation: Place both the inoculated test tube and the uninoculated control tube upright in the incubator or a warm area at 30–37 °C.4. Observation and Time-Lapse Recording: Observe the tubes at regular intervals (e.g., 0 h, 12 h, 24 h, 48 h). Focus the camera on the test tubes and record time-lapse images or video. Compare the inoculated tube with the control, noting any color change and visible fungal growth.5. Completion: After final observation, document results. Dispose of cultures according to biosafety guidelines and clean the workspace.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: Both tubes show clear to slightly translucent phenol red malt extract medium with a red or orange color; no visible growth.2. During Incubation (Inoculated Tube): Gradual appearance of cottony or fluffy white mycelial growth characteristic of Rhizopus on the surface or within the medium. The medium color gradually shifts from red/orange toward yellow due to acid production.3. Control Tube: No fungal growth; medium color remains unchanged throughout incubation.V. Summary of Experimental PrincipleRhizopus metabolizes carbohydrates in malt extract, producing organic acids as metabolic byproducts. Phenol red is a pH indicator that is red/orange at neutral pH and turns yellow under acidic conditions. As Rhizopus grows and produces acid, the pH of the medium decreases, leading to a visible color change. The uninoculated control confirms that observed changes are due to fungal metabolism rather than environmental factors. This method demonstrates both fungal growth characteristics and biochemical activity relevant to pathological diagnosis.VI. Experimental Precautions1. Maintain strict aseptic technique to avoid contamination.2. Ensure equal medium volumes and identical incubation conditions for experimental and control tubes.3. Do not open tubes unnecessarily during incubation.4. Handle Rhizopus cultures following laboratory biosafety rules.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate Rhizopus detection using phenol red malt extract medium, emphasizing fungal metabolism–induced pH change. Phased Storyline: (1) Initial setup with two identical test tubes of red/orange medium, one labeled as control; (2) sterile loop inoculation of Rhizopus into the experimental tube only; (3) placement into a warm incubation environment; (4) accelerated time-lapse showing emergence of cottony mycelium and gradual color change to yellow in the inoculated tube; (5) final comparison frame highlighting unchanged control versus altered experimental tube. manual: Experimental Instruction Manual (TXT)I. Basic InformationExperiment Title: Squat-to-Lift Grocery Box Using Hip HingeSubject: Healthcare – PhysiotherapyObjective: Demonstrate safe lifting mechanics using a hip hinge to move a grocery box from floor to counter in one continuous motion, suitable for time-lapse recording.II. Equipment and EnvironmentKitchen setting with clear floor space; standard kitchen counter; medium-sized grocery box (rectangular, closed, neutral color); adult participant; camera on tripod with fixed focus and fixed position.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the grocery box flat on the kitchen floor near the counter. Set the camera at a side-front angle, ensure the entire body, box, and counter are in frame, and lock focus and exposure for time-lapse.2. Starting Posture: Adult stands close to the box with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly outward, spine neutral, eyes forward.3. Squat and Hip Hinge: Adult pushes hips back and bends knees simultaneously, hinging at the hips while keeping the back straight and chest open.4. Grasp and Lift (Core Operation): Adult grips the box firmly, engages core, and extends hips and knees together to lift the box in one smooth motion.5. Placement: Without pausing, the adult continues the motion to place the box securely onto the counter.6. Finish: Adult releases the box and returns to upright standing posture.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Box rests on the floor; adult stands upright.During Operation: Hips move backward first, knees bend, spine remains neutral; box rises smoothly as hips and knees extend.Final State: Box rests stably on the counter; adult stands upright without visible strain.V. Experimental Principle SummaryThis experiment demonstrates proper lifting biomechanics in physiotherapy. The hip hinge shifts load to the hips and legs, reduces spinal flexion, and minimizes lumbar stress. Coordinated hip and knee extension generates force efficiently, allowing safe transfer of an external load from floor to counter.VI. PrecautionsAvoid rounding the back; keep the box close to the body; ensure the camera remains fixed to preserve time-lapse consistency.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Dissolution Comparison of Enteric-Coated and Uncoated Tablets in Acidic LiquidI. Basic Experiment InformationExperiment Title: Dissolution Behavior of Enteric-Coated vs Uncoated Tablets in Acidic LiquidSubject: Healthcare - PharmacyObjective: To visually compare the dissolution behavior of an enteric-coated tablet and an uncoated tablet in an acidic environment and understand the protective function of enteric coatings.II. Experimental MaterialsClear glass beaker (250 mL), acidic liquid (simulated gastric fluid or dilute hydrochloric acid, clear), one enteric-coated tablet (glossy surface), one uncoated tablet (matte surface), forceps, camera with tripod (for fixed-focus time-lapse recording).III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place the beaker on a stable, well-lit surface and pour acidic liquid into the beaker to a depth sufficient to fully submerge both tablets.2. Placement: Using forceps, gently place the enteric-coated glossy tablet and the uncoated matte tablet side by side at the bottom of the beaker, ensuring they do not touch each other.3. Recording Setup: Fix the camera on a tripod, adjust focus to clearly capture both tablets and the surrounding liquid, and ensure the frame remains static.4. Core Operation: Start time-lapse recording. Do not stir or disturb the beaker. Allow the tablets to remain submerged and undisturbed.5. Completion: After clear differences in dissolution are observed, stop recording and dispose of the liquid according to laboratory safety guidelines.IV. Observation of Experimental PhenomenaInitial State: Both tablets are intact at the bottom of the beaker; the liquid is clear.During Observation: The uncoated tablet gradually absorbs liquid, swells, and begins to disintegrate, creating turbidity or particulate matter around it. The enteric-coated tablet remains intact with minimal visible change.Later Stage: The uncoated tablet shows significant dissolution, while the enteric-coated tablet largely retains its shape and glossy surface.V. Experimental Principle SummaryUncoated tablets dissolve readily in acidic environments because their active ingredients are directly exposed to the liquid. Enteric-coated tablets are covered with a pH-sensitive polymer that resists dissolution in acidic conditions but dissolves in the higher pH of the intestine. Therefore, in acidic liquid, the uncoated tablet dissolves faster, while the enteric-coated tablet remains protected.VI. PrecautionsEnsure the liquid is clear for visibility; avoid stirring or shaking; handle acidic solutions with care; maintain fixed camera focus throughout the experiment.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target Concept: Demonstrate the functional difference between enteric-coated and uncoated tablets in acidic conditions, assuming basic knowledge that enteric coatings resist gastric acid.Minimum Mechanistic Assumptions: Acidic liquid simulates gastric environment; coating integrity correlates with delayed dissolution; no external agitation affects dissolution.Phased Storyline: (1) Static setup with both tablets fully submerged and clearly visible; (2) Early phase where the uncoated tablet begins to swell or erode while the enteric-coated tablet remains unchanged; (3) Later phase showing pronounced disintegration of the uncoated tablet contrasted with the intact enteric-coated tablet.Visibility Constraints: Transparent beaker, clear liquid, side-by-side placement, fixed camera angle and focus to allow direct visual comparison and causal verification.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Lactophenol Cotton Blue Staining (Fungal Observation)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Lactophenol Cotton Blue Staining for Fungal Observation2. Subject: Healthcare – Pathology (Medical Mycology)3. Experiment Objective: To prepare a temporary stained mount of fungi using Lactophenol Cotton Blue, observe fungal morphology under a microscope from low to high magnification, and understand the staining principle that enhances visualization of fungal structures.II. Experimental Equipment and ReagentsClean glass slides, coverslips, Lactophenol Cotton Blue stain, inoculating needle or teasing needle, fungal specimen (culture or clinical sample), light microscope, absorbent paper, gloves.III. Experimental Procedure1. Preparation: Place a clean glass slide on a flat surface. Put on gloves to avoid contamination.2. Staining: Using a dropper, place one small drop of Lactophenol Cotton Blue in the center of the slide.3. Specimen Transfer: Sterilize the inoculating needle if required. Pick a very small amount of fungal specimen and transfer it into the stain drop.4. Teasing: Use the needle to gently tease and spread the specimen within the stain to separate hyphae and spores.5. Mounting: Hold a coverslip at an angle and carefully lower it onto the preparation to avoid air bubbles. Blot excess stain with absorbent paper.6. Microscopic Observation: Place the slide on the microscope stage. Observe first under low magnification to locate the specimen, then switch to higher magnification to examine details. Adjust focus gradually.7. Time-lapse/Focusing Demonstration: Record or demonstrate gradual focusing and magnification change from low to high power to show clearer structural details over time.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial View (Low Magnification): Blue-stained fungal mass visible against a light background; overall arrangement of hyphae observed.2. High Magnification View: Individual fungal structures become clear, including blue-stained hyphae, septa, and spores/conidia with sharp contrast.3. Focusing Effect: As focus improves, outlines of fungal elements become sharper and more distinct.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesLactophenol Cotton Blue acts as both a mounting and staining medium. Phenol kills and preserves fungal cells, lactic acid preserves morphology, glycerol prevents drying, and cotton blue binds to chitin in the fungal cell wall. This selective staining enhances contrast, allowing clear microscopic observation of fungal structures from low to high magnification.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of correct Lactophenol Cotton Blue fungal staining and microscopic observation. Minimum assumptions: presence of a slide, blue stain, fungal specimen, coverslip, and light microscope with adjustable magnification and focus. Phased storyline: (1) Preparation phase—clean slide with a visible blue stain drop; (2) Manipulation phase—fungal specimen transferred and teased within the stain; (3) Mounting phase—coverslip applied smoothly without bubbles; (4) Observation phase—microscope view transitions from low to high magnification with improved focus; (5) Result phase—clear blue-stained fungal hyphae and spores visible. Visibility constraints: camera alternates between bench-level operation view and microscope field view; focus and zoom changes must be visually apparent to verify causal progression.

manual: Instructions for the Experiment: Achilles Tendon Reflex (Sitting Position)I. Basic Experiment Information1. Experiment Title: Achilles Tendon Reflex (Sitting Position)2. Discipline and Subject: Medicine and Health – Human Physiology3. Experiment Objective: To demonstrate and observe the Achilles tendon (ankle jerk) reflex in a relaxed seated subject, understand the basic method for eliciting a deep tendon reflex, and comprehend the physiological principle of spinal reflex arcs.II. Experimental EquipmentReflex hammer (standard rubber-headed), chair of appropriate height, cooperative human subject, camera or recording device positioned for side view (optional for teaching/demonstration).III. Experimental Procedure1. Subject Preparation: Ask the subject to sit relaxed on a chair, with thighs supported and lower legs hanging freely. Ensure the feet are not touching the ground and the subject is calm and not voluntarily contracting the leg muscles.2. Examiner Positioning: Stand or sit slightly to the side of the subject to obtain a clear lateral view of the lower leg and ankle.3. Tendon Localization: Visually and manually locate the Achilles tendon, which lies just above the heel at the posterior aspect of the ankle.4. Core Operation: Using the reflex hammer, strike the Achilles tendon once with a quick, controlled, and smooth motion. Avoid repeated or excessively forceful strikes.5. Recording (Optional): Record the foot movement from the side view, ensuring a clear view of the lower leg, ankle, tendon, and hammer action. Time-lapse or slow-motion may be used for teaching clarity.IV. Observation of Experimental Phenomena1. Initial State: The foot hangs freely in a neutral position, with no active movement.2. Immediately After Tapping: A brief, involuntary plantar flexion of the foot occurs (the foot moves downward).3. Completion: The foot returns to its resting position after the reflex movement.V. Summary of Experimental PrinciplesThe Achilles tendon reflex is a stretch (myotatic) reflex mediated by the spinal cord. Tapping the Achilles tendon stretches the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles, activating muscle spindle receptors. Sensory (afferent) impulses travel via the tibial nerve to the S1–S2 segments of the spinal cord, where they synapse directly with motor neurons. Motor (efferent) impulses then return to the same muscles, causing a brief contraction and resulting in plantar flexion of the foot. This reflex does not require conscious control and is used clinically to assess peripheral nerve and spinal cord function.
high_level_evaluation_guide: Target concept: Demonstration of the Achilles tendon (ankle jerk) reflex as a spinal stretch reflex in human physiology. Minimum mechanistic assumptions: a relaxed seated subject, gravity-assisted hanging lower legs, correct identification of the Achilles tendon, and a single controlled reflex hammer strike eliciting an involuntary response.Phased storyline: (1) Setup phase – subject sits relaxed with lower legs hanging freely; side view establishes visibility of lower leg and ankle. (2) Action phase – examiner locates and taps the Achilles tendon once with a reflex hammer in a smooth motion. (3) Response phase – immediate plantar flexion of the foot occurs due to muscle contraction. (4) Resolution phase – foot returns to resting position. Visibility constraints: side view must clearly show tendon contact, hammer motion, and foot movement to verify causal linkage between action and reflex response.
